articles.t: 재활용 면화의 상업적 규모 확보
articles.o: Unlocking commercial scale for recycled cotton
articles.s: Fashion for Good has launched the Cotton Reloop Matrix Project, a cross-industry initiative designed to accelerate the commercial adoption of recycled cotton by benchmarking yarn quality, recycled content and price against the requirements of fashion brands. The project brings together Fashion for G
articles.x: Fashion for Good has launched the Cotton Reloop Matrix Project, a cross-industry initiative designed to accelerate the commercial adoption of recycled cotton by benchmarking yarn quality, recycled content and price against the requirements of fashion brands. The project brings together Fashion for Good partners Arvind, Bestseller, C&A, Interloop, Reformation and Shahi, alongside textile testing specialist Uster. It aims to establish a shared, evidence-based understanding of where mechanically recycled cotton can be used commercially and how higher recycled content can be achieved without compromising product performance. Cotton accounts for approximately 19% of global fibre production but incorporating significant quantities of mechanically recycled cotton into new yarns remains challenging. During mechanical recycling, textile waste is shredded and reopened into fibres, shortening and weakening them. According to Fashion for Good, only 45–50% of the original material survives as usable fibre. The resulting shorter fibres limit the proportion of recycled cotton that can be incorporated into new yarns, with many commercial applications currently restricted to around 10% recycled content. Increasing this proportion can affect yarn strength, fabric durability and handle. Although recycling capacity is available, brands and manufacturers frequently work with fragmented testing data and differing quality specifications. The technology is one of just 16 innovations chosen for the curated showcase of new materials, technologi
articles.x: The Lycra Company is highlighting its latest Coolmax CloakFX fibre technology at this week’s Performance Days in Munich (13-14 October), following its selection for the event’s Innovation Forum. The technology is one of just 16 innovations chosen for the curated showcase of new materials, technologies and developments. Coolmax CloakFX uses optical masking technology to diffuse light at fibre level, reducing the visibility of sweat marks while providing moisture-wicking and cooling performance. The fibre now contains 100% recycled polyester and is Global Recycled Standard (GRS) certified. “Visible sweat on apparel is a leading pain point for consumers across demographics, often forcing them to compromise between performance, comfort, and appearance,” said Tara Maurer-Mackay, Product Category Director, Branded Specialty Products, The Lycra Company. “Consumers want one fabric that does it all, and Coolmax CloakFX fibre is designed to help garments look drier while helping keep the wearer cool and dry.” The company is also presenting fabrics and garments incorporating renewable Lycra fibre, which contains 70% plant-based content and is designed to reduce the carbon footprint of apparel while maintaining the performance characteristics of conventional elastane. Among the featured developments is Set the Pace, a collaboration with Italian textile manufacturer Brugnoli and cycling apparel specialist PISSEI. The project combines Brugnoli’s patented Br4 technology and bio-based polyamide with renewable Lycra fibre to produce a technical stretch fabric containing up to 89% bio-based materials. articles.o: One in, three out at Cedro Têxtil
articles.s: Brazilian fabric manufacturer Cedro Têxtil has been able to decommission three older stenters following the installation of a new Brückner finishing line, while also reducing natural gas consumption by more than 20%. The investment forms part of an ongoing modernisation programme at the vertically i
articles.x: Brazilian fabric manufacturer Cedro Têxtil has been able to decommission three older stenters following the installation of a new Brückner finishing line, while also reducing natural gas consumption by more than 20%. The investment forms part of an ongoing modernisation programme at the vertically integrated company, which produces more than 60 million linear metres of fabric annually and is one of South America’s largest suppliers of workwear textiles. The new Brückner line, commissioned just over a year ago, has enabled Cedro to substantially increase production speeds while improving energy efficiency and reducing maintenance requirements. It has also delivered improvements in the finishing of super-stretch fabrics, where uniform temperature distribution and precise process control are essential to achieving consistent dimensional stability. The resulting productivity gains have enabled Cedro to consolidate production previously handled by three older stenters onto the new line, reducing the number of machines required and associated operating costs. The investment followed several years of evaluating machinery suppliers from Europe and Asia, including visits to manufacturing facilities and reference customers worldwide. The Brückner stenter SFP-4 at Cedro Têxtil © Brueckner Cedro assessed the competing technologies on productivity, maintenance requirements, energy consumption, spare parts availability and the provision of technical support in Brazil. The company ultimately selected Brückner on the basis of its combination of production performance, energy efficiency and local service capabilities. articles.t: Unifi, 방수 원사 기술 도입
articles.o: Unifi introduces water-resistant yarn technology
articles.s: US yarn manufacturer Unifi is launching two new yarn technologies at Performance Days in Munich on 13-14 October, including a water-resistant yarn designed to eliminate conventional topical durable water-repellent (DWR) treatments. Resist2O Pro incorporates water resistance directly into the yarn, m
articles.x: US yarn manufacturer Unifi is launching two new yarn technologies at Performance Days in Munich on 13-14 October, including a water-resistant yarn designed to eliminate conventional topical durable water-repellent (DWR) treatments. Resist2O Pro incorporates water resistance directly into the yarn, minimising water absorption without topical treatments or fluorinated chemistry. Compatible with different fabric formation methods, the technology could simplify textile production by eliminating a separate finishing stage. Unifi says Resist2O Pro is fluorine-free and PFOA-free, with PFOA levels below five parts per billion (ppb). Potential applications include apparel, footwear, furnishings and industrial textiles. The company’s second innovation, Cofira, combines the aesthetics and handle of spun yarns with the performance characteristics of filament yarns. It can be tailored using synthetic, blended and functional fibres to deliver different fabric properties and effects. Suitable for apparel, furnishings, equipment and accessories, Cofira can also incorporate Unifi’s existing technologies, including AMT moisture management, ChillSense cooling and ReFlexx stretch and recovery. Cofira is available globally in virgin and Repreve recycled polyester versions, including material produced using Unifi’s Repreve Takeback textile-to-textile recycling technology. Recycled versions can be traced using the company’s FiberPrint technology and are available with GRS and SCS recycled-content certification. “These new products bring multifunctional capabilities that help reduce complexities associated with high-performance products,” said Unifi CEO Eddie Ingle. Both innovations will be showcased at Performance Days in Munich at booth J18, followed by the Functional Fabric Fair in Portland

articles.o: FibreTrace® Physical Verification Now Available Across North And Central America As Regional Producers Launch YarnProof™
articles.s: LONDON — October 13, 2026 — North and Central American polyester filament manufacturers today announced a collective initiative, launching YarnProof™ powered by FibreTrace® technology. YarnProof, powered by FibreTrace, enables physical verification of regional origin at any point across the value ch
articles.x: LONDON — October 13, 2026 — North and Central American polyester filament manufacturers today announced a collective initiative, launching YarnProof powered by FibreTrace® technology. YarnProof, powered by FibreTrace, enables physical verification of regional origin at any point across the value chain, giving brands, manufacturers, and regulators increased confidence in supply chain compliance. By embedding an invisible, persistent tracer directly into polyester filament yarn during extrusion, YarnProof-enabled materials carry a verifiable origin signature that stays in the material from production through the life of the product. The FibreTrace handheld scanner detects the tracer in real time, whether in yarn, fabric, or final product. Each scan by an authorized participant creates a verification event that connects the physical material with supporting production and sourcing records. Working alongside existing documentation, YarnProof facilitates a layer of physical proof of origin to strengthen trade integrity, protect compliant supply chains, and support regional manufacturing. For YarnProof, this capability creates an additional layer of assurance supporting the yarn-forward requirements of CAFTA-DR and USMCA. North and Central American polyester filament manufacturers have united to protect the integrity of manufacturing in region. These manufacturers are: Aquafil O’Mara, Inc. CS America, Inc. CS Central America, S.A. de C.V. Nan Ya Plastics Corporation America, Premiere Fibers, LLC Skytex México, S.A. de C.V. Tecnología Textil Avanzada S.A. Textufil S.A. de C.V. Unifi Manufacturing, Inc. articles.x: CARY, N.C. — October 13, 2026 — INDA, the Association of the Nonwoven Fabrics Industry, has opened registration for IDEA®27, the premier global event for the nonwovens and engineered fabrics industry, taking place March 23-25, 2027, at the Kansas City Convention Center in Kansas City, Missouri. articles.o: Pontetorto wins Performance Days Eco Award
articles.s: Italian warp knitted textiles manufacturer Pontetorto has won the Performance Days Eco Award for its innovative 6140/Biobased fleece fabric, developed using bio-based polyester fibres from Finnish company UPM. The award will be presented at Performance Days in Munich, Germany, on 13 and 14 October 2
articles.x: Italian warp knitted textiles manufacturer Pontetorto has won the Performance Days Eco Award for its innovative 6140/Biobased fleece fabric, developed using bio-based polyester fibres from Finnish company UPM. The award will be presented at Performance Days in Munich, Germany, on 13 and 14 October 2026, recognising the company’s efforts to develop lower-impact textile solutions for the outdoor, sportswear and performance apparel sectors. Founded in 1952, Pontetorto has established a strong reputation for developing technical fleece fabrics and other innovative textiles. Its latest development replaces conventional fossil-based raw materials with wood-derived bio-PET, offering an alternative to traditional polyester while maintaining the performance, comfort and technical characteristics required for demanding applications. The 6140/Biobased microfleece incorporates innovative fibres produced using raw materials derived from residues generated by the wood industry, including small branches, leaves and sawmill by-products. These resources are converted into bio-based polyester feedstocks, helping to reduce dependence on fossil-based materials. According to Pontetorto, the resulting fabric offers a lower carbon footprint than conventional polyester while retaining the functional properties expected of high-performance fleece materials. The wood used in the production process is sourced from forests certified under FSC and PEFC schemes, supporting responsible forest management and traceability throughout the supply chain. articles.o: Jiwarajka’s New Technical-Textile Frontier: From Yarn to Performance
articles.s: By Jayshri Ramani With more than four decades of polyester expertise, Jiwarajka Textile Industries is moving beyond conventional yarn manufacturing into application-driven, high-performance yarn solutions for technical textiles The global… The post Jiwarajka’s New Technical-Textile Frontier: From Ya
articles.x: By Jayshri Ramani With more than four decades of polyester expertise, Jiwarajka Textile Industries is moving beyond conventional yarn manufacturing into application-driven, high-performance yarn solutions for technical textiles The global textile industry is undergoing a fundamental shift from commodity products towards materials engineered for specific performance requirements. For Jiwarajka Textile Industries, this is opening a new avenue of growth—one that builds on its more than four decades of experience in polyester yarn manufacturing while taking the company deeper into technical textiles. Anish Jiwarajka, Director, Jiwarajka Textile Industries In an exclusive interaction with The Textile Magazine , Anish Jiwarajka, Director, Jiwarajka Textile Industries, explains the company’s evolving strategy, including its expansion into Industrial Drawn Yarn (IDY), Mother Yarn, Monofilament and other specialised yarns. At the heart of the strategy is a simple change in the customer’s question—from “What is the price of this yarn?” to “What can this yarn do?” From commodity yarn to performance materials Technical textiles are fundamentally different from conventional textiles because their primary purpose is functionality rather than aesthetics or fashion. Whether it is a seat belt designed for safety, a geotextile used to strengthen infrastructure or a medical textile requiring specific protective properties, performance is the defining criterion. This is creating opportunities across automotive, infrastructure, agriculture, healthcare, industrial manufacturing, safety and protection, sports and packaging. articles.t: Lycra CloakFX를 사용하면 수분 흔적이 덜 눈에 띕니다
articles.o: Moisture marks less visible with Lycra CloakFX
articles.s: A polyester fibre designed to make sweat marks less visible on clothing is among the technologies being highlighted by The Lycra Company at this week’s Performance Days in Munich (October 13-14). Coolmax CloakFX uses optical masking technology to diffuse light at the fibre level, reducing the visibl
articles.x: A polyester fibre designed to make sweat marks less visible on clothing is among the technologies being highlighted by The Lycra Company at this week’s Performance Days in Munich (October 13-14). Coolmax CloakFX uses optical masking technology to diffuse light at the fibre level, reducing the visible appearance of moisture on fabrics. Rather than simply managing perspiration, the technology aims to make garments look drier during exercise and everyday wear. The fibre, which is now made from 100% recycled polyester and is Global Recycled Standard (GRS) certified, is one of 16 products selected for the exhibition’s Innovation Forum. The technology addresses a familiar problem in sportswear, where sweat marks can remain highly visible even when fabrics are designed to transport moisture away from the skin. By incorporating the masking effect into the fibre itself, Lycra aims to reduce this visibility without compromising moisture management. Turkish textile manufacturer Ekoten will demonstrate how CloakFX can be incorporated into commercially developed fabrics and garments. Lycra will also present two collaborative projects exploring the use of bio-based and recycled materials in performance apparel. The first, Set the Pace, brings together Italian textile manufacturer Brugnoli and cycling apparel specialist Pissei in the development of a technical cycling kit containing up to 89% bio-based materials. The fabrics combine Brugnoli’s patented Br4 technology and bio-based polyamide with renewable Lycra elastane which contains 70% plant-based content. The project demonstrates how bio-based fibres can be combined in stretch fabrics designed to meet the demands of technical cycling apparel. articles.o: Knitting and weaving a new future for green hydrogen
articles.s: North Wales-based KnitMesh Technologies and German technical mesh specialist GKD are combining knitted and woven metallic structures in complete cell assemblies for hydrogen electrolysers, bringing two long-established textile technologies into the rapidly developing green hydrogen industry. The com
articles.x: North Wales-based KnitMesh Technologies and German technical mesh specialist GKD are combining knitted and woven metallic structures in complete cell assemblies for hydrogen electrolysers, bringing two long-established textile technologies into the rapidly developing green hydrogen industry. The companies will jointly showcase their technologies at Hydrogen Technology World Expo in Hamburg from October 20-22, building on a strategic partnership first announced in March 2025. For KnitMesh, the development represents a significant new application for technology it has been developing since 1957. The Greenfield, Flintshire-based company is supplying knitted wire mesh as porous transport layers (PTLs), gas diffusion layers, electrodes and elastic elements for electrolysers used to produce hydrogen. The potential of the technology has been highlighted by research from the German Aerospace Center (DLR) Institute of Engineering Thermodynamics into the performance of porous transport layers in water electrolysis. In controlled single-cell testing, DLR compared a KnitMesh knitted-wire PTL with a standard configuration and recorded a 33% increase in current density. Cell voltage was also reduced indicating lower energy requirements under the test conditions. articles.o: Dutch AWARE™ signs agreement with Chinese textile hub Shengze to bring material innovation to global markets
articles.s: Government-backed traceability initiative launches as carbon-capture yarn from China is transformed into a jacket in Bangladesh with a Digital Product Passport for Europe. Dutch textile traceability company AWARE™ has signed a cooperation agreement with the Shengze Town People’s Government to develo
articles.x: Government-backed traceability initiative launches as carbon-capture yarn from China is transformed into a jacket in Bangladesh with a Digital Product Passport for Europe. Dutch textile traceability company AWARE™ has signed a cooperation agreement with the Shengze Town People’s Government to develop international supply-chain traceability and help bring the region’s advanced synthetic textile innovations to global markets. The agreement was announced on 10 October during the opening of the 15th Jiangsu (Shengze) Textile Expo, which also celebrated the 40th anniversary of the China Eastern Silk Market. The collaboration will establish a large-scale pilot connecting textile producers through a neutral, cross-border data infrastructure. The initiative aims to make production origin, material composition and sustainability evidence accessible to international buyers, while allowing producers to retain control of their own data. As a first step, the partners will launch the first recycled polyester Digital Product Passport. Shengze is one of China’s most important textile manufacturing centres, home to major producers including Shenghong and Hengli. The China Eastern Silk Market generates approximately RMB 200 billion in annual trading activity. From carbon-capture yarn in China to a jacket for Europe The first practical example was presented during the event. Fuhua Weaving received Wujiang District’s first carbon-capture fabric material Digital Product Passport (mDPP) label, powered by STCP first-mile traceability and AWARE™, demonstrating how innovative materials can be connected to digital production evidence. articles.s: Brussels, 6 October 2026 – EURATEX has submitted its contribution to the European Commission’s public consultation on the future European Partnerships under Horizon Europe 2028–2034, calling for the continuation of a dedicated European research and innovation partnership for the textile and clothing
articles.x: Brussels, 6 October 2026 – EURATEX has submitted its contribution to the European Commission’s public consultation on the future European Partnerships under Horizon Europe 2028–2034, calling for the continuation of a dedicated European research and innovation partnership for the textile and clothing industry. As the European Commission prepares the next EU research and innovation framework, the future of sector-specific partnerships is under discussion. EURATEX stresses that textiles must remain a strategic priority , ensuring that European companies, particularly SMEs, can access the research, technologies and funding needed to strengthen their competitiveness. The European textile and clothing industry generates €166 billion in annual turnover and employs 1.2 million people across approximately 194,000 companies. With 99.8% of businesses being SMEs, dedicated European cooperation is essential to translate research into practical industrial solutions. Keeping Textiles of the Future at the heart of European innovation EURATEX calls for the continuation and reinforcement of Textiles of the Future , the co-programmed European Partnership launched under Horizon Europe’s 2025–2027 Strategic Plan. The partnership connects companies, research organisations and technology providers to address common industrial challenges. It is expected to mobilise at least €60 million in its initial phase, with projects running until 2030. Discontinuing the partnership after 2027 would risk interrupting this momentum before its first projects have delivered their full results. articles.o: Barmag puts repeatability at the heart of productivity
articles.s: Barmag’s new Wings POY 2.0 1920/16 winding concept increases the number of winding positions from 12 to 16, enabling polyester spinning plants to achieve up to 33% higher production density. For Georg Strausberg, however, the more important development is the automation needed to sustain this increa
articles.x: Barmag’s new Wings POY 2.0 1920/16 winding concept increases the number of winding positions from 12 to 16, enabling polyester spinning plants to achieve up to 33% higher production density. For Georg Strausberg, however, the more important development is the automation needed to sustain this increased output without compromising process stability, yarn quality or operating efficiency. Speaking at the recent Dornbirn Global Fiber Congress, Strausberg emphasised that the objective of automation should not simply be to introduce additional functions, robots or more sophisticated machinery, but to eliminate the variability that can undermine production performance. “The real question is not how to achieve higher productivity once but how to achieve it every day,” he said. “This is where automation becomes decisive.” The distinction is particularly relevant to polyester filament production, where higher production density places additional demands on process control, yarn handling and operating personnel. “If higher productivity leads to more breaks, more waste, greater operator dependency, or less stable quality, it is not real progress,” Strausberg said. Redesigning the process First introduced to a selected audience at ITMA Asia + CITME 2025 in Singapore, POY 2.0 represents a redesign of Barmag’s production technology for partially oriented yarn, covering the entire process from spinning and filament cooling through to winding and digital monitoring. Rather than concentrating solely on increasing winding capacity, Barmag has modified several core components to improve their combined performance. articles.o: Polartec® Introduces The Next Generation Of Polartec Alpha™ Active Insulation
articles.s: SPARTANBURG, S.C. — October 13, 2026 — Polartec®, a Milliken & Company brand and global supplier of innovative performance textiles, introduces the next generation of Polartec Alpha™ active insulation, featuring a new patent-pending construction engineered to deliver greater durability and design ve
articles.x: SPARTANBURG, S.C. — October 13, 2026 — Polartec®, a Milliken & Company brand and global supplier of innovative performance textiles, introduces the next generation of Polartec Alpha active insulation, featuring a new patent-pending construction engineered to deliver greater durability and design versatility while preserving the breathability and dynamic thermoregulation that has made Alpha a benchmark for active insulation. Polartec Alpha was born from an unusually complex performance challenge: create insulation for highly active military users who move rapidly between periods of intense exertion and lower activity in cold environments. Traditional insulation could provide warmth, but often at the expense of breathability and moisture management as activity increased. Polartec Alpha approached the problem differently. Its open, highly breathable construction was engineered to balance insulation with airflow, helping manage excess heat and moisture as exertion and environmental conditions change. That combination helped establish Polartec Alpha within military and special operations communities around the world and ultimately helped create an entirely new category of active insulation. Over the following decade, the same performance principle moved into outdoor, endurance and lifestyle apparel. Polartec Alpha became known for its combination of lightweight warmth, exceptional breathability, fast drying, and packability – forever changing how designers approached insulation for people in motion. Now, Polartec is advancing the platform once again. At the center of the next generation is a patent-pending construction engineered to improve the structural integrity of the fabric while maintaining the open architecture fundamental to Polartec Alpha performance. articles.t: Eurojersey와 Petratex는 성능에 대한 새로운 접근 방식을 취합니다.
articles.o: Eurojersey and Petratex take new approach to performance
articles.s: Italian warp-knitted fabric specialist Eurojersey and Portuguese technical apparel manufacturer Petratex have joined forces to develop Optical Motion, a new performance wear project that integrates textile innovation, garment engineering and advanced manufacturing from the earliest stages of product
articles.x: Italian warp-knitted fabric specialist Eurojersey and Portuguese technical apparel manufacturer Petratex have joined forces to develop Optical Motion, a new performance wear project that integrates textile innovation, garment engineering and advanced manufacturing from the earliest stages of product development. Using cycling as its starting point, the collaboration explores how fabrics, garment construction and technologies can be developed together to optimise aerodynamics, comfort, breathability and freedom of movement. The project, developed under the concept ‘Engineered Together’, combines Eurojersey’s expertise in technical warp-knitted fabrics with Petratex’s capabilities in garment design, engineering and production. Rather than treating fabric and garment development as separate processes, the partners have created an integrated approach in which material selection, construction and fit are developed simultaneously. Optical Motion incorporates different textile structures positioned according to the demands of the body and movement. Mesh fabrics enhance ventilation, structured surfaces are designed to improve aerodynamics, while high-density materials provide support and stability. The resulting garments are engineered to maintain comfort and performance over long distances. © Eurojersey The capsule also features a distinctive visual identity inspired by Op Art, using three-dimensional textures, contrasting surfaces and reflective elements to create a sense of movement and speed. These aesthetic features are developed alongside the technical characteristics of the garments rather than added during the final design stages. articles.o: North And Central American Polyester Filament Yarn Producers Launch Yarnproof™ To Strengthen Regional Trade Compliance And Supply Chain Integrity
articles.s: GREENSBORO, N.C. — October 13, 2026 — Unifi, Inc., together with polyester filament yarn manufacturers across North and Central America, today announced the launch of YarnProof™, an industry-wide initiative designed to provide immediate, physical verification of polyester filament yarn origin throug
articles.x: GREENSBORO, N.C. — October 13, 2026 — Unifi, Inc., together with polyester filament yarn manufacturers across North and Central America, today announced the launch of YarnProof , an industry-wide initiative designed to provide immediate, physical verification of polyester filament yarn origin throughout the supply chain. YarnProof, powered by FibreTrace® technology, embeds an invisible and permanent tracer into polyester filament yarn during extrusion. The tracer remains with the material throughout its lifecycle and can be immediately detected using a proprietary FibreTrace handheld scanner at designated points across the supply chain, including yarn, fabric, and finished goods. By linking physical verification to origin claims, YarnProof supports compliance with the yarn-forward requirements of the CAFTA-DR and USMCA trade agreements. Working alongside existing documentation and certification systems, YarnProof adds a layer of verifiable evidence that strengthens trade integrity, protects compliant supply chains, and supports regional manufacturing. “Supply chain integrity is a top priority for our brand,” said Nick Pence, Senior Director of Material Supply at Under Armour. “As we continue to rely on yarn manufacturers in the region to fulfill our brand’s strategic goals, we are encouraged by the proactive steps the industry is taking to enhance transparency and reliability throughout the supply chain, and to provide physical evidence to support sourcing history.” As concerns over non-compliant trade continue to grow, trade regulators like U.S. Customs and Border Protection have emphasized the importance of private-sector solutions that help strengthen supply chain traceability and support enforcement efforts. “Traditional methods of fraud detection, such as document

articles.o: Munich Fabric Start expands digital reach
articles.s: Munich Fabric Start is expanding its role beyond the traditional trade fair calendar with a year-round digital platform, new industry partnerships and a government-backed initiative supporting emerging German textile and fashion businesses. The organiser says its latest developments reflect a strate
articles.x: Munich Fabric Start is expanding its role beyond the traditional trade fair calendar with a year-round digital platform, new industry partnerships and a government-backed initiative supporting emerging German textile and fashion businesses. The organiser says its latest developments reflect a strategy to strengthen international connections, encourage innovation and provide greater value to the global fashion and textile industry between its twice-yearly exhibitions in Munich. Central to the strategy is the launch of 365 Days Munich Fabric Start, a digital platform building on the organiser’s 30th anniversary campaign, 30 Years. 30 Stories. The initiative will provide year-round industry insights, emerging trends and perspectives through podcasts, editorial content, video and an expanded social media presence. The platform is designed to extend industry dialogue beyond the physical exhibitions, creating additional opportunities for knowledge exchange, networking and collaboration across the international textile supply chain. A further development is a partnership with Future Fashion Assembly, beginning with an industry webinar entitled What Comes Next for European Fashion Supply? on 28 October 2026. Bringing together brands, retailers, textile manufacturers and specialists in sourcing, technology and innovation, the webinar will examine practical solutions for improving the competitiveness of European fashion supply chains. Discussions will focus on the commercial benefits of artificial intelligence and digitalisation, preparations for Digital Product Passports, compliance with sustainability claims legislation and the implications of evolving EU regulations. articles.x: ₹344-crore spinning expansion completed, weaving capacity to rise to 65 million metres; company sharpens focus on asset utilisation, circularity, seamless garments and capital efficiency Sangam (India) Limited is entering a new phase of its growth journey. After several years of investment and capacity creation, the integrated textile manufacturer is now shifting its focus from project execution to operational excellence , with the objective of extracting higher returns from the assets already deployed. R. P. Soni, Chairman The company’s consolidated revenue from operations rose 13.22% to ₹3,234.53 crore in FY2025-26 , from ₹2,856.95 crore in the previous year. This performance comes as Sangam completes or advances a series of strategic investments spanning spinning, weaving, recycled polyester and downstream textile and apparel businesses. Chairman R. P. Soni describes the transition as more than a change in operational priorities. Having moved from a phase of adding capacity to one focused on making every spindle and loom contribute to the bottom line, Sangam is now seeking to build a self-sustaining model of high-yield growth. The strategy is centred on three broad priorities: improving utilisation of existing assets, increasing value addition and strengthening financial efficiency. Building scale across the textile value chain Sangam has developed an integrated textile platform extending from fibre and yarn manufacturing to weaving, processing, denim and garments. The company’s portfolio includes grey yarn, cotton blends, PV dyed yarn, denim, knitted fabrics, woven and processed fabrics and garments. articles.x: As the textile and apparel industries look beyond standalone automation, Taiwan-based OSHIMA is building closer connections between fabric inspection, production planning and cutting-room operations. In an exclusive interview at TITAS 2026, CEO Mr. Florian Finke discusses the company’s expanding technological capabilities, opportunities in technical textiles and its growing ambitions for the Indian market. BY Nithin Kumar H A fabric defect identified during inspection can still become an expensive production problem if the information never reaches the cutting room. The fabric may be inspected, graded and approved for production, yet the precise location of an imperfection can remain disconnected from the marker and spreading plan. By the time it is discovered on a cut component, the opportunity to address it efficiently may already have passed. Mr. Florian Finke , CEO For Mr. Florian Finke, CEO of OSHIMA, this gap between inspection and production represents an important opportunity for the next generation of textile and garment machinery. His vision is not simply to make individual machines faster or more automated, but to enable them to exchange information that manufacturers can use to improve their operations. Speaking to The Textile Magazine at TITAS 2026 in Taipei, Mr. Finke outlined how OSHIMA is bringing together its expertise in garment machinery, artificial intelligence and software development to create a more connected manufacturing environment. articles.o: Unifi moves water resistance into the yarn
articles.s: Unifi is moving water resistance from the finishing stage into the yarn itself with a new technology designed to eliminate the need for conventional topical durable water-repellent (DWR) treatments. The US manufacturer will introduce Resist2O Pro alongside a second new yarn technology, Cofira, at Pe
articles.x: Unifi is moving water resistance from the finishing stage into the yarn itself with a new technology designed to eliminate the need for conventional topical durable water-repellent (DWR) treatments. The US manufacturer will introduce Resist2O Pro alongside a second new yarn technology, Cofira, at Performance Days in Munich this week (October 13-14). Resist2O Pro is engineered to minimise water absorption without the use of topical treatments or fluorinated chemistry and can be employed with different methods of fabric formation. This potentially gives textile manufacturers greater flexibility in developing water-resistant fabrics while removing a separate finishing treatment from the production process. Unifi says the technology is fluorine-free and PFOA-free – defined as containing less than 5 ppb (parts per billion) – and is targeting applications ranging from apparel and footwear to furnishings and industrial textiles. The company is also launching Cofira, a yarn designed to combine characteristics normally associated with spun and filament constructions. Cofira has been developed to provide the aesthetics and handle of a spun yarn while retaining the performance characteristics available from filament yarns. It can be tailored using synthetic, blended and functional fibre technologies to create different fabric properties and effects. Potential applications include apparel, furnishings, equipment and accessories, and the yarn can also be combined with existing Unifi technologies including AMT (moisture management), ChillSense (cool-to-the-touch properties) and ReFlexx (stretch and recovery). articles.o: Why regulations need to consider how clothes are used
articles.s: By the International Wool Textile Organisation BRUSSELS – A garment can pass demanding strength tests and still be worn only a handful of times. It may fit badly, feel uncomfortable or no longer be considered ‘current’. Put another way, a strong fabric offers limited benefit if the garment made from
articles.x: By the International Wool Textile Organisation BRUSSELS – A garment can pass demanding strength tests and still be worn only a handful of times. It may fit badly, feel uncomfortable or no longer be considered ‘current’. Put another way, a strong fabric offers limited benefit if the garment made from it spends most of its life unworn. Understanding this gap is essential if Europe’s textile policies are to deliver the environmental benefits they promise. At the International Wool Textile Organisation, we believe the development of EU textile rules needs to give much greater weight to what happens to clothing in everyday life. While physical testing provides useful evidence about a garment’s ability to withstand use, it cannot, on its own, establish how much use that garment will receive. Extrinsic durability Researchers describe these wider influences on continued use as “extrinsic durability.” The term, which has become increasingly prevalent in recent years, covers considerations all of us will be familiar with. These include whether clothing fits, whether people enjoy wearing it, how they value it and whether it remains relevant as their lives change. The evidence to support the concept of extrinsic durability can be found in a review by researchers at Oslo Metropolitan University which drew together 17 studies of clothing disposal. Excluding other or unknown reasons, physical quality accounted for 37 per cent of disposal motivations, fit for 28 per cent and perceived value for 35 per cent. These findings do not suggest that quality is unimportant, but they do show how much a policy based predominantly (or only) on physical performance would miss. articles.o: John Smedley and MOON celebrate wool
articles.s: Luxury knitwear manufacturer John Smedley has partnered with historic Yorkshire woollen mill Abraham Moon & Sons (MOON) to launch a limited-edition collection of knitwear and homeware, bringing together more than four centuries of combined British textile manufacturing expertise. Launched on 8 Octob
articles.x: Luxury knitwear manufacturer John Smedley has partnered with historic Yorkshire woollen mill Abraham Moon & Sons (MOON) to launch a limited-edition collection of knitwear and homeware, bringing together more than four centuries of combined British textile manufacturing expertise. Launched on 8 October 2026, the John Smedley x MOON collection marks the first capsule in a planned long-term partnership between the two heritage brands. Combining John Smedley’s fine knitwear expertise with MOON’s woollen textile manufacturing capabilities, the collaboration celebrates the versatility, durability and enduring appeal of wool. © John Smedley The collection also represents John Smedley’s first venture into homewares, extending the brand’s established knitwear offering into interior textiles. Featuring woollen throws, cushions, a chunky knit and a woollen hat, the range combines traditional textile craftsmanship with contemporary styling. A colour palette of ginger, grey, cream and midnight blue is complemented by variegated stripes and plain textures, reflecting the growing interest in natural materials and timeless interior design. John Smedley CEO Jess Mcguire-Dudley said the partnership was a natural extension of the companies’ shared manufacturing heritage and commitment to quality. “John Smedley and MOON share generations of specialist knowledge, British manufacturing, and a belief in creating beautiful products that are made to last. articles.s: The Remod collection, to be introduced at Kingpins Amsterdam this week (October 14-15), explores how three different types of Tencel Lyocell fibre can be used to create contrasting denim textures, weights and finishes, including constructions containing no cotton. articles.x: The Remod collection, to be introduced at Kingpins Amsterdam this week (October 14-15), explores how three different types of Tencel Lyocell fibre can be used to create contrasting denim textures, weights and finishes, including constructions containing no cotton. The fabrics have been woven at Kaihara’s vertically integrated mill in Hiroshima, building on a relationship with Lenzing that dates back to the 1990s. The collection includes heavyweight men’s jackets, mid-weight wide-leg and stretch jeans and casual shirting. It combines conventional denim manufacturing techniques with different fibre blends to achieve specific fabric characteristics. Central to the development is Tencel Lyocell HV100, first introduced at Kingpins Amsterdam in October 2025 as a cotton-like alternative to standard lyocell fibres. The fibre employs Lenzing’s Variocut technology to introduce controlled variations in fibre length, creating the subtle irregularities and more opaque, matte appearance associated with cotton denim. A second fibre, Tencel Lyocell dtex 2.2, has a coarser structure and a fibre length of 51mm. It produces a drier, stiffer handle and natural slub effects resembling linen, adding body and structure to fabrics without significantly increasing weight. Standard Tencel Lyocell, meanwhile, contributes softness, drape and colour depth. articles.o: Livinguard cuts reactive dyeing wash-off time
articles.s: Swiss textile technology company Livinguard has demonstrated how its +DYE SC after-treatment can reduce the conventional nine-stage wash-off process following reactive dyeing of cotton to just six steps, cutting water consumption by 32% and processing time by 23%. The results come from an independen
articles.x: Swiss textile technology company Livinguard has demonstrated how its +DYE SC after-treatment can reduce the conventional nine-stage wash-off process following reactive dyeing of cotton to just six steps, cutting water consumption by 32% and processing time by 23%. The results come from an independent assessment commissioned by Fashion for Good and conducted by technical consultancy BluWin at a knitwear processing mill in India. Steam consumption was reduced by up to 88%, while calculated greenhouse gas emissions fell by 29%. Crucially, the simplified process was achieved using existing dyeing equipment, recipes and dyestuffs, without machinery modifications. Wash-off challenge The reactive dyeing of cotton and other cellulosic fibres requires extensive washing and soaping after dye application to remove hydrolysed dyes that have not bonded permanently with the fibres. These processes are often carried out at high temperatures and account for a substantial proportion of the water and energy consumed during dyeing. Livinguard +DYE SC addresses this problem through a cationic after-treatment that binds to both the fibre and hydrolysed dye, forming a charged, crosslinked network that restricts dye release during subsequent washing. This allows the conventional wash-off sequence to be shortened considerably while maintaining the required colour fastness. In the Indian trial, the mill’s existing nine-stage process, which included two soaping baths at 95°C and hot washes at 80°C and 90°C, was reduced to six stages incorporating a single warm wash at 60°C. Water consumption during wash-off fell from 37.44 to 25.33 litres per kilogram of fabric, while processing time decreased from 5.72 to 4.42 hours. articles.o: Arclin Introduces Kevlar® EXO™ XP E480
articles.s: ALPHARETTA, Ga. — October 12, 2026 — Arclin, a materials science company, today announced the launch of Kevlar® EXO™ XP E480, the latest innovation in its personal protection portfolio. Combining the proven ballistic and trauma-reduction performance of Kevlar® XP technology with the advanced capabil
articles.x: ALPHARETTA, Ga. — October 12, 2026 — Arclin, a materials science company, today announced the launch of Kevlar® EXO XP E480, the latest innovation in its personal protection portfolio. Combining the proven ballistic and trauma-reduction performance of Kevlar® XP technology with the advanced capabilities of Kevlar® EXO fiber, the new solution enables body armor manufacturers to achieve significantly lighter weight while meeting NIJ Level IIIA/HG2 protection requirements, helping improve wearer comfort, mobility, and operational effectiveness. “Protective equipment is only effective if users can wear it comfortably throughout their entire mission,” said Joe Hovanec, Arclin’s Vice President of Kevlar® EXO . “With Kevlar® EXO XP E480, manufacturers can achieve armor that is up to 25% lighter and provides up to 40% greater comfort*, helping reduce fatigue while maintaining the trusted protection users depend on.” Engineered to perform in demanding field conditions, Kevlar® EXO XP E480 combines high stopping power, excellent bullet-flattening performance, and exceptional durability in a lighter-weight construction. The material’s unique fiber architecture also helps reduce layer counts and stitching requirements, enabling streamlined armor designs and potentially lowering manufacturing complexity and labor costs. Kevlar® EXO XP E480 is now available for evaluation to customers worldwide. To learn more, visit XPE480 – Arclin. *vs. XP K520 for level IIIA/HG2 NIJ. Kevlar® and Kevlar® EXO are registered trademarks of Arclin. Posted: October 12, 2026 Source: Arclin

articles.x: Mini garments entrepreneurs met on Friday, 9 October 2026, at Hotel Platinum in Banani, Dhaka. The meeting focused on forming the convening committee of the Bangladesh Mini Garments Manufacturers Association and discussing future initiatives to develop the sector. Md. Rubel Miah, Managing Director of Sixem Fashion, was appointed Convenor, while S M Sumon Bappy, Managing Director of Sordar Garments, was appointed Member Secretary. The other representatives included in the committee were designated as Members. Participants emphasized developing the mini garments sector through training, skills enhancement, knowledge and experience sharing, and stronger cooperation among entrepreneurs. Participants also discussed plans to develop an association website to facilitate communication, information sharing, and connections among members. The discussion also covered improvements in production practices, product quality and business management, along with new market opportunities and possible solutions to common challenges faced by mini garments manufacturers. Participants expressed their commitment to working together to develop the sector. After forming the convening committee and discussing future plans, the meeting concluded with a cake-cutting ceremony. articles.s: The Hong Kong Research Institute of Textiles and Apparel (HKRITA) celebrated its 20th anniversary with an Innovation and Technology Symposium at the Hong Kong Convention and Exhibition Centre on 9 October 2026, bringing together government, academic and industry leaders to explore the future of text
articles.x: The Hong Kong Research Institute of Textiles and Apparel (HKRITA) celebrated its 20th anniversary with an Innovation and Technology Symposium at the Hong Kong Convention and Exhibition Centre on 9 October 2026, bringing together government, academic and industry leaders to explore the future of textile innovation and sustainable development. Held under the theme ‘Weaving 20 Years | Threading New Paths. Building to Last’, the event highlighted HKRITA’s achievements in applied research, technology transfer and commercialisation, while examining emerging opportunities in artificial intelligence, green innovation, circularity and talent development. A key highlight was the signing of a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) between HKRITA and Ocean Park Corporation to strengthen collaboration in sustainability, innovation, education and knowledge exchange. The partnership will explore opportunities in green technology and circular economy initiatives, combining HKRITA’s research expertise with Ocean Park’s conservation, education and public engagement capabilities. In her welcome address, HKRITA Chairman Teresa Yang emphasised the growing importance of innovation in maintaining industrial competitiveness and supporting sustainable development. “Innovation and technology are reshaping industries at an unprecedented pace. Amid growing global competition and sustainability challenges, innovation is no longer an option, but a key driver of industrial upgrading and long-term value creation,” she said. articles.s: High-performance, durable functional textiles require innovative solutions that meet a wide range of consumer expectations, from lasting freshness and superior comfort to reliable protection against adverse weather conditions. SANITIZED and RUDOLF are introducing their latest innovations, demonstrat
articles.x: High-performance, durable functional textiles require innovative solutions that meet a wide range of consumer expectations, from lasting freshness and superior comfort to reliable protection against adverse weather conditions. SANITIZED and RUDOLF are introducing their latest innovations, demonstrating how specialized textile technologies can enhance the functional durability, comfort, and long-term wearability of modern apparel. Addressing Consumer Expectations Through Textile Innovation Consumers expect more from textiles than ever before. Functional apparel, outdoor clothing, and technical textiles must remain comfortable, functional, and reliable even after repeated wear and use. Freshness, weather protection, and long-lasting performance have become important factors influencing purchasing decisions and perceptions of product quality. In response to these growing expectations, SANITIZED and RUDOLF continue to develop technologies that address the practical challenges faced by brands, manufacturers, and end consumers. Their latest innovations are designed to enhance the long-term functionality of textiles while improving comfort, protection, and overall wearability. Long-Lasting Freshness for Functional Apparel Functional clothing is repeatedly exposed to sweat, environmental conditions, daily wear, and frequent washing. Over time, these factors can compromise the perceived comfort and performance of garments, even when the textile remains physically intact. One of the key challenges is persistent odor. Sebum and odor-causing residues can accumulate on textile fibers, resulting in unpleasant smells that may remain even after multiple washing cycles. articles.x: The Bangladesh Export Processing Zones Authority (BEPZA) has launched three dedicated country desks for investors from China, South Korea and Japan to strengthen investor services and attract new investment to its export processing zones (EPZs) and economic zones. The desks were formally inaugurated at the ‘Meet the Investors’ event held in Dhaka on Saturday (October 10), attended by more than 100 local and foreign investors. Investors from 38 countries have invested in BEPZA’s eight EPZs and two economic zones, with China, South Korea and Japan emerging as the top three investor countries. The newly launched desks will provide direct assistance, investment-related information and guidance to existing and prospective investors from the three countries, helping streamline investment processes and strengthen communication. Speaking at the event, BEPZA Executive Chairman Major General Mohammad Moazzem Hossain said the initiative would help strengthen partnerships, address investors’ concerns and make Bangladesh’s investment environment more competitive and business-friendly. Despite global trade uncertainties and economic challenges, BEPZA signed investment agreements with 36 enterprises in the fiscal year 2025–26. Exports from its zones reached US$8.41 billion during the fiscal year, marking a 2.22 percent increase from the previous year. The executive chairman also highlighted the declaration of BEPZA Economic Zone-1, BEPZA Economic Zone-2, Jashore EPZ and Patuakhali EPZ as full-fledged zones, urging investors to expand their operations in the new zones in collaboration with supply-chain partners. articles.o: CottonConscience combines satellite data and DNA to trace cotton
articles.s: Fashion brands could gain better evidence of cotton origins and water-related risks through a satellite-based tracking system developed by Brand Conscience. Its CottonConscience project has completed...
articles.x: Fashion brands could gain better evidence of cotton origins and water-related risks through a satellite-based tracking system developed by Brand Conscience. Its CottonConscience project has completed a feasibility study supported by the European Space Agency (ESA), paving the way for live supply chain testing. The system combines satellite imagery, DNA tagging, farmer surveys, and digital records to trace cotton from farms to initial processing. It uses Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 satellite data from the European Union’s Copernicus program to identify cotton fields and assess environmental conditions. The initiative targets a key supply chain challenge: verifying sustainability claims beyond supplier declarations and paper-based audits. DNA analysis and digital records can help connect satellite-based farm information with physical cotton. Water accountability is another priority. Cotton production accounted for 8% of the global blue water footprint of crop production, according to a July 2026 analysis by Chatham House. Better farm-level data could help brands identify water risks and support more responsible sourcing. The project involves supply chain partners across Egypt, India, Türkiye, Pakistan and China. It aims to help brands verify sourcing claims and support responsible farming practices. However, the technology needs more real-world testing. It must prove that it can track products reliably, keep costs reasonable and work with existing supply chain systems before brands can use it for compliance and sustainability reporting.

articles.o: Precision spray finishing test base established in Pakistan
articles.s: Pakistan’s textile mills are to gain local access to precision spray finishing trials under a new initiative involving BW Converting, Archroma and Monforts. BW Converting plans to install a laboratory-scale spray-finishing unit at Archroma’s Pakistan laboratory, enabling mills to test finishing chem
articles.x: Pakistan’s textile mills are to gain local access to precision spray finishing trials under a new initiative involving BW Converting, Archroma and Monforts. BW Converting plans to install a laboratory-scale spray-finishing unit at Archroma’s Pakistan laboratory, enabling mills to test finishing chemistries and applications on their own fabrics without initially having to carry out trials overseas. The three companies will outline the initiative at IGATEX Pakistan, taking place at the Expo Centre Lahore this week (October 15-18), where they will exhibit jointly through their local representative Al-Ameen Trading Corporation. The planned facility will use BW Converting’s non-contact spray application technology alongside Archroma’s textile chemistry and application expertise. Applications showing potential at laboratory level could subsequently move to larger-scale trials at the Monforts Advanced Technology Center (ATC) in Mönchengladbach, Germany. Direct route The arrangement is intended to provide a more direct route from initial formulation and application development through to testing under industrial finishing conditions. BW Converting’s Baldwin TexCoat G4 technology applies controlled quantities of finishing chemistry to one or both sides of a fabric using non-contact precision spraying. Compared with conventional processes involving higher wet pick-up, applying only the required amount of chemistry can reduce the volume of water subsequently needing to be evaporated during drying. This can lower water, chemical and energy consumption while potentially allowing higher production speeds, depending on the fabric and finishing application. Pakistan is regarded as a particularly relevant market for the technology because of the scale of its textile processing industry

articles.x: Steven Collet, Vice-Minister for International Cooperation of the Netherlands, visited 4A Yarn Dyeing Ltd., a concern of TEAM Group, to discuss sustainability, clean energy, supply chain traceability, and Bangladesh’s post-LDC transition. Figure: Netherlands delegation explores green initiatives at 4A Yarn Dyeing Collet was accompanied by Wampie Libon, Ambassador for Sustainable Development, and Joris van Bommel, Ambassador of the Netherlands to Bangladesh. Representatives from Swisscontact Bangladesh, Solidaridad Network Bangladesh, Fair Wear Foundation and AWARE Bangladesh also joined the visit. The delegation toured the Savar-based facility and observed its rooftop solar plant, rainwater harvesting system, fair-price shop, childcare facility and production floor. The facility is LEED Platinum certified and was the first outerwear manufacturer to sign the UN Fashion Industry Charter for Climate Action. Afroza Shahin, Managing Director of TEAM Group, Abdullah Hil Nakib, Deputy Managing Director, and senior management officials welcomed the delegation. The visit also included a presentation on the group’s sustainability strategy and a discussion on future cooperation. Key topics included Bangladesh’s graduation from least developed country (LDC) status, the proposed Bangladesh-EU Free Trade Agreement, industrial decarbonization, traceability, digital product passports (DPPs) and upcoming EU regulations. The participants also discussed potential partnerships with Dutch brands and development cooperation in clean energy, circularity and workforce development. “The Netherlands has long been a partner in our industry’s journey toward safer, fairer and greener production,” said Afroza Shahin. The project will be located within Huafon’s industrial footpr
articles.x: DANVILLE, V.A. — October 8, 2026 — Circ® and Huafon, a leading spandex producer in China, are partnering to build and scale a new multi-phase textile-to-textile recycling site in China, expanding Circ’s global pathway to industrial scale. The project will be located within Huafon’s industrial footprint and will use Circ’s technology to process polycotton textile waste and recycle both inputs, recovering recycled PTA, recycled MEG and recycled cellulosic pulp for use in new textiles. The site will be developed in phases, with Phase 1 designed for approximately 200 metric tons of textile waste per day and additional capacity planned. The partnership brings together Circ’s polycotton recycling technology with Huafon’s manufacturing capabilities, infrastructure, and China market position. Huafon is also investing directly in the project alongside Circ and other selected investors. Huafon’s engineering, procurement, logistics, and commercial experience provide an efficient path to industrial deployment. Circ brings an established network of global brands, textile manufacturing partners, and downstream customers ready to adopt the materials the platform produces. “China is at the center of global textile production, making it a critical location for scaling textile-to-textile recycling. Huafon brings the industrial capabilities, experience, and investment to move quickly and build a platform that can scale well beyond this first site,” said Peter Majeranowski, CEO of Circ. Competitions, discussions with industry figures, career seminars, a job fair, a fashion show and cultural performances kept the campus lively for two days. The program began on Thursday (October 8) with registration at 8:30 am. Dhaka-19 MP Dr Dewan Mohammad Salahuddin Babu was the chief guest, and Bangladesh Textile Mills Corporation (BTMC) Chairman Brig Gen S M Zahid Hasan was the special guest. Speakers included Md Safayat Hossain, General Manager of Epyllion Group, who presented the "7E" formula; Kazi Feroz Hossain; Prof Dr Md Shah-e-Alam, Vice-Chancellor of Shanto-Mariam University of Creative Technology; BTMC Director (Finance and Audit) Noore Khaja Alamin; and NITER Director Prof Dr Ashequl Alam Rana. Banna, convener of the NITER Textile Club, pledged to continue the club's activities to increase student engagement. Guests visited the stalls around noon while judging continued. articles.o: Lycra advances plant-based spandex with 70% renewable content
articles.s: The Lycra Company is advancing plant-based spandex with 70% renewable content from US-grown field corn. The fiber can reduce its carbon footprint by up to 45% while maintaining the stretch and recover...
articles.x: The Lycra Company is advancing plant-based spandex with 70% renewable content from US-grown field corn. The fiber can reduce its carbon footprint by up to 45% while maintaining the stretch and recovery performance of conventional Lycra fiber, according to a third-party-reviewed life cycle assessment. Figure: Global fiber production reached an estimated 139 million tons in 2025, while textile-to-textile recycling accounted for only 0.76% of total fiber production. The fiber has entered commercial applications, including swimwear by Italian brand Arena and denim by Danish brand Only & Sons. Lycra also showcased a plant-based denim collection during Climate Week in New York in September 2026, combining its renewable fiber with lower-footprint cotton. The development comes as textile manufacturers face growing pressure to reduce material-related emissions. Global fiber production reached an estimated 139 million tons in 2025, while textile-to-textile recycling accounted for only 0.76% of total fiber production, according to Textile Exchange’s Materials Market Report 2026 . Alongside renewable feedstocks, Lycra is developing pilot-stage technology to recover spandex from textile waste blended with nylon and polyester. Commercial-scale recycling remains a challenge because these fibers are difficult to separate efficiently. For apparel manufacturers, renewable spandex offers a potential route to lower the carbon footprint of stretch fabrics without compromising performance. However, wider adoption will depend on cost, supply availability and credible environmental data. Scaling fiber recovery from blended textiles will also be critical to advancing circular production beyond the use of renewable raw materials.

articles.x: The Nature Conservancy (TNC) has launched the Microfiber Action Alliance (MAA), bringing together major apparel and outdoor brands to reduce microfiber pollution across the textile value chain. Nike, Patagonia, Under Armour, lululemon, Cotopaxi and REI Co-op are among its founding participants. Announced on October 6, 2026, the initiative aims to accelerate the adoption of science-based solutions, test practical interventions, and share findings across the industry. It will work with participating companies to identify where microfiber pollution occurs and determine which measures can deliver meaningful reductions at scale. Microfiber pollution extends beyond synthetic textiles. Fibers can be released from polyester, nylon, and acrylic, as well as natural materials such as cotton and wool. Dyeing, softeners, and other textile treatments can also affect the environmental behavior of released fibers. Pollution can occur during textile manufacturing, garment use, washing, and disposal. Research published in PLOS ONE found substantial differences in microfiber shedding among textile samples. In tests covering 37 materials, fiber loss ranged from 9.6 milligrams to 1,240 milligrams per kilogram of textile per wash. The findings highlight the role of fabric construction, material selection, and finishing in reducing fiber release. These results are specific to the tested samples and do not represent all textiles. The alliance builds on existing industry research and collaboration, including work by The Microfibre Consortium, which develops scientific tools and methods to measure fiber fragmentation and support reductions across textile supply chains. articles.o: How technology upgradation can help Bangladesh’s textile sector regain competitiveness
articles.s: Bangladesh’s textile industry has built much of its strength on a solid backward linkage base, with spinning playing a particularly important role in supporting the country’s ready made garment secto...
articles.x: Bangladesh’s textile industry has built much of its strength on a solid backward linkage base, with spinning playing a particularly important role in supporting the country’s ready made garment sector. For decades, investment in spinning capacity helped reduce dependence on imported yarn, shorten sourcing lead times and strengthen the domestic textile value chain. Today, however, the economics of spinning have become much more difficult. Gas and electricity costs have risen sharply. Wages are higher, financing remains expensive, imported raw materials are costly, and competition from regional suppliers continues to put pressure on yarn prices. At the same time, many mills are still operating with machinery and production systems installed more than a decade ago. Under these conditions, technology upgradation is no longer simply about producing more. It is increasingly about producing at a cost that allows a mill to remain competitive. The challenge becomes even more serious when working capital is considered. In Bangladesh, textile mills often operate with much longer working capital cycles than competitors in countries such as India and China. When capital remains tied up for several months, financing costs rise and operating flexibility declines. This means that mills cannot depend only on volume growth. The next phase of competitiveness will have to come from better energy efficiency, higher machine productivity, lower waste, more automation and a broader product mix. Energy efficiency must come first Energy is now one of the most important factors affecting spinning cost. Older machinery generally consumes significantly more power than modern systems. articles.x: AMSTERDAM — October 9, 2026 — TNO today launches polySCOUT, an independent Dutch AI company that designs polymers to specification. Target properties and regulatory constraints go in; lab-validated candidate materials come out. Where the design and selection phase of a new polymer typically takes years, polySCOUT brings it down to weeks. The technology has been developed within TNO since 2022, and TNO becomes a shareholder in the new company. To mark the launch, the founders ring the gong at Euronext Amsterdam this morning. Why now Plastics are everywhere: 431 million tonnes were produced worldwide in 2024 (PlasticsEurope). Yet the molecules the industry relies on are largely a century old, and regulation is now changing faster than the chemistry. Since 20 July 2026, bisphenol A has been banned in food contact materials in the EU. The European microplastics restriction phases out synthetic polymer microparticles category by category through 2035. A broad PFAS restriction is in preparation. Every deadline means the same thing: a material has to go, and its replacement has to perform at least as well.”Forced substitution is a performance problem with a deadline,” says Michaël van der Jagt, co-founder and CEO of polySCOUT. “Conventional polymer development succeeds in five to ten percent of cases. Not because chemists lack skill, but because the search space is unimaginably large: more than 1060 possible polymer structures. We don’t make R&D faster. We make it start in the right place.” How it works polySCOUT turns the classical development process around. articles.x: Spanish textile recycling company Recover™ has launched RecoverOne, a recycled cotton and polyester fiber blend designed to eliminate downstream overdyeing and simplify textile production. The company said the ready-to-spin blend combines mechanically recycled cotton with recycled polyester in color-matched ratios tailored to different textile applications. By matching the fiber colors during blending, RecoverOne is designed to remove the need for additional dyeing after fabric production. The launch highlights an approach to integrating color selection into recycled fiber development, potentially helping textile manufacturers simplify processing and reduce reliance on downstream overdyeing. For textile manufacturers, the blend offers an option to incorporate recycled fibers while addressing production requirements related to color consistency and processing efficiency. Its application-specific formulation also allows the blend to be adapted to different textile uses. Recover™, based in Spain, develops recycled textile materials, with mechanical cotton recycling forming part of its product portfolio.

articles.x: Trützschler Group has expanded the international customer network for its TRUECYCLED textile recycling technology, adding new reference installations in Bangladesh, Pakistan and the United States. Announced as the industry marked World Circular Textiles Day on October 8, the latest customers are Akij Textile Mills in Bangladesh, Material Return in the United States and Artistic Denim Mills in Pakistan. The additions reflect growing interest in technologies capable of transforming pre-consumer and post-consumer textile waste into secondary fibres suitable for producing new yarns. TRUECYCLED Connects Recycling With Spinning Preparation TRUECYCLED is Trützschler’s integrated solution for the mechanical recycling and spinning preparation of textile waste. The process can cover cutting and tearing textile waste, opening, cleaning and blending the recovered fibres, carding and drawing the resulting material before it enters the spinning process. One of the main technical challenges in mechanical textile recycling is the loss of fibre length. Cutting and tearing fabrics create fibres that are generally shorter and more variable than virgin raw materials. Unopened yarn and fabric particles can also remain in the material stream. If these secondary fibres undergo overly aggressive processing, additional fibre damage can reduce usable yield and make it more difficult to produce stable, homogeneous yarn. Trützschler addresses this challenge by coordinating the tearing and spinning-preparation stages. Machine settings and process configurations are selected to limit unnecessary fibre shortening while ensuring that the recovered material is sufficiently opened, cleaned and blended. articles.x: US textile recycling technology developer Circ is joining forces with Chinese chemicals and fibre manufacturing giant Huafon to establish a large-scale textile-to-textile recycling operation in China, with an initial processing capacity of approximately 200 tons of textile waste per day. The project will be developed within Huafon’s existing industrial infrastructure, combining Circ’s technology for recovering both polyester and cellulose from blended fabrics with the Chinese group’s manufacturing capabilities, engineering resources and established supply chains. Significantly, Huafon will also invest directly in the venture alongside Circ and other selected investors, providing both industrial expertise and financial backing for its development. The new facility will be built in phases, with the first designed to process approximately 200 tons of textile waste daily, equivalent to around 73,000 tons annually if operated continuously at full capacity. Further expansion is planned. The partnership represents another major step in Circ’s efforts to commercialise its recycling technology, alongside the company’s first industrial-scale facility currently under development in France. © Huafon Industrial backing Headquartered in Wenzhou, Zhejiang Province, Huafon is one of China’s largest chemical and advanced materials manufacturers and a major global producer of spandex and polyurethane materials. Founded in 1991, the group employs more than 20,000 people worldwide and operates across polyurethane, polyamide, bio-based materials and other industrial sectors. Entitled Archivi Punti Aperti (Open Archives – Knit Stitch Collection), the appointment-only event will take place at Milano Trend’s showroom in Via Visconti di Modrone 33, offering designers, fashion brands and textile professionals an opportunity to explore the latest developments in knitwear materials and design. The event will feature premium yarns from leading European manufacturers, particularly Italian suppliers, alongside selected materials from companies participating in Shima Seiki’s yarnbank online platform. yarnbank provides comprehensive yarn information and digital yarn data from manufacturers worldwide, enabling designers and knitwear producers to explore materials and integrate them into digital product development workflows. Visitors will have the opportunity to examine yarns and knitted fabrics normally viewed online, experiencing their colours, textures and handle first-hand. In a special feature, selected fabric samples will be available for visitors to cut and take away, providing physical references for subsequent design and product development projects. The event will also demonstrate how digital yarn data can be used to create realistic virtual knitwear prototypes through Shima Seiki’s APEXFiz design software. articles.s: AMSTERDAM — October 6, 2026 — Fashion for Good today announces the launch of the Cotton Reloop Matrix Project, a cross-industry initiative that will map and physically validate the quality of commercially available recycled cotton yarns against brand specifications, giving the industry a data-backed
articles.x: AMSTERDAM — October 6, 2026 — Fashion for Good today announces the launch of the Cotton Reloop Matrix Project, a cross-industry initiative that will map and physically validate the quality of commercially available recycled cotton yarns against brand specifications, giving the industry a data-backed overview of how quality, price, and recycled content intersect. The project is convened with Fashion for Good partners Arvind, BESTSELLER, C&A, Interloop, Reformation, Shahi, and ecosystem partner Uster. Cotton accounts for 19% of global fibre production and a core part of the material mix. Although alternative recycling pathways exist to utilise cotton-rich textile waste feedstock, they do not make a cotton output. Therefore, mechanical recycling is a crucial pathway to utilise waste and create recycled cotton yarns and fabrics. Through the mechanical recycling process, textile waste is shredded and re-opened into loose fibres that can be respun into yarn. However, shredding shortens and weakens the fibres, so only 45 to 50% of the input survives as usable material. The rest is lost as short fibres and processing waste, and because the surviving fibres are shorter than virgin cotton, spinners can only blend a limited share back into new yarn. In practice, that caps most yarns at around 10% recycled content: any higher and the fabric isn’t durable enough for commercial use. While recyclers have available capacities, integrating a meaningful percentage of recycled cotton remains complex for brands navigating trade-offs around quality and price. Testing happens in isolation, with recyclers and brands working from separate data sets, and no shared reference comparison to close the gap between them. articles.o: Building a stronger domestic textile value chain
articles.s: The government's decision to raise the cash incentive from 1.5 percent to 5 percent for the use of domestically produced yarn and fabric in Bangladesh's Ready-Made Garment (RMG) industry is timely. Am...
articles.x: The government's decision to raise the cash incentive from 1.5 percent to 5 percent for the use of domestically produced yarn and fabric in Bangladesh's Ready-Made Garment (RMG) industry is timely. Amidst intense global competition in the apparel sector, rising production costs, and various challenges facing the country's spinning and textile industries, this move could strengthen the local textile sector. An increase in demand for locally produced yarn and fabric could yield benefits for spinning, dyeing, knitting, and other allied industries. Furthermore, it could create new market opportunities for spinning mills that are currently operating below full capacity or facing financial difficulties. However, this decision should not be viewed merely as an increase in export incentives. Its significance is far-reaching, as it is directly linked to Bangladesh's long-term industrial capacity, local value addition, reduction of import dependency, and foreign currency savings. Consequently, a significant portion of the entire value chain—from yarn to fabric and fabric to the final garment—can be completed within Bangladesh. Increased use of local inputs can help reduce import reliance, save foreign currency, generate demand for related industries, and boost local value addition. This is where the 5 percent incentive holds significant potential. Additionally, the government's decision to withdraw the zero-duty import facility for 10–30 count cotton yarn under the bonded warehouse system should also be viewed in this context. The National Board of Revenue (NBR) issued the gazette notification on September 7, with the stated aim of protecting domestic textile and spinning mills. Italian circular knitter Brugnoli, meanwhile, will show Explosive Amni V550, combining Amni Soul Eco polyamide with Roica V550.
