articles.x: Thermore’s EVOdown recycled insulation is being used across five men’s and women’s styles in the new Patagonia Heyes Peak collection. Designed for everyday wear in changing and transitional weather, the Heyes Peak range includes a jacket, parka, hoody and three-in-one parka. The garments combine layer-friendly linings with EVOdown insulation to provide warmth and softness without excessive bulk. The Heyes Peak Jacket uses 80 gsm EVOdown with a shell made from NetPlus 100% post-consumer recycled nylon ripstop. NetPlus material is produced from recycled fishing nets, while the shell also has a durable water-repellent treatment made without intentionally added PFAS. Thermore EVOdown is made with fibres 100% recycled from PET bottles and has been developed to combine the soft handle and loft associated with down with the durability and easy care of synthetic insulation. The insulation is certified to Oeko-Tex Standard 100, the Global Recycled Standard (GRS) and bluesign requirements. articles.x: The Lycra Company will highlight progress in producing spandex from renewable raw materials and developing textile-to-textile recycling technology at the Textile Exchange Conference 2026, taking place in Vancouver, Canada, from October 12-16. The company has now reached commercial-scale production of its Renewable Lycra fibre, which contains 70% plant-based material, while continuing to develop processes for recovering and recycling spandex from waste textiles. The renewable fibre uses dent corn grown primarily in Iowa, USA, as a feedstock to replace a significant proportion of the petroleum-derived raw materials traditionally used in spandex production. According to a comparative life cycle assessment conducted by Ramboll this year, the bio-based fibre can reduce its carbon footprint by up to 45% compared to conventional Lycra fibre, while maintaining equivalent stretch and recovery properties. The assessment specifically compares fibres made with bio-derived and fossil-derived polytetramethylene ether glycol (PTMEG), a key component in spandex production. Alongside this commercial development, Lycra is working with textile recycling specialists to address one of the more difficult challenges facing the industry – the recovery of elastane from blended fabrics. Spandex is widely used in combination with polyester, nylon and other fibres to provide stretch and shape retention, but its presence complicates conventional textile recycling processes. Over the past few years, Lycra has collaborated with recycling companies worldwide to develop methods of separating spandex from other fibres in pre-consumer textile waste and processing the recovered material into new spandex fibres. articles.o: From mass production to precision cutting at Edwin Base
articles.s: Japanese denim manufacturer Akita Hose has transformed a former mass-production jeans factory into a specialist operation producing smaller batches of high-value garments, supported by automated cutting technology from Shima Seiki. Established in 1973, Akita Hose is part of the Edwin Group’s Japanes
articles.x: Japanese denim manufacturer Akita Hose has transformed a former mass-production jeans factory into a specialist operation producing smaller batches of high-value garments, supported by automated cutting technology from Shima Seiki. Established in 1973, Akita Hose is part of the Edwin Group’s Japanese manufacturing operations and previously employed around 100 people producing approximately 3,000 pairs of jeans a day. Today, its workforce has been reduced to around 30, while production has shifted almost entirely from jeans to more complex garments such as denim jackets. The factory now handles orders as small as 50-100 garments for brands including Edwin, Lee, Wrangler and Something, as well as jackets destined for overseas markets. The transformation culminated in October 2024, when equipment previously distributed across three buildings was consolidated into a single facility and the operation was relaunched as Edwin Base. P-CAM R Central to the reorganisation was the replacement of two ageing industrial cutting machines with a single, more compact Shima Seiki P-CAM R automated cutting system. The previous machines dated from the factory’s high-volume production era and occupied considerable floor space. Their age was also creating concerns about maintenance, safety and the availability of technical support. Akita Hose needed a replacement capable of handling denim accurately at relatively high speeds, while accommodating frequent changes in styles and production quantities. Compatibility with its existing CAD data was another important consideration. articles.x: The country’s largest textile festival, ‘Textile Fest Bangladesh 1.0’, has been held for the first time at the campus of the National Institute of Textile Engineering and Research (NITER) in Savar. Organized by the NITER Textile Club, the event aimed to bring textile and apparel students, industry representatives, and corporate leaders together on one platform. On the first day of the two-day event, more than 3,000 students from universities and institutions across the country and over 150 industry and corporate representatives took part. The festival focused on the sector’s potential, innovation, careers, and industry-academia linkage. Dewan Mohammad Salahuddin, Member of Parliament for Dhaka-19, attended as chief guest. Special guests included Brigadier General S M Zahid Hasan, Chairman of the Bangladesh Textile Mills Corporation (BTMC), among others. A key attraction was the series of career seminars and talk shows, where experienced professionals discussed the industry’s current state, opportunities, and career paths with students. A job fair and career networking sessions gave participants direct access to company representatives. To showcase young people’s creativity and skills, the festival featured a textile and apparel exhibition and a fashion show. Competitions included TexOlympiad, TexTech Hackathon, a 180-Second Innovative Pitch, Mock Interview, and Photography, with a total prize pool of BDT 2.5 lakh. The festival closes with a mega live concert and stand-up comedy, along with a raffle draw for visitors. As the first event of the NITER Textile Club, the festival has generated strong interest among students and textile stakeholders. articles.x: The textile industry is entering a groundbreaking era. Manufacturers face rising energy prices, growing sustainability demands, increasing labor shortages, and an unprecedented need for flexibility. For a globally active textile industry, where competitiveness is closely linked to production efficiency and cost leadership, this means that technology is no longer merely a means of improving operational processes – it is increasingly becoming a strategic differentiator. Against this backdrop, Barmag will present a innovation portfolio at India ITME that goes far beyond incremental machine upgrades. From December 4 to 9, 2026, Barmag’s experts will be presenting next-generation spinning concepts, smart factory platforms, and groundbreaking technologies for filament, staple fibers and nonwovens at their booth C15 in Hall 10 at India Expo Centre & Mart in Greater Noida, Uttar Pradesh, India. In doing so, the company is laying the foundation for what it calls “A New Era” of textile production. At the center of this transformation stands one development in particular: Barmag POY 2.0. André Wissenberg, Head of Marketing, Corporate Communications and Public Affairs at Barmag Every few years, an innovation emerges that fundamentally changes how an industry thinks about production. Barmag believes POY 2.0 represents exactly such a moment. The new spinning concept is the result of a complete re-evaluation of the entire POY process chain, from spinning and quenching to winding, parallel with a digital process control. Rather than improving isolated components, engineers reimagined the interaction between all process steps. Sans will operate alongside Spinnere as a sister company within Reshoring Textiles, and industry veteran John Garner has been named its
articles.x: STONEVILLE, N.C. — October 8, 2026 — Reshoring Textiles has acquired Sans Technical Fibers, an American producer of high tenacity LDI nylon 6.6 and polyester yarns. Sans will operate alongside Spinnere as a sister company within Reshoring Textiles, and industry veteran John Garner has been named its CEO. Robert Antoshak has been named Chief Marketing Officer of Reshoring Textiles. The acquisition adds domestic filament production for technical and specialty uses, including sewing thread and industrial textiles, giving Reshoring more to offer manufacturers in apparel and industrial markets. “Reshoring is dedicated to helping American textile manufacturing grow,” said Josh Nieuwsma, CEO of Reshoring Textiles. “Customers need reliable long-term domestic sources of the raw materials their products require. Sans gives us an established operation with deep experience in specialty nylon and polyester. Alongside Spinnere, it will help us supply more of those needs from U.S. facilities, and support manufacturers and startups looking to grow and build their businesses here.” Based in Stoneville, North Carolina, Sans has supplied high tenacity filaments for more than two decades. Its nylon yarns range from ultrafine to heavier deniers and offer UV stabilization and favorable dyeing characteristics. The company expanded into polyester in 2017, with new production equipment entering service in 2018 and in 2024. Sans now offers polyester yarns from fine deniers to heavy denier industrial. With new extrusion equipment on its way, Sans will be able to offer significantly more and different polymers to its customers. articles.x: Kornit Digital Ltd., a global pioneer in on-demand digital fashion and textile production, will showcase the possibilities of digital, on-demand production at PERFORMANCE DAYS 2026, October 13–14 at Messe München, Hall 6, Booth E08. Under the theme “Growth at the speed of demand,” Kornit Digital will demonstrate how digital production can combine design freedom, durability and production flexibility across textile, leather and footwear applications. Together with colortex, Kornit will present a range of real-world applications, including printed leather and footwear, giving visitors the opportunity to see the quality and creative possibilities of digital production firsthand. The applications on display will demonstrate high-definition digital printing across detailed designs, gradients and vibrant colors, alongside custom pattern mapping for individual shoe silhouettes. Visitors will also be able to explore Kornit DuraTech and its possibilities for durable digital applications. “PERFORMANCE DAYS is an opportunity to show what digital production can make possible for performance applications,” said Guy Yaniv, President Kornit Digital Europe. “We’re looking forward to meeting with brands, designers and producers in Munich and demonstrating how on-demand production can bring together creativity, durability and flexibility.” Kornit’s presence at the show will also highlight its broader vision for digital, on-demand production: removing overproduction and manufacturing digitally, in real time. Now operating at Long John Group’s plant in Indonesia, the machine employs th
articles.x: The growing sophistication of engineered textile structures for athletic footwear is being taken a step further with the first industrial installation of Karl Mayer’s new RDJ 7/3 jacquard double needle bar raschel machine. Now operating at Long John Group’s plant in Indonesia, the machine employs three wireless jacquard bars to enable different structures, functional zones and design effects to be positioned within individual footwear fabrics. This allows manufacturers to move beyond uniform textile constructions and engineer different properties into specific areas of a shoe upper, while also introducing complex patterns and three-dimensional effects during fabric production. Among the possibilities are larger and more precisely formed openings, integrated functional and design zones, two-colour jacquard effects and three-dimensional embossed surfaces. The first machine was officially inaugurated at Long John’s Indonesian plant in August in the presence of representatives from international athletic footwear brands and Karl Mayer. Long John celebrates the commissioning of the new RDJ 7/3. © Karl Mayer Taiwan-headquartered Long John is a major supplier of textiles to the global athletic footwear industry, with manufacturing operations in Taiwan, China, Vietnam and Indonesia and a sales office in the USA. Its vertically integrated production encompasses spinning, weaving, knitting, warp knitting, dyeing and finishing, with warp knitting used for open-structure stretch fabrics for shoe uppers and linings as well as spacer fabrics with plain and jacquard-patterned mesh surfaces. articles.x: Swedish textile machinery companies are accelerating innovation ahead of ITMA Asia + CITME 2026. Their latest technologies focus on automation, recycling, lower resource use, and better production control. Courtesy: Collected The exhibition will run from Nov. 20 to 24 at the National Exhibition and Convention Center in Shanghai. More than 1,800 companies have applied to exhibit, with nearly 90% of applicants originating from China. The show will also place a stronger emphasis on recycling, automation, digital platforms, and traceability. This makes Shanghai an essential proving ground for the next wave of textile machinery investment across Asia. Members of the Textile Machinery Association of Sweden (TMAS) have introduced several groundbreaking technologies throughout 2026. ACG Kinna has expanded its facility in Skene by 1,000 square meters to support soaring global demand for automated textile and finished-product production systems. Imogo has opened a new showroom, test center, and production facility. Its Dye-Max spray dyeing system processes about 3 tons of fabric per day while using as little as 0.7 liters of dye liquor per kilogram of fabric. This directly targets one of the industry's biggest resource challenges by drastically reducing water, energy, chemical consumption, and wastewater generation. ReSpin implements a different circular approach through its RespinJenny technology. The system mechanically converts textile waste into high-grade fibers for new yarn production and is currently being installed at Sweden’s first industrial spinning mill dedicated entirely to recycled textile fibers. articles.x: Bangladesh’s garment manufacturers’ association has urged the World Bank to expand funding and the scope of a water security programme to help the country’s apparel industry adopt sustainable water management technologies. The call came at a high-level meeting on Wednesday between Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BGMEA) President Mahmud Hasan Khan and a World Bank delegation led by Mara K. Warwick, Regional Director for Sustainable Development in South Asia, at the BGMEA complex in Uttara, Dhaka. BGMEA Director Dr. Md. Hasib Uddin also attended the meeting. The World Bank delegation included Lead Water Specialist David Melcom Lord, Senior Water Supply and Sanitation Specialist Rokeya Ahmed, Water Specialist Md. Mahadi Hasan and Environmental Specialist Bushra Nishat. Khan said water management was no longer only an environmental issue but was directly linked to Bangladesh’s international trade and global competitiveness. International buyers, particularly European brands, are increasingly looking for data on water consumption reduction, wastewater treatment and water recycling at different stages of garment production, he said. “There is no alternative to adopting modern water-efficient technologies, both to protect Dhaka’s rivers and groundwater levels and to maintain access to export markets,” Khan said, according to the statement. The meeting reviewed the World Bank-supported Dhaka Water Security and Resilience Program (D-Water) and a $5 million Viability Gap Funding ( VGF ) pilot project under the programme. BGMEA had initially proposed a list of 31 factories for the project, from which the World Bank will begin work with eight factories. articles.o: High fruit yields with 3D fabric
articles.s: A new knitted textile developed at North Carolina State University and used to cover strawberry plants has more than tripled strawberry yields in tunnel field tests – without negatively impacting plant health. The technology could also significantly reduce water and pesticide usage in strawberry fie
articles.x: A new knitted textile developed at North Carolina State University and used to cover strawberry plants has more than tripled strawberry yields in tunnel field tests – without negatively impacting plant health. The technology could also significantly reduce water and pesticide usage in strawberry fields. The cover, known as Plant Armor, is a carefully designed fabric that is draped over strawberry plants. The material’s three-dimensional structure prevents insects from reaching the plants beneath, but its multiple layers allow sunlight, rain and airflow to reach the plant. Tunnel field tests found that Plant Armor increased strawberry yields by as much as 3.56 times, without negatively impacting relative humidity or light access. “To produce fruit, plants need sunlight,” said Gabriel Olawuyi, a graduate research assistant at NC State and lead author of a paper on Plant Armor. “We expected that Plant Armor’s seemingly opaque fabric would lead to an increase in vegetative biomass at the expense of fruiting, because reduced sunlight would trigger a ‘shade-avoidance’ response, making the plant divert energy toward stem and leaf growth rather than fruit production. However, we found the fabric did not impede access to light at all, and fruit production increased significantly.” Growing degree days Plant Armor also provided a consistent warming effect over the three seasons that the plant grows, which Olawuyi said helped the bushes reach the fruiting stage earlier than those without the cover. “Plants require a certain amount of accumulated heat, calculated as ‘growing degree-days’, to progress through developmental stages including fruiting. articles.s: The newly approved Institute of Textile Professional Development can do what a garment-export economy has never managed to do: produce the engineers who start medical, geo, aerospace, and electronic t...
articles.x: The newly approved Institute of Textile Professional Development can do what a garment-export economy has never managed to do: produce the engineers who start medical, geo, aerospace, and electronic textile businesses. For four decades, Bangladesh has competed on volume. Readymade garments earned USD 39.35 billion in FY2024-25, according to Export Promotion Bureau data, about four-fifths of the country's USD 48.28 billion merchandise exports. Few countries have built so much export capacity so fast. But in the faster-growing, higher-margin market for technical textiles, Bangladesh is almost invisible. A GIZ feasibility study released with BGMEA in 2021 put the country's share of a global technical textile market worth about USD 180 billion at under half a percent. That is the same country that accounts for more than 6 percent of the world's apparel trade. The recent approval of the Institute of Textile Professional Development (ITPD) at the Bangladesh University of Textiles (BUTEX) is a chance to close that gap. How it is used matters. If ITPD becomes another provider of short courses in merchandising and compliance, it will reinforce the model we already have. If it is designed as a launch pad for advanced textiles, it could become the place where Bangladesh's next export industries are first imagined, tested, and staffed. The constraint is people, not machines The case for ITPD starts with a diagnosis. The GIZ study named five barriers holding back Bangladeshi technical textiles: lack of awareness of market requirements, inadequate technical expertise, difficulty in sourcing high-performance raw materials, compliance and certification requirements, and the need for capital investment. Even before tariffs made relying heavily on China too expensive, experienced buyers knew that sourcing from only one country is risky. Most compan
articles.x: Author: Stanislas Teisseire, VP of Operations for Inspections & Audits at QIMA For years, the main supply chain story has been China +1, or China + many. Even before tariffs made relying heavily on China too expensive, experienced buyers knew that sourcing from only one country is risky. Most companies now build diversification into their plans, and many are acting on it. Our 2026 Sourcing Survey found 43% of businesses with international sourcing networks changed the countries they sourced from last year. Among US businesses, it was two in three. A lot of investment went into building alternatives. Not many people asked what happens when those alternatives come under pressure too. In our Q3 Barometer , published in July, we saw the first sign of that. Two months later, here’s what has changed and what hasn’t. What we’re seeing In Q2, China represented 35% of our inspections and audits for North American buyers, the highest level in six quarters, while Southeast Asia fell back to pre-2025 levels. The same pattern was visible among EU buyers, but more pronounced. Demand for Southeast Asian inspections weakened every month of the quarter, from 14% growth in April to a 5% decline by June. July, August and early September data suggests this was not a one-time blip. For North American buyers, China’s share kept rising while Southeast Asia’s continued to fall. Likely trigger for the Q2 shift: capacity When the Hormuz crisis cut fuel supply, factories across Southeast and South Asia struggled to keep up. Buyers with peak-season orders had two options. They could accept the delay and risk missing delivery dates, or move some orders to a supplier who could take them. articles.o: Evidence defines next fibre generation
articles.s: Good Earth Cotton (GEC) is advocating a move from broad environmental claims towards measurable evidence as new European Union rules raise the requirements for substantiating sustainability claims. articles.x: Good Earth Cotton (GEC) is advocating a move from broad environmental claims towards measurable evidence as new European Union rules raise the requirements for substantiating sustainability claims. From 27 September, measures implementing the EU’s Empowering Consumers for the Green Transition Directive (EmpCo) began to apply across EU Member States. The rules restrict generic environmental claims that cannot demonstrate recognised environmental performance and prohibit sustainability labels that are not based on approved certification schemes or established by public authorities. The regulatory changes come amid concerns about the credibility of environmental marketing. European Commission analysis has found that 53% of green claims examined in the EU market provide vague, misleading or unfounded information, while 40% have no supporting evidence and half of green labels offer weak or non-existent verification. For Good Earth Cotton, the shift reflects an approach it has been developing over eight years, moving away from practice-based assumptions towards measured outcomes, primary farm-level data, independent verification and fibre physically verified at source. The Australian cotton producer is also deliberately moving beyond the terminology of regenerative agriculture, arguing that describing farming practices does not necessarily demonstrate their environmental outcomes. “For years, we used the language of regenerative agriculture because it helped describe the direction farming needed to take. But a practice is an intervention; an outcome is the evidence,” said Danielle Statham, founder and owner of Good Earth Cotton and FibreTrace. “The next generation of fibre will not be defined by the practice it claims. articles.s: 무신사가 운영하는 패션·라이프스타일 플랫폼 '29CM'가 한글날 제정 100주년을 맞아 국립한글박물관이 소장한 보물인 시조집 '청구영언'을 현대적인 라이프스타일 상품으로 재해석한다.'모든 마음곁에, 한글' 기획전은 29CM 입점 브랜드 13개와 공모전 당선 브랜드 8개 등 총 21개 브랜드가 참여하며 오는 29일부터 서울 성수동에서 협업 상품과 콘텐츠를 선보이는 전시를 연다. 29CM는 국립한글박물관·세종시문화관광재단과 함께 한글문화상품을 개발하고 유통·판매까지 지원하는 프로젝트 ‘모든 마음 곁에, 한글’을 진행한다고 8일 밝혔다.

articles.o: Syre Appoints Tim King As CEO
articles.s: STOCKHOLM, Sweden — October 7, 2026 — Syre, the textile impact company on a mission to scale textile-to-textile recycling, today announces the appointment of Tim King as its new Chief Executive Officer. Tim King, currently Syre’s Chief Operating Officer, will with his deep experience of Syre’s indus
articles.x: STOCKHOLM, Sweden — October 7, 2026 — Syre, the textile impact company on a mission to scale textile-to-textile recycling, today announces the appointment of Tim King as its new Chief Executive Officer. Tim King, currently Syre’s Chief Operating Officer, will with his deep experience of Syre’s industrial development, operational leadership, and strategic priorities, lead the company through its next phase of advancement. Tim King Founded in 2023, Syre has established a strong business platform with the industry’s largest commercial agreements, leading industrial partnerships, and a committed investor base. Next step is all about building on that momentum. “We have built a strong foundation, and our focus is to continue turning that into an industrial reality” says Tim King, new CEO of Syre. “I am excited to take on this responsibility and privileged to be working with an exceptional team, supportive customers, and leading partners. Syre’s mission is important for the planet, and we are committed to navigating a challenging market to make circularity a reality at scale”. Tim King has been leading Syre’s industrial development and the execution of strategy since joining Syre in its early days. articles.o: Yarn Expo Spring eyes further growth
articles.s: Yarn Expo Spring will return to the National Exhibition and Convention Center in Shanghai from 10–12 March 2027, bringing together international yarn and fibre suppliers, manufacturers and buyers to explore new materials, technologies and sourcing opportunities. The upcoming exhibition follows a rec
articles.x: Yarn Expo Spring will return to the National Exhibition and Convention Center in Shanghai from 10–12 March 2027, bringing together international yarn and fibre suppliers, manufacturers and buyers to explore new materials, technologies and sourcing opportunities. The upcoming exhibition follows a record-breaking edition in March 2026, when more than 600 exhibitors from 12 countries and regions connected with over 25,000 visitors from 113 countries and regions. The strong participation reinforced the event’s position as an important international platform for yarn and fibre sourcing, innovation and industry exchange. Organised by Messe Frankfurt (HK) Ltd and the Sub-Council of Textile Industry, CCPIT, the exhibition will once again take place alongside Intertextile Shanghai Apparel Fabrics – Spring Edition, Intertextile Shanghai Home Textiles – Spring Edition, CHIC and PH Value, creating opportunities for businesses across the textile and apparel supply chain. The fair provided an exceptional platform for connecting with the global textile community Wilmet Shea, General Manager of Messe Frankfurt (HK) Ltd, said: “In a changing economic landscape, last year’s record participation showed how important it is for the yarn and fibre industry to meet in Shanghai, exchange ideas and understand what the market needs next.” She added that suppliers would have opportunities to present their latest developments to buyers from apparel, home textiles, knitting and related sectors, while discussing requirements and establishing long-term business relationships. The exhibition comes as the global yarn, fibre and thread market continues to evolve, with research forecasting its value to reach US$182.7 billion by 2032. articles.o: Technical textiles market set to reach $318.7 billion by 2031
articles.s: The global technical textiles market is entering a steady expansion phase as industries demand advanced, high-performance materials. Market research from BCC Research shows the sector was valued at $2...
articles.x: The global technical textiles market is entering a steady expansion phase as industries demand advanced, high-performance materials. Market research from BCC Research shows the sector was valued at $228.7 billion in 2025 and is projected to hit $318.7 billion by 2031, growing at a compound annual growth rate of 5.9% from 2026 to 2031. Figure: Technical textiles market set to reach $318.7 billion by 2031. Courtesy: Collected This growth reflects a major shift toward engineering fabrics for specific industrial needs rather than conventional apparel, leveraging strength, low weight, and durability. Asia-Pacific anchors this expansion, currently holding 38.1% of the global market with its massive manufacturing base and competitive costs. Government initiatives like India's Production Linked Incentive scheme are accelerating this momentum by approving around $1.2 to $1.3 billion to build domestic capacity. Healthcare is also fueling demand through rising medical spending and an increase in specialized surgical procedures. Medtech innovations now span advanced wound care, biocompatible implants, and wearable health-monitoring devices that require antimicrobial performance. At the same time, cutting-edge technologies are expanding capabilities, with nanotechnology projected to grow at a 7.3% compound annual growth rate and 3D weaving expected to grow at 6.7% through 2031. Ultimately, these advancements are paving the way for self-decontaminating fabrics through metal-organic framework materials and smart e-textiles. The market outlook proves that technical textiles are becoming deeply intertwined with broader industrial innovation, where long-term success relies heavily on developing specialized materials.

articles.o: Design In Bangladesh Week – Bangladesh’s Next Design Generation Takes Centre Stage With 100 Designers Runway
articles.s: “3D in BD — Discovered, Designed & Developed in Bangladesh” Design in Bangladesh Week 2026 officially opened at the United Convention Centre, Dhaka, bringing 100 Bangladeshi designers onto one collective platform and runway to showcase the country’s growing capacity in design, creativity, craftsmans
articles.x: “3D in BD — Discovered, Designed & Developed in Bangladesh” Design in Bangladesh Week 2026 officially opened at the United Convention Centre, Dhaka, bringing 100 Bangladeshi designers onto one collective platform and runway to showcase the country’s growing capacity in design, creativity, craftsmanship, innovation, product development and creative entrepreneurship. The inaugural ceremony was graced by Dr. S. M. Ziauddin Hyder, Special Assistant to the Honorable Prime Minister on Health Affairs, with the status of State Minister, as Chief Guest. In his address, Dr. Hyder welcomed the participation and work of 100 designers and encouraged the Design in Bangladesh platform to continue developing as a collaborative creative hub connecting talent, heritage, enterprise, industry and opportunity. He also highlighted the relevance of “One Village, One Product” and the 3D in BD vision — Discovered, Designed & Developed in Bangladesh — as approaches that can help create greater value from Bangladesh’s own creative capacity. Design in Bangladesh Week positions design as an important contributor to Bangladesh’s creative economy — connecting original ideas and cultural knowledge with research, product development, manufacturing, branding, entrepreneurship and market access. The initiative seeks to complement the country’s wider ambition to strengthen innovation, value addition and creative enterprise by building stronger connections between creative talent and Bangladesh’s established production ecosystem. 100 DESIGNERS — ONE PLATFORM At the heart of the opening was the 100 Designers Showcase and Runway, bringing together 100 creative voices on one shared platform. articles.o: AeoniQ closes in on first commercial volumes
articles.s: Swiss cellulosic filament developer AeoniQ expects to begin supplying initial market volumes in early 2027 as it makes the transition from pilot development towards industrial production in Portugal. Returning to the Dornbirn Global Fiber Congress in Austria from September 16-18, five years after it
articles.x: Swiss cellulosic filament developer AeoniQ expects to begin supplying initial market volumes in early 2027 as it makes the transition from pilot development towards industrial production in Portugal. Returning to the Dornbirn Global Fiber Congress in Austria from September 16-18, five years after its technology was first presented at the event’s Innovation Days, AeoniQ outlined the progress made towards commercialising a biodegradable filament designed as an alternative to polyester and nylon. The technology converts cellulose into continuous filament yarn which can subsequently be texturised, dyed, woven or knitted using conventional textile machinery. Its feedstock flexibility is also central to the longer-term proposition. In addition to wood-derived cellulose, AeoniQ is exploring recycled textile cellulose, agricultural residues and bacterial cellulose as potential raw material sources. The major change since its first Dornbirn appearance has been the involvement of Portuguese pulp and forest products group Altri, which acquired a 58.7% interest in AeoniQ Holding in 2025. A pre-industrial production unit is now being established in Portugal to support product development and initial market programmes, while a larger industrial plant is planned at Altri’s Caima pulp operation in Constância. The first industrial unit is planned with annual capacity of around 1,750 tons. Altri has indicated that construction is scheduled to start in 2027, with the full project targeted to start production in 2028. AeoniQ global director of business development Carmen Danner said that initial market volumes from the pre-industrial operation are expected from January 2027. articles.x: Bangladesh is seeking to expand its readymade garment exports to Indonesia as the two countries revisit stalled trade negotiations, highlighting a largely untapped apparel market despite their position as competitors in the global textile and clothing industry. Figure: Khandakar Abdul Muktadir, Commerce Minister, made a courtesy call on a meeting with Mohammad Anis Matta, Deputy Foreign Minister, Indonesia, at the Commerce Ministry on 7th Oct. Courtesy:Collected The push gained fresh momentum on October 7 during a high-level meeting at the Commerce Ministry, where Khandakar Abdul Muktadir, Minister, Ministry of Commerce, discussed bilateral trade with visiting Mohammad Anis Matta, Deputy Foreign Minister, Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Indonesia. The trade minister noted that bilateral commerce could rise significantly if market-access barriers are removed. Bangladesh currently exports about $56 million worth of goods to Indonesia while importing around $3.5 billion, leaving a substantial trade deficit. For Bangladesh's apparel sector, Indonesia remains a relatively small destination. Yet according to UN Comtrade data, the latest product-level figures show a meaningful existing market. Indonesia imported $48.41 million worth of apparel from Bangladesh in 2025, comprising $26.26 million in non-knit garments and $22.15 million in knitwear. According to UN Comtrade data, the product mix points to opportunities across several categories. Indonesia imported $8.44 million of Bangladeshi T-shirts, $4.63 million of sweaters, pullovers and vests, and $2.07 million of men's knitted shirts in 2025. articles.o: Chloris Strengthens Commercial Readiness Of Claessen Blue™ Through An Integrated Verification Framework
articles.s: WEST JORDAN, Utah — September 23, 2026 — Chloris is strengthening the commercial readiness of its flagship bio-based dye, Claessen Blue™, through a growing international verification framework covering bio-based origin, traceability, responsible chemical management and textile application. Rather th
articles.x: WEST JORDAN, Utah — September 23, 2026 — Chloris is strengthening the commercial readiness of its flagship bio-based dye, Claessen Blue , through a growing international verification framework covering bio-based origin, traceability, responsible chemical management and textile application. Rather than treating individual certifications as standalone credentials, Chloris has organized them around the key questions brands, mills and manufacturers need to address when evaluating a new material. Bio-based Origin — USDA BioPreferred® and OK biobased provide independent verification of bio-based carbon content, supporting clear and credible renewable-material claims. Traceability — ISCC PLUS extends verification into renewable feedstocks and chain-of-custody traceability, connecting material sourcing with industrial production. Chemical Safety — ZDHC MRSL Level 3 and OEKO-TEX® support chemical management and textile chemical safety requirements relevant to global sourcing and manufacturing. Application Approval — GOTS Approved Input supports the use of Claessen Blue within GOTS-certified textile processing, subject to applicable requirements. In parallel, Chloris uses Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) as a separate layer of quantitative environmental evidence. While certification verifies attributes, processes and compliance pathways, LCA evaluates environmental performance within defined life-cycle boundaries. This provides brands and supply-chain partners with measurable evidence across relevant environmental indicators and helps translate sustainability from a material claim into data that can inform sourcing and ESG decisions. articles.s: ISTANBUL — September 29, 2026 — BTU-TECH has announced the launch of BTU-GMAX, a next-generation multiaxial production line developed to deliver the flexibility of advanced multiaxial platforms at an investment level comparable to conventional entry-level machines. With its fully programmable 0°–180
articles.x: ISTANBUL — September 29, 2026 — BTU-TECH has announced the launch of BTU-GMAX, a next-generation multiaxial production line developed to deliver the flexibility of advanced multiaxial platforms at an investment level comparable to conventional entry-level machines. With its fully programmable 0°–180° weft-angle capability, BTU-GMAX enables manufacturers to produce a wide range of multiaxial fabric architectures, mainly glass, aramid, carbon fabrics for composite industries, on a single platform. Operators can select new production angles directly from the interface without lengthy mechanical adjustments. One of the system’s key innovations is its ability to calculate weft paths directly on the industrial motion controller in real time. New production parameters can be applied within seconds without external computer software, CAM table generation, or a machine restart. This significantly reduces setup times and increases machine availability. BTU-GMAX uses a heavy-duty trigger-belt-driven carrier architecture instead of conventional rack-driven systems. The design reduces wear and noise, improves positional accuracy, prevents jump-offs at high speed, and simplifies maintenance. Built on BTU-TECH’s proprietary PC-free automation platform, the system combines real-time weft-curve calculation, automatic carrier synchronization at every production start, and electronic collision prevention. Integrated laser safety barriers dynamically monitor operator positioning, while Industry 4.0 connectivity allows production data and machine parameters to be transferred to ERP systems and factory networks via industrial communication protocols. articles.o: Recover recycled fibre blend eliminates overdyeing
articles.s: MADRID – Recover has launched a new range of cotton-polyester fibre blends made from recycled materials which it says can eliminate the need for downstream overdyeing. The Spanish textile recycler’s product range, Recover One, combines its mechanically recycled cotton with colour-matched, dope-dyed
articles.x: MADRID – Recover has launched a new range of cotton-polyester fibre blends made from recycled materials which it says can eliminate the need for downstream overdyeing. The Spanish textile recycler’s product range, Recover One, combines its mechanically recycled cotton with colour-matched, dope-dyed recycled polyester to create ready-to-spin blends for textile manufacturers. The technology uses an intimate blending process that harmonises the colours of recycled textile feedstocks with recycled polyester fibres. According to Recover, this produces a consistent material without the need for additional overdyeing, potentially reducing processing time, water consumption and production costs. The blends are available in different cotton-polyester ratios, depending on the intended application. They can be supplied either as fibre or finished fabric through Recover’s supply chain partners. Applications include single jersey, French terry and fleece fabrics, with solid, heather and mélange colour options available. “With Recover One, we are making it easier for brands and manufacturers to use recycled materials at scale,” said Enes Adak, co-CEO and chief product officer at Recover. “By combining our recycled cotton with recycled polyester, we deliver a consistent blend that simplifies production and helps reduce costs. This brings sustainability and business value together.” Recover says the product builds on the environmental advantages of its recycled cotton, while delivering additional savings by removing the overdyeing stage. articles.o: Selenis acquires Polisan Hellas
articles.s: Selenis, the only specialty copolyester producer manufacturing in Europe, has acquired the production assets of Polisan Hellas in Greece for installation in Portugal. Including these assets, Selenis will operate more than 200,000 metric tons of annual installed specialty copolyester capacity by 2028
articles.x: Selenis, the only specialty copolyester producer manufacturing in Europe, has acquired the production assets of Polisan Hellas in Greece for installation in Portugal. Including these assets, Selenis will operate more than 200,000 metric tons of annual installed specialty copolyester capacity by 2028, across production sites in Portugal, Italy, Tunisia and the United States. The acquisition adds continuous polymerisation to a manufacturing base built on flexibility. Continuous production serves the high-volume markets, where standardisation, consistency and cost per ton matter, while batch production serves speciality and custom grades, where smaller volumes, fast changeovers and formulation depth are key. With both technologies now part of its manufacturing platform across four countries, Selenis can serve the full spectrum of the market, from high-volume applications to specialised grades, combining the scale and efficiency of continuous production with the flexibility of batch manufacturing. “We believe Europe needs a strong speciality materials manufacturing base and we are investing to build it,” said Duarte Matos Gil, CEO of Selenis. “When customers qualify our materials, they make a long-term commitment. Our responsibility is to invest ahead of their needs, to put more than one plant behind every grade and to give them a cost base that lets them compete. This acquisition puts industrial capacity behind that commitment, and further steps will follow.” Selenis will work with customers to qualify selected grades at more than one manufacturing site, so a converter can hold the same specification from two plants, with no dependency on a single line or region and with the flexibility to move volume between sites as demand and logistics change. articles.x: As textile fiber production volumes increase annually, and new and upcoming regulations in the EU and US reshape approaches to waste management, Reju is helping to accelerate the transition to textile-to-textile recycling through its innovative regeneration hubs, where textile waste is given a new life. Reju CEO Patrik Frisk shares his perspective on regionalization, investment in infrastructure, policy, and how collaboration and coordination are the key to building a more circular textile system. The theme of the 2026 Textile Exchange Conference is The Implementation Era—do you believe that our industry is at the point now where we are ready to begin implementing change at scale? Not yet actually. When it comes to dealing with all the regulation that’s on the horizon, transitioning from where we have been, and specifically, moving recycled polyester from using bottles to post-consumer textiles, we’re not there yet. The reason why Reju is here and has always been here is to deal with the problem of the creation of post-consumer textile waste. We’ve been doing that for a very long time, and now we are making sure that we’re compliant, and we’re helping the industry become compliant, with all the regulation that’s coming down the pipeline. It’s going to take time to prepare, not just for Reju, but also upstream, as there is a lot of work to do, such as organizing feedstock, aggregation, sorting, and the preparation of feedstock, to create the pipeline of the future. So, if you were to ask me: is it today? No. Is it tomorrow? Yes. In this interview, Liz Hershfield, […] The post Scaling Regenerative Cotton from Field to Suppl
articles.x: As certified cotton production continues to grow around the world, the industry is increasingly embedding traceability and environmental considerations into everyday production and supply-chain decisions. In this interview, Liz Hershfield, Executive Director of COTTON USA and Co-Director of the U.S. Cotton Trust Protocol, and Marjory Walker, Co-Director of the U.S. Cotton Trust Protocol, discuss what the 2026 Textile Exchange Conference theme, The Implementation Era, means in practice —from the growing scale of field-level data collection and the adoption of regenerative practices, to new approaches to physical verification and supply-chain transparency. Our conference theme this year is The Implementation Era, moving from ambition and commitments toward measurable action. What does that shift look like in practice across the US cotton industry? What steps are working particularly well and what challenges are you facing along the way? Liz Hershfield: The Implementation Era is about moving from pilots and proof points to programs that can operate at the scale needed by brands and retailers. Over the past several years, the industry has made continued progress in developing the frameworks, data, and verification systems needed to measure and demonstrate sustainability outcomes. Now, the focus is on expanding participation and embedding those efforts more deeply across the supply chain. What’s working is the growing alignment around data, transparency, and outcome-based approaches. articles.t: X-Pac, 범포 기술을 야외용 직물에 접목
articles.o: X-Pac takes sailcloth technology into outdoor fabrics
articles.s: Dimension-Polyant is extending the sailcloth-derived technology behind its X-Pac technical fabrics with a new family of lightweight laminates aimed at mountaineering, climbing, skiing and bikepacking equipment. The new X-Pac hyperTEC range will make its European debut at Performance Days in Munich f
articles.x: Dimension-Polyant is extending the sailcloth-derived technology behind its X-Pac technical fabrics with a new family of lightweight laminates aimed at mountaineering, climbing, skiing and bikepacking equipment. The new X-Pac hyperTEC range will make its European debut at Performance Days in Munich from October 13-14, where the company will show its first UX10 and UX20 sT constructions. The X-Pac fabrics originated from Dimension-Polyant’s experience in high-performance sailcloth, applying similar precision lamination techniques to fabrics. At the centre of the construction is a 100% Ultra-PE face fabric combined with X-Pac’s Ultra-PE X-Ply reinforcement. The laminate construction also provides inherent waterproofing. “Using advanced fibres allows us to produce laminates that are ultra-light and have a tremendous strength-to-weight ratio, while maintaining the durability and reliability that X-Pac is known for,” said Dimension-Polyant president Kenneth Madsen. Two versions will initially be highlighted in Munich. X-Pac hyperTEC UX10, available in translucent white, has been developed as the more versatile of the two, balancing low weight and durability for packs across a range of outdoor applications. UX20 sT, in black, places greater emphasis on strength and load-bearing performance for more highly stressed applications. The “sT” refers to a single polyester taffeta backing layer positioned behind the polyester film, improving handling and durability and giving the otherwise lightweight laminate a more opaque appearance. One of the first commercial adopters is Belgian bikepacking specialist Moga Bags, which is introducing products manufactured with hyperTEC fabrics. articles.t: Fashion for Good, 재활용 면 사용 확대를 위해 Cotton Reloop Matrix 출시
articles.o: Fashion for Good launches Cotton Reloop Matrix to scale recycled cotton use
articles.s: Fashion for Good has launched the Cotton Reloop Matrix Project to improve the use of mechanically recycled cotton in textile production. The project aims to connect the capabilities of cotton recycle...
articles.x: Fashion for Good has launched the Cotton Reloop Matrix Project to improve the use of mechanically recycled cotton in textile production. The project aims to connect the capabilities of cotton recyclers with the quality requirements of fashion brands. It will also address gaps in testing and data sharing across the supply chain. Major stakeholders, including Arvind, Bestseller, C&A, Interloop, Reformation, Shahi, and Uster, are taking part in the project. The initiative has two main tracks. The first will assess recycled cotton yarn performance for knit and woven fabrics. It will focus on whether the yarn is suitable for its intended use rather than comparing it directly with virgin cotton. The project will also explore performance levels beyond the current typical 10% recycled cotton blend limit. The second track will include trials to produce 10 demonstration fabrics and conduct five process-optimization trials. The findings will be published in an open-source Standard Operating Procedure (SOP). This will help standardize spinning parameters across different supply chains. The project aims to create clearer quality benchmarks and help overcome fiber degradation challenges. It could support wider and more commercial use of recycled cotton in the global textile industry.

articles.o: Empowering and Equipping Cotton Farmers with Regenerative Practices in Maharashtra
articles.s: Words by Zoë Goodhead, with photography by Abhishek Khedekar In villages in the Amravati region in Maharashtra, India, farmers are coming together to share knowledge and learn regenerative practices for […] The post Empowering and Equipping Cotton Farmers with Regenerative Practices in Maharashtra a
articles.x: Words by Zoë Goodhead, with photography by Abhishek Khedekar In villages in the Amravati region in Maharashtra, India, farmers are coming together to share knowledge and learn regenerative practices for their small-scale cotton farms. As the scheme grows, they are discovering that these practices can not only save them money, but also save their soil. At Nagpur airport, welcome signs declare it the City of Oranges, but driving through the Maharashtra landscape towards the Amravati region, it’s not just orange trees that can be seen growing in the fields, but cotton, with balls of white catching the light of the sun. The connection with this cotton is deeply felt by those who spend their days sowing, growing, and picking it. Madhuri Anil Dugane, from Kati, a small village in Amravati, describes her special relationship with the soil. “My connection with the soil feels like one between a mother and a daughter,” she explains in Marathi, the local language. “Unless you work hard at it, unless you love your mother, how can you expect to get anything out of it?” Madhuri has always lived in Kati, surrounded by cotton fields. She now lives with her husband and two children, farming cotton on her own land and also picking up shifts as a laborer on other nearby farms for extra income. Along with others in her village, she has recently signed up to CottonConnect’s REEL Regenerative program. CottonConnect works with local partner Apeksha Homoeo Society to roll out the program in villages across the region, working with around 4,500 farmers in just this area alone. This is just one of many projects for Apeksha, a local charitable organization ensuring the sustainable development of women, children, farmers, and landless communities. articles.o: Cotton remains vital to a changing global textile industry
articles.s: World Cotton Day 2026 is being observed on October 7, highlighting the continued importance of cotton to global agriculture, textile production, international trade and the livelihoods of millions of...
articles.x: World Cotton Day 2026 is being observed on October 7, highlighting the continued importance of cotton to global agriculture, textile production, international trade and the livelihoods of millions of people. The United Nations officially designated October 7 as World Cotton Day through a resolution adopted by the UN General Assembly on August 30, 2021. The initiative was originally proposed by four major African cotton-producing countries—Benin, Burkina Faso, Chad and Mali, collectively known as the Cotton-4. The day aims to raise global awareness of cotton’s contribution to economic development and highlight the challenges faced by farmers, producers, processors and workers across the cotton value chain. The Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO), International Trade Centre, UN Conference on Trade and Development and International Cotton Advisory Committee supported the initiative before its formal adoption by the UN. Cotton remains one of the world's most important natural fibers and a key raw material for the global textile and apparel industry. Around 80% of cotton is used for clothing, while another 15% is used for home textiles and other household products, according to FAO data. Beyond its role as a textile fiber, cotton is an important source of income for millions of farming households. Around 24 million producers are involved in cotton cultivation globally, while the wider sector supports more than 100 million families through farming, processing, manufacturing and trade. For many developing economies, cotton exports are also an important source of foreign exchange. As a result, changes in global cotton prices, production and demand can have a direct impact on farmers and national economies. Global cotton production remains substantial.

articles.t: 압소바, ‘마이멜로디’ 앞세워 신세계 하남 팝업
articles.o: 압소바, ‘마이멜로디’ 앞세워 신세계 하남 팝업
articles.s: 해피랜드 코퍼레이션(대표 임남희)이 전개하는 프랑스 프리미엄 유아동복 브랜드 ‘압소바’가 산리오캐릭터즈와 손잡고 오프라인 고객 접점 확대에 나선다. 압소바는 오는 10월 9일부터 22일까지 신세계 하남에서 팝업스토어를 열고 26FW 산리오캐릭터즈 협업 컬렉션을 선보인다.이번 팝업은 26FW 시즌 메인 캐릭터인 ‘마이멜로디’를 전면에 내세운다. 마이멜로디 특유의 사랑스러운 분위기에 압소바의 프렌치 감성을 접목한 가을·겨울 스타일을 비롯해 헬로키티, 폼폼푸린, 포차코 등 산리오캐릭터즈의 개성을 유아동 감성으로 풀어낸 다양한 제품을 한자

articles.t: 아넥스2027 “한국서 미래 산업용 부직포 소재 경쟁 펼친다”
articles.o: 아넥스2027 “한국서 미래 산업용 부직포 소재 경쟁 펼친다”
articles.s: 인공지능 시대, 산업 구조가 빠르게 재편되면서 부직포 산업의 경쟁 무대도 달라졌다. 과거 위생용품과 소비재 중심이던 부직포가 반도체 배터리 자동차 바이오헬스 항공우주 등 첨단 제조 산업에 고기능성 소재 영역으로 넓히면서 기능과 기술력이 새 경쟁력으로 떠오른다.이 같은 변화 속에 아시아 부직포 산업의 주요 전시회인 아넥스 2027이 내년 6월 서울에서 열린다. 2027년 6월 23일부터 25일까지 서울 코엑스 C홀과 D홀에서 열리는 이번 전시회는 부직포 원료와 원단부터 제조설비 산업용 응용제품 완제품과 관련 서비스까지 산업 전반을 아

articles.s: 글로벌 패션·섬유 수출기업 신원(대표 박정주)이 13년간 축적한 웨이더(Wader) 생산 기술을 기반으로 고기능성 테크니컬 웨어 사업 경쟁력을 강화한다. 방수·투습 소재 가공과 심실링 등 고난도 제조 기술을 고도화하고 드라이수트(Drysuit) 등으로 생산 영역을 넓혀 글로벌 아웃도어·퍼포먼스 브랜드의 OEM·ODM 수요를 공략한다.신원은 2013년 웨이더 생산을 시작한 이후 약 13년간 고기능성 방수 의류 제조 역량을 축적해왔다. 웨이더는 강이나 호수, 바다 등에서 낚시와 수상 활동을 할 때 착용하는 기능성 방수 의류다. 장시간

articles.s: By K. articles.x: By K. Gopalakrishnan As textile manufacturers move towards connected, data-driven production, EAS is bringing together ERP, MES, industrial automation, machinery connectivity and automated dosing systems to create a more integrated Industry 4.0 environment. Francesc López, Area Manager – India & Asia, EAS, outlines how the company is helping mills improve visibility, traceability, productivity and resource efficiency, with India emerging as a strategic market for its next phase of growth. For more than three decades, EAS – Escarré Automatización y Servicios has focused on applying automation and digital technologies to solve practical challenges in textile manufacturing. Founded in Barcelona in 1991, the company has evolved from a specialist in industrial automation and process control into a technology partner offering production-management software, MES solutions, data acquisition, industrial connectivity, automated chemical and dye preparation systems and specialised machinery. Its solutions today operate in more than 35 countries. Francesc López, Area Manager – India & Asia, EAS According to Francesc López, Area Manager – India & Asia, EAS, the company’s evolution has been driven by a simple principle: technology must serve the production process. This philosophy is particularly relevant as textile manufacturers seek to connect increasingly complex machinery environments while gaining greater control over productivity, quality, traceability and resource consumption. From Automation Supplier to Digital Ecosystem EAS brings together three areas that are often managed independently: software, industrial automation and machinery. articles.o: 3D in Bangladesh calls at the inaugural ceremony of DIBW 100 designers’ runway
articles.s: “3D in BD — Discovered, Designed & Developed in Bangladesh” Design in Bangladesh Week 2026 officially opened at the United Convention Centre, Dhaka, bringing 100 Bangladeshi designers onto one collective platform and runway to showcase the country’s growing capacity in design, creativity, craftsmans
articles.x: “3D in BD — Discovered, Designed & Developed in Bangladesh” Design in Bangladesh Week 2026 officially opened at the United Convention Centre, Dhaka, bringing 100 Bangladeshi designers onto one collective platform and runway to showcase the country’s growing capacity in design, creativity, craftsmanship, innovation, product development and creative entrepreneurship. The inaugural ceremony was graced by Dr. S. M. Ziauddin Hyder, Special Assistant to the Honorable Prime Minister on Health Affairs, with the status of State Minister, as Chief Guest. In his address, Dr. Hyder welcomed the participation and work of 100 designers and encouraged the Design in Bangladesh platform to continue developing as a collaborative creative hub connecting talent, heritage, enterprise, industry and opportunity. He also highlighted the relevance of “One Village, One Product” and the 3D in BD vision — Discovered, Designed & Developed in Bangladesh — as approaches that can help create greater value from Bangladesh’s own creative capacity. Design in Bangladesh Week positions design as an important contributor to Bangladesh’s creative economy — connecting original ideas and cultural knowledge with research, product development, manufacturing, branding, entrepreneurship and market access. The initiative seeks to complement the country’s wider ambition to strengthen innovation, value addition and creative enterprise by building stronger connections between creative talent and Bangladesh’s established production ecosystem. 100 DESIGNERS — ONE PLATFORM At the heart of the opening was the 100 Designers Showcase and Runway, bringing together 100 creative voices on one shared platform. articles.o: EverDye gains industry recognition
articles.s: French textile technology start-up EverDye has secured ZDHC certification and been selected for a CEMATEX Start-Up Grant, providing further industry recognition for its low-energy, bio-based approach to textile dyeing. Founded in 2021, EverDye has developed a pigment dyeing process designed to opera
articles.x: French textile technology start-up EverDye has secured ZDHC certification and been selected for a CEMATEX Start-Up Grant, providing further industry recognition for its low-energy, bio-based approach to textile dyeing. Founded in 2021, EverDye has developed a pigment dyeing process designed to operate at room temperature while consuming significantly less energy than conventional textile dyeing. The company says its technology can reduce CO2 emissions by 90% and cut energy consumption eightfold compared with traditional processes. The company is led by founder Dr Amira Erokh, a materials chemist who has developed an approach based on bio-based pigments and green chemistry. EverDye’s ZDHC certification confirms that its chemical product complies with the ZDHC Manufacturing Restricted Substances List (MRSL). The Zero Discharge of Hazardous Chemicals initiative works globally to support the elimination of hazardous chemicals from textile, apparel, leather and footwear manufacturing. According to EverDye, the certification validates its approach to using bio-based pigments while limiting chemical residues during processing. “The ZDHC certification confirms that it is possible to transform the dyeing process without compromising on chemical control,” said Erokh. “At EverDye, we want to drive a profound shift in the industry towards a more responsible model, starting with dyeing. This recognition gives brands and manufacturers a concrete guarantee for partnering with us.” EverDye’s technology uses a chemistry based on affinity, with pigments rapidly anchoring to fibres. This enables dyeing to take place quickly and at room temperature, with the company claiming reduced chemical residues, lower water and energy consumption and rich, durable colours. articles.x: TEXAS – A major new research project has produced the first harmonised global picture of textile recycling potential. The work estimates that between three and five million tonnes of recycled spinnable fibre could be produced annually by 2030. The new Textile-to-Textile Recycled Fiber report was published by Textile Exchange in collaboration with Reverse Resources, Fashion for Good and TEXroad. articles.o: Global Cotton Consumption Trending Up, Production Trending Down for 2026/27 Season
articles.s: Global cotton consumption is projected to exceed production in the 2026/27 season as production, trade, and ending stocks decline modestly, according to the latest estimates from the International Cotton Advisory Committee (ICAC). The decline in production is largely attributed to reduced cotton are
articles.x: Global cotton consumption is projected to exceed production in the 2026/27 season as production, trade, and ending stocks decline modestly, according to the latest estimates from the International Cotton Advisory Committee (ICAC). The decline in production is largely attributed to reduced cotton area across most major producing countries. Global cotton production is projected at approximately 25.94 million tonnes in 2026/27, down 3.8% from 26.98 million tonnes in 2025/26. Consumption, meanwhile, is expected to increase by approximately 1.1%, from 25.85 million tonnes to 26.14 million tonnes. The projections represent a notable shift in the global cotton balance. In 2025/26, production is estimated to exceed consumption by approximately 1.13 million tonnes. In 2026/27, that relationship is projected to reverse, with consumption exceeding production by approximately 201,000 tonnes. Global Cotton Trade Projected to Ease World cotton exports are projected to decline modestly in 2026/27, from approximately 9.87 million tonnes to 9.70 million tonnes, a decrease of about 1.7%. The projected decline comes despite slightly higher global cotton consumption, highlighting a market in which overall mill use is expected to strengthen even as international trade volumes ease. Ending Stocks Expected to Decline Global ending stocks also are projected to decrease, from approximately 17.70 million tonnes in 2025/26 to 17.50 million tonnes in 2026/27, a decline of about 1.1%. The combination of lower production, slightly higher consumption, and declining ending stocks points to a somewhat tighter global cotton balance in the coming season. articles.o: Climate policies and plans must translate into effective projects, financing and measurable results: Environment Minister
articles.s: Minister for Environment, Forest and Climate Change Abdul Awal Mintoo emphasized the need to translate national climate policies and plans into coordinated programmes, quality projects, appropriate financing and measurable results. He said that today’s development decisions would shape climate risks
articles.x: Minister for Environment, Forest and Climate Change Abdul Awal Mintoo emphasized the need to translate national climate policies and plans into coordinated programmes, quality projects, appropriate financing and measurable results. He said that today’s development decisions would shape climate risks for decades to come. Every major investment must therefore take the climate conditions of the relevant area into account. The Minister made these remarks as the chief guest at the opening ceremony of the two-day Bangladesh Climate Development Partnership (BCDP) Knowledge Conference 2026 at the Pan Pacific Sonargaon Hotel in Dhaka today, Wednesday. On the occasion, he launched the BCDP Web Portal. Through real-time project monitoring, the digital portal will help manage information on climate-related projects and investments, enhance transparency and improve processes for developing domestic and international climate finance pipelines. The Minister said that adaptation investments often deliver significant public benefits even when they do not generate direct revenue. Climate financing arrangements must reflect Bangladesh’s development priorities and fiscal capacity. He also called for private investment in clean energy and sustainable infrastructure. Emphasizing the importance of drawing on local communities’ experience in planning, the Minister said that women, young people, persons with disabilities and marginalized communities must have meaningful opportunities to participate in project design, implementation and monitoring. Alongside effective institutions, sound investment decisions and transparent use of resources, Bangladesh would continue to call for international support and climate justice in addressing adaptation and climate-related loss and damage. articles.o: Parkdale acquires CiCLO to advance lower-persistence synthetic fibers
articles.s: Parkdale Advanced Materials has acquired full ownership of CiCLO technology, a patented additive designed to reduce the environmental persistence of microplastic fibers. Figure: Parkdale acquires CiC...
articles.x: Parkdale Advanced Materials has acquired full ownership of CiCLO technology, a patented additive designed to reduce the environmental persistence of microplastic fibers. Figure: Parkdale acquires CiCLO to advance lower-persistence synthetic fibers. CiCLO technology is integrated into polyester and nylon during the extrusion or spinning process. The acquisition gives Parkdale full control of the technology and expands its polymer and fiber portfolio. According to Knitting Trade Journal, the technology is intended to support further development in knitted textiles and related industrial markets. CiCLO is designed for use in synthetic fibers, including polyester and nylon. These fibers can shed microfibres during textile use and washing. The technology aims to make these fibers less persistent in the environment. The acquisition also allows Parkdale to further develop CiCLO technology for textile and industrial applications. It could support the company’s work on synthetic fiber solutions with lower environmental persistence. Parkdale Advanced Materials is a subsidiary of Parkdale, a textile and fiber producer. The company’s expanded technology portfolio now includes full ownership of the patented CiCLO additive. The deal reflects growing industry interest in technologies that can address the environmental impact of synthetic fibers while maintaining their use in textile applications.

articles.o: Virgin polyester rises 7%, global fiber output hits 139m tons
articles.s: Global textile fiber production reached a record 139 million tons in 2025, up from 132 million tons a year earlier, with growth again driven largely by virgin fossil-based fibers, according to Textil...
articles.x: Global textile fiber production reached a record 139 million tons in 2025, up from 132 million tons a year earlier, with growth again driven largely by virgin fossil-based fibers, according to Textile Exchange’s Materials Market Report 2026 . Virgin fossil-based fiber production rose from 81 million tons in 2024 to 86 million tons in 2025. Polyester remained the world’s dominant fiber. Production increased from 77.7 million tons to 82.5 million tons, maintaining a 59% share of global fiber output. Of that volume, 72.8 million tons, or 88%, was virgin fossil-based polyester. The figures underline a widening gap between the textile industry’s circularity ambitions and actual fiber production trends. While brands and manufacturers are increasingly setting recycled-material and lower-impact sourcing targets, the absolute volume of virgin polyester continues to grow. Recycled polyester production increased only modestly, from about 9.4 million tons in 2024 to 9.7 million tons in 2025. Around 97% still came from plastic bottles, rather than discarded textiles. Textile-to-textile recycled fiber production across all fiber types accounted for just 0.76% of global fiber output in 2025, up only marginally from 0.61% in 2021. This is important because bottle-based recycled polyester can reduce reliance on virgin fossil feedstock, but it does not by itself create a closed-loop textile system. The industry’s longer-term circularity challenge is therefore not simply to increase recycled polyester volumes, but to scale fiber-to-fiber recycling capable of turning textile waste back into textile raw material. articles.o: First mountain biking range from Ortovox
articles.s: The new Sequence Series mountain biking collection from German brand Ortovox is based on 100% textile-to-textile recycled polyester, marking a significant departure for a company that has built much of its technical apparel identity around the advanced performance properties of wool. Synthetic fibre
articles.x: The new Sequence Series mountain biking collection from German brand Ortovox is based on 100% textile-to-textile recycled polyester, marking a significant departure for a company that has built much of its technical apparel identity around the advanced performance properties of wool. Synthetic fibres used in high-intensity sportswear, however, can retain sweat-related odours, prompting Ortovox to incorporate Microban International’s Scentry Revive odour-capture technology directly into the fabric during manufacture. Rather than relying on an antimicrobial mechanism, the technology captures and neutralises odour molecules before they become established in the fabric. Microban says its effectiveness is retained for up to 50 domestic washes. For Ortovox, the development provides a way of combining textile-to-textile recycled polyester with the performance requirements of clothing intended for prolonged trail riding. Reducing persistent odours can potentially also reduce the frequency with which garments need to be washed, potentially extending garment life. Scentry Revive has Eco Passport by Oeko-Tex and bluesign certification and does not require biocidal registration. Founded in 1980 and headquartered in Taufkirchen near Munich, Ortovox has traditionally concentrated on ski touring, freeriding, alpine climbing and high-alpine activities, with mountain biking being added to its portfolio for the first time in summer 2026. articles.s: Fashion for Good announces the launch of the Cotton Reloop Matrix Project, a cross-industry initiative that will map and physically validate the quality of commercially available recycled cotton yarns against… The post Fashion for Good launches the Cotton Reloop Matrix Project appeared first on The
articles.x: Fashion for Good announces the launch of the Cotton Reloop Matrix Project, a cross-industry initiative that will map and physically validate the quality of commercially available recycled cotton yarns against brand specifications, giving the industry a data-backed overview of how quality, price, and recycled content intersect. The project is convened with Fashion for Good partners Arvind, BESTSELLER, C&A, Interloop, Reformation, and Shahi, together with ecosystem partner Uster. Cotton accounts for 19% of global fibre production and a core part of the material mix. Although alternative recycling pathways exist to utilise cotton-rich textile waste feedstock, they do not make a cotton output. Therefore, mechanical recycling is a crucial pathway to utilise waste and create recycled cotton yarns and fabrics. Through the mechanical recycling process, textile waste is shredded and re-opened into loose fibres that can be respun into yarn. However, shredding shortens and weakens the fibres, so only 45 to 50% of the input survives as usable material . The rest is lost as short fibres and processing waste, and because the surviving fibres are shorter than virgin cotton, spinners can only blend a limited share back into new yarn. In practice, that caps most yarns at around 10% recycled content: any higher and the fabric isn’t durable enough for commercial use. While recyclers have available capacities, integrating a meaningful percentage of recycled cotton remains complex for brands navigating trade-offs around quality and price. Testing happens in isolation, with recyclers and brands working from separate data sets, and no shared reference comparison to close the gap between them. articles.o: Neumühle takes monomaterial design down to the thread
articles.s: Zurich, Switzerland-based clothing label Neumühle has extended its monomaterial approach with a new hoodie made entirely from cotton, including the sewing thread, and with no elastane incorporated into its construction. The Circular Mono Hoodie has been designed with eventual textile-to-textile recy
articles.x: Zurich, Switzerland-based clothing label Neumühle has extended its monomaterial approach with a new hoodie made entirely from cotton, including the sewing thread, and with no elastane incorporated into its construction. The Circular Mono Hoodie has been designed with eventual textile-to-textile recycling in mind, addressing one of the persistent obstacles to recovering fibres from garments – the presence of multiple materials within a single product. Its heavyweight fabric is made from 100% organic cotton, while the sewing thread is also cotton and Cradle to Cradle Certified. By eliminating elastane, Neumühle avoids introducing an additional fibre that would subsequently have to be separated or accommodated during recycling. The approach reflects growing attention to the relationship between garment design and the practicalities of fibre-to-fibre recycling. Neumühle points to a 2026 study from Wageningen University and Research examining discarded textiles in the Dutch clothing system, which found that 61% consisted of material blends. The researchers concluded that monomaterial products, or garments incorporating components that can easily be separated, are considerably better suited to efficient, high-quality textile-to-textile recycling. The Circular Mono Hoodie is consequently intended to address end-of-life requirements at the initial material-selection and design stages rather than attempting to deal with incompatible components once a garment enters the waste stream. Neumühle co-founder Andreas Fehr said the objective is for clothing to remain in use for years before eventually returning to a material stream, requiring the company to work backwards from a garment’s eventual end of life when developing products. The new pillow line expands the wellness-focused bedding brand’s growing line of domestically made pillows, filled and finished at its Phoenix, Arizona campus. articles.s: FORT BENTON, Mont. — October 1, 2026 — IND HEMP, a producer, processor and supplier of industrial hemp materials in the USA, today announced a significant investment in new fiber processing equipment at its IH Fiber decortication facility in Fort Benton, Montana. The investment adds a secondary proc
articles.x: FORT BENTON, Mont. — October 1, 2026 — IND HEMP, a producer, processor and supplier of industrial hemp materials in the USA, today announced a significant investment in new fiber processing equipment at its IH Fiber decortication facility in Fort Benton, Montana. The investment adds a secondary processing line, featuring multiple fiber refining technologies to perform opening, cleaning and cottonizing, that brings IND HEMP’s hemp fiber to a ready-to-spin quality directly at the source. Yarn is the foundation from which nearly every fabric application is built. Once hemp fiber is spun into yarn, it can be woven or knit into a wide range of end products, from garments and home goods to technical fabrics such as composites. Historically, reaching that spinnable quality has required additional refining beyond standard decortication, work that has fallen to third-party processors, or to the spinners themselves, upgrading standard decorticated technical fiber before it can run on their equipment. The commissioning of IND HEMP’s new processing line brings that refining capability in-house, at the fiber’s source. “Consumers are increasingly looking for natural materials and more transparent supply chains, and brands are moving quickly to try to meet that demand. Hemp is an incredible plant-based solution, but until now the U.S. hasn’t been capable of consistently delivering the quality and scale the global textile industry requires,” explains IND HEMP CEO Morgan Tweet. “By supplying ready-to-spin fiber directly from Montana, we’re removing one of the biggest barriers for manufacturers wanting to work with hemp. articles.s: Bangladesh Jamaat-e-Islami Ameer and Leader of the Opposition in Parliament, Dr. Shafiqur Rahman, held a meeting with leaders of the Bangladesh Textile Mills Association (BTMA) to discuss the current challenges and future prospects of the country’s textile industry.
