articles.x: Bangladesh Jamaat-e-Islami Ameer and Leader of the Opposition in Parliament, Dr. Shafiqur Rahman, held a meeting with leaders of the Bangladesh Textile Mills Association (BTMA) to discuss the current challenges and future prospects of the country’s textile industry. The meeting was held on Tuesday afternoon at the official residence of the Leader of the Opposition at 29 Minto Road in the capital. The discussions focused on several key issues affecting the textile sector, including incentives, gas and electricity supply, challenges following Bangladesh’s graduation from the Least Developed Country (LDC) category, taxes and duties, and various policy-related complexities. Speaking at a press briefing after the meeting, Jamaat Secretary General and former Member of Parliament Mia Golam Parwar said Dr. Shafiqur Rahman emphasized that the opposition does not intend to oppose every government initiative. He said the party wants to play a constructive role by supporting initiatives that serve the public interest while highlighting and opposing policies that are against national interests. According to Mia Golam Parwar, BTMA leaders presented various challenges faced by the textile industry. Dr. Shafiqur Rahman highlighted the importance of ensuring raw materials for export-oriented industries, protecting the capacity of the primary textile sector, increasing local value addition, safeguarding employment, conserving foreign exchange and government revenue, and preventing misuse of bond facilities and illegal imports. He said such balanced and coordinated policies could help strengthen Bangladesh’s primary textile industry, export capacity and overall industrial base. He also assured that the concerns raised by the sector would be brought to Parliament and discussed with the gov

articles.s: BKMEA President Mr. Mohammad Hatem attended the ‘DIU Textile Grand Carnival’, organised by the Department of Textile Engineering of Daffodil International University, as the Chief Guest, where he shared valuable guidance with the students on professional integrity, skills and future opportunities. A
articles.x: BKMEA President Mr. Mohammad Hatem attended the ‘DIU Textile Grand Carnival’, organised by the Department of Textile Engineering of Daffodil International University, as the Chief Guest, where he shared valuable guidance with the students on professional integrity, skills and future opportunities. Addressing the students, he emphasised the importance of honesty, sincerity and dedication in professional life. He reminded them that the task they are performing deserves their utmost attention and that they themselves are equally important. Therefore, every responsibility should be carried out with full concentration, commitment and sincerity. He also encouraged students to build their knowledge and skills in Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Sustainability, highlighting that the young generation will shape the future of the apparel industry. He further called for extending the internship period for textile students from three months to six months. He mentioned that BKMEA will take initiatives to facilitate internship opportunities across its member factories, enabling students to gain practical industry experience and develop the skills required to become industry-ready professionals. Also present at the event were DIU Vice Chancellor Prof. Dr. Engr. M. R. Kabir, Dean of the Faculty of Engineering Prof. Dr. M. Shamsul Alam, Head of the Department of Textile Engineering Dr. Engr. Tanvir Ahmed Chowdhury, along with faculty members and students. articles.s: To accelerate sustainable manufacturing, enhance environmental compliance, and improve resource efficiency across Bangladesh’s industrial value chains, Amin & Jahan Corporation Limited (A&J) a...
articles.x: To accelerate sustainable manufacturing, enhance environmental compliance, and improve resource efficiency across Bangladesh’s industrial value chains, Amin & Jahan Corporation Limited (A&J) and SGS Bangladesh Ltd. held a strategic coordination meeting at their Karwan Bazar Office. The meeting focused on establishing a collaborative framework to roll out globally accredited ZDHC Academy Training programs, specifically addressing Chemical Management and Wastewater Management across the textile, apparel, leather, and tannery manufacturing sectors in Bangladesh. Figure: Officials from SGS Bangladesh Ltd. and Amin and Jahan Corporation Ltd. following the strategic planning session for ZDHC Academy Training. Submit an Expression of Interest (EOI) to join this program: https://bit.ly/zdhc-bd During the discussion, both organizations agreed on a phased implementation structure tailored to regional supply chain requirements. Participating facilities will first undergo comprehensive Chemical Management modules, followed by advanced Wastewater Management training once core chemical stewardship practices are embedded on the factory floor. The curriculum will also incorporate sector-specific adaptations for textile mills and leather tanneries, ensuring targeted alignment with the ZDHC Roadmap to Zero guidelines, discharge standards, and international compliance benchmarks. To maximize shop-floor absorption while maintaining international technical rigor, the interactive capacity-building initiative will blend global course materials with localized, bilingual delivery. SGS Bangladesh will also conduct baseline technical assessments to identify common operational bottlenecks across facilities prior to program execution. articles.o: Bangladesh Launches Initiative to Advance Textile Traceability and Decarbonization
articles.s: Solidaridad Asia, in partnership with the Embassy of the Kingdom of the Netherlands in Bangladesh, the Netherlands Enterprise Agency (RVO), Dutch retail brands, technology innovators and Bangladesh’s apparel industry bodies, has officially launched a 2.5-year initiative titled “Circular Textiles Ban
articles.x: Solidaridad Asia, in partnership with the Embassy of the Kingdom of the Netherlands in Bangladesh, the Netherlands Enterprise Agency (RVO), Dutch retail brands, technology innovators and Bangladesh’s apparel industry bodies, has officially launched a 2.5-year initiative titled “Circular Textiles Bangladesh: Advancing Traceability and Decarbonization.” Photo: Guests, speakers, industry leaders, brand representatives, technology partners and stakeholders pose for a group photograph at the launch of “Circular Textiles Bangladesh: Advancing Traceability and Decarbonization”. The initiative aims to support Bangladesh’s textile and apparel sector in responding to emerging global sustainability and regulatory requirements, particularly those linked to the European Union market. It will focus on practical solutions for product-level traceability, carbon data, transparency and decarbonization across textile and apparel supply chains. The initiative brings together Dutch retailers Zeeman, Wibra and XD Connects, technology providers Aware, tex.tracer, OneTrueValue and Colubris, and industry bodies BGMEA and BKMEA. It will work with manufacturers to test practical solutions around supply chain traceability, circularity, decarbonization and sustainability data. The initiative brings together Dutch retail brands including Zeeman, Wibra and XD Connects; technology innovators Aware, tex.tracer, OneTrueValue and Colubris; and industry organizations including BGMEA and BKMEA. The launch comes as global regulations are increasingly shifting from traditional factory-level compliance toward verified product-level information. The upcoming fair follows its strongest edition to date, held in March this year, when over 600 exhibitors from 12 c
articles.x: SHANGHAI — October 6, 2026 — Yarn Expo Spring will welcome the global yarn and fibre industry back to the National Exhibition and Convention Center (Shanghai) from 10 – 12 March 2027. The upcoming fair follows its strongest edition to date, held in March this year, when over 600 exhibitors from 12 countries and regions connected with more than 25,000 visitors from 113 countries and regions. The record turnout reaffirmed the fair’s role as a key venue for sourcing, innovation and industry exchange. Returning alongside Intertextile Shanghai Apparel Fabrics – Spring Edition, Intertextile Shanghai Home Textiles – Spring Edition, CHIC and PH Value, the comprehensive yarn and fibre trade fair will create further opportunities for the textile value chain to connect around changing material and sourcing priorities. Prior to the fair, Ms Wilmet Shea, General Manager of Messe Frankfurt (HK) Ltd, commented: “In a changing economic landscape, last year’s record participation showed how important it is for the yarn and fibre industry to meet in Shanghai, exchange ideas and understand what the market needs next. In March, suppliers will have the opportunity to present their latest developments to buyers from apparel, home textiles, knitting and related sectors, discuss requirements and build business relationships for the long term.” Yarn and fibre markets evolve with changing sourcing needs As the yarn, fibre and thread market expands towards a projected USD 182.7 billion by 2032, Asia-Pacific remains central to spinning, filament and textile production, as well as downstream demand. China’s integrated fibre, yarn, textile and equipment segments further strengthen Shanghai’s role as a location for industry exchange. articles.o: Vardhman bets ₹3,660 crore on scale, integration and value-added growth
articles.s: By K. Gopalakrishnan Major investment cycle spans spinning, weaving, processing, technical textiles, garments and green energy as Vardhman positions itself for the next phase of India’s textile growth For more… The post Vardhman bets ₹3,660 crore on scale, integration and value-added growth appeared
articles.x: By K. Gopalakrishnan Major investment cycle spans spinning, weaving, processing, technical textiles, garments and green energy as Vardhman positions itself for the next phase of India’s textile growth For more than six decades, Vardhman Textiles has grown alongside India’s textile industry, building one of the country’s most extensive vertically integrated textile manufacturing platforms. Today, as global sourcing patterns undergo a structural shift and India strengthens its position as a preferred textile and apparel sourcing destination, the company is embarking on one of the most significant investment cycles in its recent history. Suchita Oswal Jain, Vice-Chairman and Joint Managing Director of Vardhman Textiles Vardhman has committed approximately ₹3,660 crore to a broad-based growth and modernisation programme, covering spinning and fabric, technical textiles, fabric processing, garment manufacturing and green-energy infrastructure. Rather than being a conventional capacity expansion programme, the investment is designed to move the company further up the textile value chain, improve productivity and margins, strengthen sustainability credentials and create a more resilient business model. The scale and breadth of the programme underline Vardhman’s confidence in the long-term prospects of the Indian textile industry. The company believes that global supply chains are being redrawn as brands and retailers diversify sourcing away from concentrated geographies and increasingly seek large, compliant and technologically capable manufacturing partners. articles.o: US-Grown Hemp Meets Supima
articles.s: Hemp is steadily moving from a sustainability-led niche towards a commercially viable fibre for mainstream textile manufacturing, and Heartland USA is seeking to accelerate this transition through scalable fibre solutions… The post US-Grown Hemp Meets Supima appeared first on The Textile Magazine .
articles.x: Hemp is steadily moving from a sustainability-led niche towards a commercially viable fibre for mainstream textile manufacturing, and Heartland USA is seeking to accelerate this transition through scalable fibre solutions and strategic blends. Its recent innovation combining US-grown Imperium hemp fibre with Supima® cotton demonstrates the potential to integrate hemp into commercial spinning systems while creating premium textile possibilities around performance, natural fibres and a distinctive “Grown in America” proposition. According to Mr. Amey Padma, Head – India Business, Heartland USA, the next phase of hemp adoption will depend on consistent fibre quality, reliable supply, technical compatibility and, ultimately, commercial economics. Hemp is gaining renewed attention as textile manufacturers and global brands search for natural fibre alternatives that can deliver sustainability as well as commercially relevant performance. For Heartland USA, the opportunity extends beyond positioning hemp as another sustainable fibre. The company is focused on making hemp compatible with existing textile manufacturing infrastructure and developing commercially viable fibre blends for apparel and home textiles. Mr. Amey Padma, Head – India Business, Heartland USA According to Mr. Amey Padmas, the global hemp market is gradually moving “from niche to industrial”, particularly through applications involving cotton, lyocell and other fibre blends. However, he believes that mainstream adoption will ultimately depend on three factors: consistency, economics and supply reliability. “Sustainability gets attention; performance and economics drive adoption,” says Padma. articles.o: LAPP at 30 in India: Building the Next Phase of Growth Through Localisation, Innovation and Sustainability
articles.s: By K. Gopalakrishnan Three decades after entering India, LAPP has made the country its second-largest market globally and its biggest investment base in Asia. With India emerging as a major… The post LAPP at 30 in India: Building the Next Phase of Growth Through Localisation, Innovation and Sustaina
articles.x: By K. Gopalakrishnan Three decades after entering India, LAPP has made the country its second-largest market globally and its biggest investment base in Asia. With India emerging as a major manufacturing hub, the company is expanding local production, developing application-specific solutions and investing in technology, sustainability and talent to drive its next phase of growth. When LAPP established its presence in India 30 years ago, many European companies were looking primarily towards China and other Asian markets. LAPP, however, chose to make a long-term bet on India. Three decades later, that decision has paid off handsomely. Matthias Lapp, CEO, LAPP Group India is now LAPP’s second-largest market globally, after Germany, and its largest investment destination in Asia. The company’s growing commitment is reflected in the expansion of its Bhopal manufacturing facility, which is set to become LAPP’s largest factory globally. For Matthias Lapp, CEO, LAPP Group, India’s importance goes beyond its size as a market. The country has become an important manufacturing, engineering and talent hub within the global LAPP network. “Celebrating 30 years is awesome. It feels great,” says Lapp. “India is our number one invested country from an Asia perspective.” He describes the country increasingly as a second home for LAPP. A Long-Term Bet on India LAPP’s decision to invest in India was driven by the opportunity to participate in a market where the industrial landscape was still developing. “There were opportunities, not everything was yet distributed and set in stone, so we could really participate in the growth, in the future growth,” Lapp recalls. articles.x: ‘’A buyer asks for 500 pieces per style/Colour The factory merchandiser asks whether they meant 50,000 pcs’’ Somewhere between those two questions, an opportunity disappears. This small exchange captures a bigger challenge facing Bangladesh’s ready-made garment industry. The country has built a powerful business around producing large quantities efficiently. But the next generation of orders will require greater flexibility, stronger product development and dependable delivery. The question is changing from “How much can we produce?” to “How well can we respond?” The pressure is real. The picture is mixed. According to BGMEA’s published figures, Bangladesh exported $38.701 billion in garments in FY2025–26, down 1.64%** from the previous year. Garments still accounted for 80.62% of national merchandise export earnings. When the industry struggles, the effects reach workers, transport businesses, banks and households. Figure: Ruhul Talukder, Managing Director, Ruhrose RBT Ltd. London HQ, Bangladesh Manufacturing. However, the figures do not support the claim that buyers everywhere are leaving Bangladesh. EPB data reported by BSS and The Business Standard show garment exports to the EU fell 3.31% to $19.06 billion. Meanwhile, exports to the US increased 2.63% to $7.74 billion, and UK shipments rose 0.91% to $4.39 billion. These figures describe goods shipped, though. They cannot guarantee a healthy order book tomorrow. India, Vietnam and Pakistan remain serious competitors. Yet Bangladesh still attracts interest. In USFIA’s 2026 survey of 30 leading US fashion companies, 46.7% planned to increase sourcing from Bangladesh over the following two years. articles.t: Parkdale, CiCLO 기술의 완전한 소유권 획득
articles.o: Parkdale takes full ownership of CiCLO technology
articles.s: Parkdale has acquired full ownership of CiCLO technology and plans to extend its use beyond apparel and home textiles into nonwovens, filtration, geotextiles and other technical applications. The Gastonia, North Carolina-based textile group has acquired the technology through its Parkdale Advanced M
articles.x: Parkdale has acquired full ownership of CiCLO technology and plans to extend its use beyond apparel and home textiles into nonwovens, filtration, geotextiles and other technical applications. The Gastonia, North Carolina-based textile group has acquired the technology through its Parkdale Advanced Materials subsidiary, adding CiCLO to its growing portfolio of polymer and fibre technologies. CiCLO is a patented additive technology incorporated into polyester and nylon during fibre manufacture. It is designed to enable synthetic fibres that shed into the environment to biodegrade more readily in biologically active conditions, addressing the long-term persistence of microplastic fibres. The technology is already commercially used in apparel, home, hospitality and workwear products, but Parkdale sees considerable scope for expansion into markets where synthetic fibres are widely employed. These include industrial and hygiene nonwovens, geotextiles, filtration, insulation and furnishings. “We believe CiCLO fibres have the potential to address microplastic fibre persistence at meaningful scale,” said Davis Warlick, chief operating officer of Parkdale. “Our focus now is to continue investing in the technology, develop new applications with our customers, open new markets and broaden adoption.” CiCLO technology is incorporated into polyester and nylon at the polymer stage, creating pathways within the resulting fibres that allow naturally occurring microorganisms to break down the polymer in biologically active environments. articles.o: Spider silk moves into major sportswear trial
articles.s: Recombinant spider silk is moving a step closer to a commercial textile applications following the first customer shipment of yarn from US developer Kraig Biocraft Laboratories. The Ann Arbor, Michigan-based company has shipped a small quantity of custom-engineered spider silk yarn to an unnamed glo
articles.x: Recombinant spider silk is moving a step closer to a commercial textile applications following the first customer shipment of yarn from US developer Kraig Biocraft Laboratories. The Ann Arbor, Michigan-based company has shipped a small quantity of custom-engineered spider silk yarn to an unnamed global performance sports brand, which plans to develop it into a new performance textile. The order forms part of a confidential pilot development programme focused on high-performance athletic apparel. Kraig said the yarn had been processed to the customer’s specifications, although it has disclosed neither the identity of the brand nor the quantity supplied. The shipment is nevertheless significant for the company as its first commercial order for recombinant spider silk yarn and moves the technology beyond production development and into testing for an end-use textile application. Kraig produces its spider silk proteins using genetically engineered silkworms, an approach intended to combine some of the mechanical properties associated with natural spider silk with the established infrastructure and scalability of conventional silk production. Spider silk has long attracted interest from textile and materials developers because of its combination of strength, toughness, flexibility and low weight. Producing it economically and consistently at useful volumes, however, has proved considerably more difficult. Kraig believes specialist performance applications offer an appropriate starting point because relatively small quantities of material can potentially provide a meaningful performance benefit. “The volume is small by design,” said founder and CEO Kim Thompson. “This is a precision application, not a bulk order. articles.x: GREENSBORO, N.C.— September 30, 2026 — UNIFI, Inc., the makers of REPREVE® and one of the world’s innovators in recycled and synthetic yarns, today launches Cofira , a versatile yarn that can be tailored with synthetic, blended, and functional fiber technologies for enhanced performance. This innovation within UNIFI®’s portfolio delivers a fusion of filament and spun characteristics in one yarn, offering the advantage of spun yarn comfort with filament functionality. Cofira offers broad design flexibility that supports the integration of sustainable performance technologies. Designed for versatility, it is ideal for applications including apparel, furnishings, gear, and accessories. Key features of Cofira: Combines spun yarn aesthetics with filament yarn performance in one construction; Enables unique fabric aesthetics and hand feel; Can be combined with other UNIFI technologies including: A.M.Y. ® , ChillSense ® , and ReFlexx ® ; and Available globally in virgin and REPREVE polyester yarns, including REPREVE Takeback , with REPREVE options fully traceable via FiberPrint ® technology and certified by U-TRUST ® , GRS, and SCS for recycled content. In addition, UNIFI also announces the launch of Resist 2 O Pro, an expansion of water-resistant offerings engineered for all types of fabric formation. Designed to deliver durable water resistance without compromising fabric performance, Resist 2 O Pro gives brands and manufacturers greater freedom to develop water-resistant fabrics for a wide range of textile applications, without the use of topical treatments or fluorinated chemistry. articles.s: Rancon Lubricants Limited today signed a land lease agreement with Invest Bangladesh for 6.5 acres of developed land at the National Special Economic Zone in Mirsarai, Chattogram. The company proposes to invest USD 19.65 million in an industrial unit expected to create more than 250 jobs. Nahian Rah
articles.x: Rancon Lubricants Limited today signed a land lease agreement with Invest Bangladesh for 6.5 acres of developed land at the National Special Economic Zone in Mirsarai, Chattogram. The company proposes to invest USD 19.65 million in an industrial unit expected to create more than 250 jobs. Nahian Rahman Rochi, Member (Investment Development), signed on behalf of Invest Bangladesh, while Imran Zaman Khan, Managing Director, signed for Rancon Lubricants Limited. “This is Invest Bangladesh’s first land lease agreement following the merger of three investment promotion agencies,” said Nahian Rahman Rochi. “Commitments from anchor investors such as Rancon Lubricants signal confidence in the new institution and help build confidence among other investors,” he added. The lease runs for 50 years from the date of possession, with provision for renewal on terms set by Invest Bangladesh. Land handover is due within 90 days of signing. Rancon Lubricants is expected to begin construction within 120 days of handover and bring the unit into operation within 36 months of handover. Invest Bangladesh will facilitate utility connections and access to applicable government-declared customs duty, VAT and tax incentives. Rancon Lubricants will obtain the necessary approvals and comply with environmental, labour and safety requirements, including the provision of effluent and sewage treatment facilities and connection to the zone’s common effluent treatment and waste management systems. The agreement provides for performance and compliance monitoring, a period to remedy breaches before termination, and arbitration under the Arbitration Act, 2001. articles.x: PARIS — October 5, 2026 — EverDye, the startup developing low-impact textile dyeing solutions, received two important recognition from the textile industry. The company secured the ZDHC Certification (Zero Discharge of Hazardous Chemicals), and is one of the 20 startups selected by CEMATEX (European Committee of Textile Machinery Manufacturers) for the CEMATEX Start-Up Grant. Founded in 2021, EverDye developed a bio-based pigment dyeing process that consumes less energy and operates at room temperature. This process reduces CO2 emissions by 90% and cuts energy consumption by 8 times compared to traditional textile dyeing methods. The company is led by Dr Amira Erokh, a materials chemist whose vision paved the way to a new approach. ZDHC certification: a labor for chemical management excellence ZDHC (Zero Discharge of Hazardous Chemicals) is a global initiative aiming to eliminate hazardous chemicals from the textile and leather industry. The certification attests to a chemical product’s compliance with the MRSL (Manufacturing Restricted Substances List), the list of substances prohibited or restricted during manufacturing. This mission resonates with EverDye, validating the technological approach of using bio-based pigments with the aim to limit chemical residues. “The ZDHC certification confirms that it is possible to transform the dyeing process without compromising on chemical control. At EverDye, we want to drive a profound shift in the industry toward a more responsible model, starting with dyeing. articles.o: Colorifix launches bacteria-based dye for wool
articles.s: British biotech firm Colorifix has launched Sunlit Clay, a warm earthy shade for wool. The dye is produced using engineered bacteria, offering a lower‑impact alternative to petrochemical dyes. The com...
articles.x: British biotech firm Colorifix has launched Sunlit Clay, a warm earthy shade for wool. The dye is produced using engineered bacteria, offering a lower‑impact alternative to petrochemical dyes. The company announced the new shade on September 29, saying Sunlit Clay is available in both yarn and fabric and is produced using its proprietary biological dyeing technology. Courtesy: Collected The color was inspired by bacteria found in soil and deep-sea sediments, with the company showcasing a 100% wool swatch. Based at Norwich Research Park, Colorifix was co-founded by University of Cambridge scientist Jim Ajioka and Chief Executive Orr Yarkoni. The company began in 2013 with research into sensors for detecting heavy metals in drinking water before turning its attention to textile dyeing after witnessing the environmental impact of conventional dyeing in Nepal and Bangladesh. Colorifix says it has developed an entirely biological process to produce, deposit and fix pigments on textiles. The technology starts with DNA instructions for a natural pigment, sourced from public databases, which are inserted into bacteria or yeast. The engineered microorganisms are grown in fermenters using agricultural by-products. The process is similar to brewing, with the resulting fermentation material pumped into conventional dyeing machines together with yarn, fabric or garments. Heat breaks open the microbial cells and releases the pigment, allowing it to bond with the textile fiber. The remaining cells are subsequently washed away. The company says its technology can be used on cotton, wool, silk, polyester, nylon and lyocell and can operate with existing textile mill infrastructure. articles.x: SACRAMENTO, CA— October 6, 2026 — The Nature Conservancy (TNC) has launched the Microfiber Action Alliance (MAA), a new multi-stakeholder initiative to combat microfiber pollution by accelerating the adoption and scaling of effective, evidence-based solutions. Convened by TNC, the founding cohort includes Nike, Patagonia, Under Armour, lululemon, Cotopaxi and REI Co-op, among other leading brands. Microfibers are small particles that shed from both synthetic and natural textiles. Alongside use and wear, the production of clothing and textiles is a significant contributor to microfiber pollution globally, with some estimates indicating that microfibers account for over 30% of ocean microplastics. While synthetic microfibers are among the most common forms of microplastic pollution found in nature, even natural fibers, such as cotton and wool, contribute to microfiber pollution if they have been treated with dye, softeners or finishes. Once in the environment, microfibers are extremely difficult to remove because they are so small and easily dispersed, underscoring the importance of prevention. Fortunately, a range of effective solutions exist. Complementing the work of The Microfibre Consortium, which convenes across the textile industry to develop the science, data and tools needed to reduce fiber fragmentation, TNC will work with participating companies to better understand, refine and advance solutions that can meaningfully reduce microfiber pollution. articles.o: Karotoa Green Spinning builds a resource-efficient model for yarn manufacturing
articles.s: Bangladesh’s green factory movement is moving beyond buildings and certifications. The next challenge is to make production itself more resource-efficient, less carbon-intensive, and more resilient....
articles.x: Bangladesh’s green factory movement is moving beyond buildings and certifications. The next challenge is to make production itself more resource-efficient, less carbon-intensive, and more resilient. Figure1: Karotoa Green Spinning Mills Ltd, Kaliakair, Gazipur Karotoa Green Spinning Mills Ltd is taking that approach at its new manufacturing complex in Kaliakair, Gazipur. Energy, water, natural resources, and worker well-being have been incorporated directly into the design of the factory. The project is being developed on a 90-acre site with four planned production units and an estimated investment of around Tk 2,400 crore. The completed complex is planned to produce 70,000 kilograms of yarn per day. A key focus of the complex is renewable energy. Karotoa plans to generate 6 MW of solar power through rooftop installations across the factory. Solar panels have already been installed in one unit. For the textile sector of Bangladesh, this approach has growing importance as factories face pressure to reduce dependence on fossil fuels, manage energy costs, and respond to decarbonization expectations from global buyers. According to industry reports, Bangladesh already has one of the strongest green-factory bases in the world, with 290 LEED-certified RMG factories recorded by July 2026. Karotoa is also building water management into its core production model. 6 acres of land have been developed on the premises. Water from the pond will be treated and reused in the factory, while rainwater will be captured, purified, and returned to the water system. This closed-loop approach can reduce pressure on freshwater sources and improve overall resource efficiency. R Devaganeshan, Project Head, Tesco Airtechniques Engineering for Energy Efficiency, Durability and for more Sustainable solution. The global textile industry is entering an era where energy efficiency is no longer an option – it is a competitive necessity. Textile manufacturing is inherently energy-intensive, with continuous operations requiring large amounts of electricity for spinning, weaving, processing, humidification, ventilation and other auxiliary systems. At the same time, manufacturers across the world are facing increasing pressure to control production costs, improve energy efficiency and reduce their environmental footprint. Electricity demand globally continues to grow, while energy markets remain exposed to price volatility and supply-side uncertainties. The International Energy Agency (IEA) expects global electricity demand to grow by around 3.6% in 2026 and 3.8% in 2027. For energy intensive industries, every unit of electricity saved can directly contribute to improved operating economics and competitiveness. Against this backdrop, Tesco Fans has taken another step forward in fan technology – moving from Polyamide Glass Blades to Carbon Fiber Polyamide Glass Blades. articles.x: With 100% of its ring and open-end spinning machinery now connected to its AI-based data analytics platform, The Mill Mind, Sri Kannapiran Mills is converting machine data into actionable intelligence to improve productivity, quality and operational responsiveness — without investing in new equipment. For years, textile mills have installed sophisticated monitoring systems across spinning and weaving operations. However, the availability of data does not necessarily translate into better decision-making. Mr. Srihari Balakrishnan, Managing Director, Sri Kannapiran Mills, believes the industry has historically collected enormous amounts of machine data without fully exploiting its potential. Mr. Srihari Balakrishnan, Managing Director, Sri Kannapiran Mills “As spinners we all have and had data monitoring equipment. Spindle monitoring, carding monitoring, preparatory monitoring etc. Like most of us we were using it as an ornament, not using the data. Not analysing it, not mining it, not drilling down to first principles,” he says. Sri Kannapiran Mills is now attempting to bridge that gap through The Mill Mind, its AI-based data analytics platform. 100% Spinning Capacity Under AI-Based Monitoring The company has now connected its ring and open-end spinning machines across all four spinning locations to The Mill Mind. Data from the machines flows continuously into the platform, where it is analysed for consistency and deviations. Depending on the process, alerts are generated either immediately or at the end of a shift or day, allowing manufacturing teams to act on abnormal machine behaviour much faster. articles.s: Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BGMEA) President Mahmud Hasan Khan today urged Pakistan to increase imports of Bangladeshi jute yarn and pharmaceutical products to reduce the bilateral trade imbalance and expand economic cooperation between the two countries. He made the
articles.x: Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BGMEA) President Mahmud Hasan Khan today urged Pakistan to increase imports of Bangladeshi jute yarn and pharmaceutical products to reduce the bilateral trade imbalance and expand economic cooperation between the two countries. He made the call during a meeting with Pakistan High Commissioner to Bangladesh Imran Haider at the BGMEA office in the city, said a press release. At the meeting, the BGMEA president also emphasised increasing imports of chemicals and dyes from Pakistan for Bangladesh’s garment industry, highlighting the potential for expanding trade in both directions. Although Bangladesh imports a significant volume of goods from Pakistan, including raw materials for the garment industry, its exports to the neighbouring country remain comparatively low, the release said. The BGMEA president called for greater efforts to address the imbalance by exploring new export opportunities and strengthening commercial ties. Pakistan high commissioner expressed keen interest in the proposals and assured that necessary steps would be taken to promote bilateral trade. The meeting also discussed arranging visits by high-level business delegations from both countries to identify new opportunities and establish direct commercial links. Haider said the Pakistan High Commission would facilitate business-to-business meetings and matchmaking sessions with leading Pakistani importers, brands, buyers and business associations if a Bangladeshi delegation comprising garment and other sector exporters visited Pakistan. Both sides also exchanged views on expanding market access and exploring a possible bilateral preferential trade arrangement to sustain trade flows after Bangladesh’s graduation from the least developed country

articles.x: Dale of Norway has launched a limited-edition home collection in collaboration with Pernille Døsvik, bringing together Norwegian textile traditions, merino wool and a contemporary cabin aesthetic. The Pernille Døsvik x Dale of Norway Home Collection was developed alongside Døsvik’s cabin project at Skeikampen, with the aim of creating textile products designed specifically for a modern mountain interior. articles.x: On 15 September 2026 , Gtech Infrastructure Ltd. organized a seminar in Chattogram focusing on the growing potential of solar energy in Bangladesh and the role of rooftop solar in building a cleaner, more cost-effective, and reliable energy system. The seminar was attended by senior representatives of the Bangladesh Power Development Board (PDB) , including the Chief Engineer, Chattogram Zone, former PDB officials, as well as Executive Engineers and Assistant Engineers from the Chattogram Zone. The participation of experienced power-sector professionals provided an important platform for discussion on the opportunities and practical challenges associated with the wider adoption of solar energy. Solar Energy: An Opportunity for Bangladesh The seminar highlighted the significant potential of solar power as Bangladesh moves toward greater energy diversification and renewable energy adoption. Rooftop solar is particularly relevant for industrial and commercial facilities because electricity generated during daylight hours can directly support daytime consumption. With rising energy costs and the need for greater energy security, rooftop solar can help businesses reduce their dependence on conventional electricity while generating clean energy from otherwise unused rooftop space. Recent studies also identify rooftop solar as an increasingly viable solution for improving energy security and reducing carbon emissions in Bangladesh. The discussion also comes at a significant time for Bangladesh, with the country placing greater emphasis on expanding rooftop solar and attracting private-sector participation in renewable energy. articles.o: BGMEA × AWARE Digital Product Passport (DPP) Pilot and understand how their factories can participate
articles.s: BGMEA hosted an introductory session on 30 September for representatives from member factories to learn more about the BGMEA × AWARE Digital Product Passport (DPP) Pilot and understand how their factories can participate. The pilot aims to help participating factories prepare for the growing demand
articles.x: BGMEA hosted an introductory session on 30 September for representatives from member factories to learn more about the BGMEA × AWARE Digital Product Passport (DPP) Pilot and understand how their factories can participate. The pilot aims to help participating factories prepare for the growing demand for transparent, verifiable production and traceability data, particularly as the EU moves toward Digital Product Passport requirements for textiles. Through the pilot, participating factories can explore a verified, producer-owned record of production data, supported by AWARE’s Crypto TC technology. The model is designed to provide a single source of verified information that can be shared across buyer relationships, while keeping production data under the factory’s ownership. The pilot also offers guided onboarding and training, data collection and DPP creation, review and validation, with the DPP creation cost fully covered during the pilot period. The session provided factory representatives with an opportunity to better understand the pilot, its potential benefits, participation process and how digital traceability can support the Bangladesh RMG sector’s transition toward greater transparency and EU market readiness. articles.s: The rapid adoption of GLP-1 weight-loss drugs is beginning to have a measurable impact on the fashion industry, changing clothing sizes, purchasing patterns and even the balance between online and physical retail. Drugs including Ozempic, Wegovy and Mounjaro are already being associated with what ha
articles.x: The rapid adoption of GLP-1 weight-loss drugs is beginning to have a measurable impact on the fashion industry, changing clothing sizes, purchasing patterns and even the balance between online and physical retail. Drugs including Ozempic, Wegovy and Mounjaro are already being associated with what has been dubbed the ‘Ozempic economy’, as significant changes in body weight force consumers to replace clothing and reconsider what and how they buy. Research from PwC suggests the impact on apparel could be substantial. Some 73% of US GLP-1 users surveyed reported a meaningful change in clothing size, while apparel spending was 9.9% higher after users had been taking the drugs for six-to-eight months. The effects are also becoming apparent in the UK. PwC estimates that around three million British adults currently use GLP-1 medications, with 40% of users surveyed saying they were spending more on clothing. One consequence could be an unexpected revival in physical clothes shopping. A US survey of 500 GLP-1 users by returns management specialist ReturnPro found that 69% had become less confident about online sizing as their bodies changed, making the ability to try garments on in stores more important. Some 71% said they were buying more apparel as their size changed, while 58% reported increased spending on premium or higher-priced clothing. More than half expected their clothing expenditure to rise further once their weight had stabilised. The trend presents challenges as well as opportunities for retailers. ReturnPro found that 65% of GLP-1 consumers surveyed were buying several sizes of the same garment with the intention of returning those that did not fit, while 43% said their frequency of apparel returns had increased. The system and its local production were presented
articles.x: Young Labels Ltd and Japan-based Toska-Bano’k Co Ltd have started local production of the FasBano’k garment tagging system in Bangladesh, expanding the availability of the Japanese-developed technology for the country’s apparel and textile industry. The system and its local production were presented at an opening ceremony held yesterday (25 September) at the Bangla-Bano’k factory in Dhaka, bringing together representatives from Japanese organisations, Toska-Bano’k and Young Labels, according to a press release. Embassy of Japan in Bangladesh First Secretary Saori Fujimoto; Daisuke Arai of Jetro Dhaka; Yasuyuki Marahashi of Jica; Toska-Bano’k Co Ltd President Masao Terunuma; and Young Labels Ltd Managing Director S Mahmud (Mujbik) attended the event. FasBano’k is designed to attach tags using a dedicated hand tool together with specially designed tag loops or string fasteners. The system provides an alternative to conventional processes in which workers manually string or tie individual tags during garment finishing. Toska-Bano’k says its fastening mechanism allows tags to be attached more quickly than conventional manual methods, with the system designed for continuous operation. The technology can be used for garments, footwear and other textile products. Material options The tagging system is available with a range of material options, including recycled plastic, polyester, cotton, jute and paper. The different material choices allow manufacturers and brands to select tagging materials according to product specifications, sourcing requirements and sustainability considerations. For applications using recycled materials, Transaction Certificates (TCs) can also be provided where applicable for buyers and manufacturers requiring documentation relating to recycled content

articles.s: North Wales manufacturer KnitMesh Technologies is taking its specialist wire knitting technology into the rapidly developing counter-drone market with a stainless steel mesh designed to provide a physical barrier against hostile unmanned aircraft systems (UAS). The company showcased its DroneStop Co
articles.x: North Wales manufacturer KnitMesh Technologies is taking its specialist wire knitting technology into the rapidly developing counter-drone market with a stainless steel mesh designed to provide a physical barrier against hostile unmanned aircraft systems (UAS). The company showcased its DroneStop Counter-UAS Shield at the Counter-UAS Homeland Security Europe conference in London on September 30 and October 1, positioning the technology as a passive addition to the electronic detection and jamming systems increasingly being deployed to protect sensitive sites. Established in 1957 and headquartered in Greenfield, Flintshire, KnitMesh Technologies has spent almost 70 years developing knitted wire mesh for applications ranging from automotive components and filtration to hydrogen production, thermal management and industrial safety. It also operates a manufacturing facility near New Delhi, India. Developed, manufactured and tested in the UK, DroneStop employs high-strength stainless steel knitted wire mesh to create a lightweight physical barrier above or around vulnerable assets. Unlike electronic counter-drone systems, it requires no power supply and does not rely on radio-frequency interference or signal jamming. Instead, the mesh is intended to form the final physical layer of a broader counter-UAS strategy, protecting locations including military bases, ammunition and fuel storage areas, aircraft facilities, communications infrastructure, prisons and other critical national infrastructure. The approach reflects the increasing complexity of protecting sites against relatively small and inexpensive unmanned aircraft. articles.x: Wendler Interlining Bangladesh Limited officially opened its new production facility in Bangladesh on Saturday, marking a significant milestone in the German textile specialist’s long-term commitment to the country’s ready-made garment (RMG) industry. The opening ceremony brought together senior executives of Wendler Interlining Group, industry stakeholders and business partners to celebrate the company’s growing presence in Bangladesh and its vision for the future of the global interlining market. Wendler Interlining, a family-owned German company with roots dating back to 1843, has evolved from a textile finisher into a specialist in high-quality interlinings for the garment industry. The company established its own Bangladesh subsidiary in 2022, building on its production presence in the country since 2009. According to the company, Bangladesh is a strategically important market because of its position as one of the world’s largest garment-producing countries. From 180 years of heritage to a new chapter in Bangladesh: Addressing the ceremony, Dr Gerhart Wendler, Chairman of Wendler Interlining Group, highlighted the company’s long history, its transformation through successive generations and its continuing commitment to innovation and quality. He spoke about Wendler’s journey from its establishment in 1843 to becoming an international specialist in interlinings. The company shifted its strategic focus to high-quality interlining fabrics in 1974 and subsequently expanded its presence across major garment-producing markets in Asia. Dr Wendler also outlined the group’s future ambition of strengthening its position as the market leader in interlinings, with Bangladesh playing an increasingly important role in that strategy. articles.x: Author: Sultan Mahmud Sohal, Country Manager, Corporate Responsibility, KM International GmbH (Branch office of FLORETT TEXTIL GmbH & Co. KG) Ten years is long enough to change an industry, and it is certainly long enough to leave an imprint on the people who work within it. In Bangladesh, the story of garments and textiles is often presented through export earnings, factory numbers, production capacity, employment and market share. These figures are important because they demonstrate the extraordinary scale of an industry that has become central to the country’s economy and international identity. Yet numbers alone cannot capture what this sector really represents. Behind every shipment is a worker beginning a shift, an engineer solving a production problem, a merchandiser managing a demanding deadline, an entrepreneur taking a financial risk, a technician learning a new machine, or a young professional trying to build a career in an industry that connects Bangladesh with consumers across the world. Behind every factory is a community, and behind every export figure are millions of individual stories. That human dimension is what makes Bangladesh’s textile and apparel industry much more than an economic statistic. It is an important part of the country’s social and economic transformation, and for the past ten years, Textile Focus has been one of the dedicated platforms telling that story. Photo: Sultan Mahmud Sohal, Country Manager, Corporate Responsibility, KM International GmbH (Branch office of FLORETT TEXTIL GmbH & Co. KG) The 10th anniversary of Textile Focus, therefore, is more than an occasion for congratulations. It is an opportunity to recognise the value of having a newspaper whose core purpose is to remain close to Bangladesh’s garments and textile industry

articles.o: Sustainable composite buttons from textile waste
articles.s: A waste-to-value approach using cotton knit waste, wood sawdust and ETP sludge Introduction Buttons are small fastening devices commonly used in clothing and accessories to secure or decorate garments...
articles.x: A waste-to-value approach using cotton knit waste, wood sawdust and ETP sludge Introduction Buttons are small fastening devices commonly used in clothing and accessories to secure or decorate garments. They are usually made from materials like plastic, metal, shell, wood, or resin. Plastic buttons, such as those made from ABS, polyester, and nylon, are popular because they are inexpensive, durable, and easy to design. However, these synthetic materials contribute to microplastic pollution, release harmful chemicals during production, and do not break down naturally. This raises serious environmental concerns [1]. With around 60 billion buttons produced each year, even a slight change to sustainable materials can significantly impact the environment [2] At the same time, the textile and fashion industries significantly harm the environment. They contribute to solid textile waste. Textile Solid Waste (TSW) is categorized into pre-consumer, production, and post-consumer waste. The textile sector generates nearly 5% of all global waste, while millions of tonnes of textile waste are generated and disposed of in landfills each year. [3]. This study explores making composite buttons using waste fabric, wood sawdust, and ETP sludge, with epoxy resin as the binder using the Hand Lay-Up method. Findings show that these waste-based composites could serve as a sustainable and functional alternative to traditional plastic buttons in the textile industry Objectives The goal of this project is to create sustainable composite buttons using leftover textiles and assess how well they work for real-world uses. articles.o: ELGI Electric: Engineering the Future of Textile Automation
articles.s: From pioneering India’s Overhead Travelling Cleaner more than five decades ago to developing intelligent automation systems for modern spinning mills, ELGI Electric is now making automation the next major chapter… The post ELGI Electric: Engineering the Future of Textile Automation appeared first on
articles.x: From pioneering India’s Overhead Travelling Cleaner more than five decades ago to developing intelligent automation systems for modern spinning mills, ELGI Electric is now making automation the next major chapter in its engineering journey. V.S. Balasubramanian, President-Operations , ELGI Electric “Whenever we introduced a new product, we never compromised on technology. We first identified the best technology available anywhere in the world and then worked towards making it even better for Indian customers. That philosophy has remained unchanged throughout our journey.” This philosophy perhaps best explains both the longevity of ELGI Electric Industries Ltd. and the direction in which the Coimbatore-based engineering company is now heading. For more than six decades, ELGI Electric has built its reputation by identifying emerging technologies, adapting them to Indian textile manufacturing and continuously refining them in close collaboration with customers. Its pioneering introduction of the Overhead Travelling Cleaner (OHTC) to India established the company’s position in textile machinery. Subsequent developments in yarn conditioning, fire and metal detection and Bobbin Transportation Systems expanded that engineering base. Today, however, the opportunity is considerably larger. As textile manufacturing becomes increasingly automated, connected and data-driven, ELGI Electric is moving beyond individual machines towards integrated automation solutions that connect processes, reduce manual intervention and improve productivity. The shift is being driven by a fundamental change in the industry’s requirements. articles.s: 글로벌 러닝화 브랜드 호카(HOKA)의 기존 국내 총판 조이웍스 임직원 비상대책위원회(이하 비대위)가 미국 데커스(Deckers) 본사와 조이웍스 간 판권 분쟁이 국제중재 절차에서 진행 중인 가운데 이랜드의 호카 전담조직 채용에 반발하며 채용 절차 중단을 요구했다.비대위는 2일 입장문을 통해 이랜드가 상품기획·온라인MD·영업·마케팅·디자인·생산 등 호카 사업 관련 6개 직군의 경력직 채용에 나섰다며 국제중재가 끝나지 않은 상황에서 사업 준비가 진행되고 있다고 주장했다.호카의 국내 유통권을 둘러싼 갈등은 데커스와 기존 총판 조이웍스

articles.o: 트루릴리젼, 아티스트 양홍원과 두 번째 컬렉션 공개
articles.s: 글로벌 데님 브랜드 트루릴리젼(TRUE RELIGION)이 아티스트 양홍원과 함께 시즌 두 번째 컬렉션을 공개했다.양홍원 특유의 거칠고 자유로운 에너지에 트루릴리젼만의 대담한 감각을 더해, 브랜드의 정체성을 한층 강렬하게 풀어냈다. 특히 비밀스러운 공간에서 펼쳐지는 캠페인을 통해 양홍원이 지닌 날것의 분위기와 컬렉션의 독특한 서사를 시각적으로 담아냈다.캠페인은 오래된 창고를 연상시키는 공간을 배경으로 전개된다. 낡은 컨테이너 안에는 그가 놓치지 않으려했던 것, 자신만의 방식으로 손에 넣은 것들이 뒤섞여 있다. 시간이 지나며 쌓인 흔

articles.s: 제이엔케이코퍼레이션(대표 곽한별, 심희원)이 전개하는 여성 컨템포러리 브랜드 틸아이다이(TILL I DIE)가 2026 WINTER 컬렉션을 공개했다.이번 컬렉션은 차분한 색감과 부드러운 소재를 중심으로 겨울 특유의 포근한 분위기를 담았다. 클래식한 실루엣과 풍성한 텍스처를 바탕으로 핸드메이드 코트와 재킷, 퍼 점퍼, 울 니트 등 다양한 시즌 아이템을 구성했다.주력 제품인 ‘울 100 핸드메이드 하프 코트’는 울 100% 소재에 핸드메이드 봉제를 적용해 간결한 실루엣을 구현했다. 소재 중량을 높여 보온성을 강화하는 동시에 봉제 방식

articles.t: 아윌미백, 우주글로벌과 중국 총판 계약…온·오프라인 유통 확대 추진
articles.o: 아윌미백, 우주글로벌과 중국 총판 계약…온·오프라인 유통 확대 추진
articles.s: 언노운네이처의 착색 케어 브랜드 아윌미백은 우주글로벌과 중국 총판 계약을 체결했다.아윌미백 측에 따르면 ‘뱀파이어 톤업 스프레이’는 지난 7월 중국 왕홍 따따의 라이브 방송에서 준비 물량이 약 2시간 만에 소진됐다. 브랜드는 해당 기간 더우인 주간 판매 1위를 기록했으며 이후 수만 개 단위 추가 물량을 현지에 공급했다고 밝혔다.우주글로벌은 지난 6월부터 해당 제품의 중국 물량 공급을 담당해 왔으며 이번 계약을 통해 공식 총판 역할을 맡는다. 양사는 온라인 판매를 중심으로 유통을 운영한 뒤 오프라인 채널까지 단계적으로 확대할 계획이다

articles.t: 피지 모락셀라, 누적 매출 600억원 기록…쿠팡 세탁세제 부문 3개월 연속 1위
articles.o: 피지 모락셀라, 누적 매출 600억원 기록…쿠팡 세탁세제 부문 3개월 연속 1위
articles.s: LG생활건강의 세탁 브랜드 ‘피지 모락셀라’는 2024년 7월부터 2026년 9월까지 출하 실적 기준 누적 매출 600억원을 기록했다고 밝혔다.브랜드 측 집계에 따르면 ‘모락셀라 세탁세제’는 쿠팡 전체 세탁세제 관련 카테고리에서 7월부터 9월까지 3개월 연속 판매 1위를 기록했다. ‘모락셀라 냄새제거부스터’의 누적 판매량은 5000만 알을 넘어섰다.기간별 매출도 증가했다. LG생활건강에 따르면 8월 16~31일 매출은 같은 달 1~15일보다 8.6% 늘었고, 9월 1~15일 매출은 8월 같은 기간보다 13% 증가했다.제품에는 자사

articles.s: 어느새 성큼 다가온 가을, 이 좋은 계절에 섬유인의 마음은 우울하고 초조하다. 추석 명절을 보내고 계절적인 성수기를 맞은 섬유 업계는 시장이 꿈쩍 않고 오히려 나락으로 빠져들고 있어 실망을 넘어 절망을 토로하고 있다.한국의 섬유 산업중 면방· 화섬· 봉제 주력 산업은 이미 공동화(空洞化)된지 오래고 마지막 보루인 직물· 염색 산업마저 공멸의 불구덩이를 향해 속도를 내고 있다. 사람이 늙어가듯 산업도 늙어가는 것은 당연한 순리다. 고목이 쓰러지기 전에 병충해도 대비하고 거름을 줬어야 함에도 늙고 병든 섬유 산업은 골든 타임을 이미 놓

articles.t: 더퓨처, 1~3분기 글로벌본부 매출 전년 대비 841% 증가
articles.o: 더퓨처, 1~3분기 글로벌본부 매출 전년 대비 841% 증가
articles.s: 더퓨처는 2026년 1~3분기 글로벌본부 매출이 전년 동기 대비 841% 증가했다고 밝혔다.회사 집계 기준 약 9.4배 수준으로, 국가별 제품 운영과 이커머스 채널 확대가 매출 증가에 영향을 미쳤다는 설명이다. 중국에서는 현지 소비자 수요를 반영한 제품과 마케팅을 운영하고 있으며 일본에서는 이너뷰티 브랜드 ‘낫띵베럴’을 중심으로 큐텐 등 이커머스 채널에서 판매하고 있다.미국에서는 틱톡샵을 활용한 판매와 콘텐츠 운영을 진행하고 있다. 항노화 뷰티 브랜드 EOA의 글로벌 플랫폼 입점도 단계적으로 추진한다. 내년 1월 ‘CES 2027’

articles.o: Six forces reweaving the future of global textiles
articles.s: For decades, the global textile industry followed a simple formula: make more, make it faster and make it cheaper. That formula built enormous manufacturing hubs, expanded global sourcing networks and...
articles.x: For decades, the global textile industry followed a simple formula: make more, make it faster and make it cheaper. That formula built enormous manufacturing hubs, expanded global sourcing networks and made polyester the workhorse of modern textiles. But the formula is changing. Global fiber production reached a record 132 million tons in 2024 , up from around 125 million tons in 2023. Production has more than doubled since 2000 and under business-as-usual conditions could reach approximately 169 million tons by 2030 . Courtesy: Collected The industry is being pushed to use different materials, reduce waste, automate production, prove its claims and build supply chains that can withstand disruption. Six forces are changing this transition: man-made fibers, circularity, AI and automation, traceability, supply-chain regionalization and advanced materials. Together, they are rewriting the economics of textiles. MMFs If one fiber defines the modern textile economy, it is polyester. Polyester represented around 59% of global fiber production in 2024 , with output rising from approximately 71 million tons in 2023 to about 78 million tons in 2024. Yet around 88% of polyester remained fossil-based . That creates one of the industry's biggest contradictions. Sustainability ambitions are growing while dependence on virgin synthetic materials continues to increase. Replacing polyester entirely is unlikely to happen quickly. Its durability, affordability, versatility and performance have made it indispensable across sportswear, outerwear, home textiles and everyday apparel. articles.x: HELSINKI – Global synthetic fibre production could have been almost half its current level without the rise of fast fashion. This is according to new research which used computer modelling to examine how the textile industry might otherwise have developed. Researchers estimate that synthetic fibre production in 2021 could have been 47 per cent lower without the growth associated with fast fashion. articles.o: Kraig Labs ships first commercial spider silk yarn
articles.s: Kraig Biocraft Laboratories has shipped its first commercial order of recombinant spider silk yarn, marking a significant step towards the use of the company’s technology in performance textiles. The custom-engineered yarn was produced to fulfil a purchase commitment from an unnamed global performan
articles.x: Kraig Biocraft Laboratories has shipped its first commercial order of recombinant spider silk yarn, marking a significant step towards the use of the company’s technology in performance textiles. The custom-engineered yarn was produced to fulfil a purchase commitment from an unnamed global performance sports brand and will now be developed into a new performance textile. The shipment forms part of a confidential pilot development programme targeting the athletic apparel market. Kraig Labs said the yarn has been custom processed to the customer’s specifications, with the initial volume intentionally kept small for the precision application. “Completing the delivery of this spider silk yarn is a huge milestone for Kraig Labs,” said Kim Thompson, founder and CEO of Kraig Labs. “The volume is small by design. This is a precision application, not a bulk order.” Kraig Labs’ technology uses genetically engineered silkworms incorporating key spider silk proteins to produce recombinant spider silk. The company believes the resulting combination of strength, flexibility, toughness and low weight makes the material particularly suited to demanding performance applications. The commercial shipment follows the company’s work to move its spider silk technology from development and scaled production towards customer-led textile applications. Kraig Labs sees elite performance apparel as a potentially important proving ground for the technology, where improvements in strength-to-weight ratio, durability and other material properties can translate directly into product performance. “High-performance sport is where materials prove themselves,” Thompson said. “Performance wins. articles.o: Texverse 2.0 to be held at BUTEX on October 30
articles.s: The Bangladesh University of Textiles (BUTEX) will host the national competition ‘Texverse 2.0’ on October 30, bringing together students from universities, textile engineering colleges, and higher secondary institutions for competitions focused on research, innovation, creativity, and problem-solvi
articles.x: The Bangladesh University of Textiles (BUTEX) will host the national competition ‘Texverse 2.0’ on October 30, bringing together students from universities, textile engineering colleges, and higher secondary institutions for competitions focused on research, innovation, creativity, and problem-solving. Organized by the BUTEX Science Club, the day-long event will begin at 8:00 am and continue until evening. Different segments of the competition will be held at the university’s Auditorium, Seminar Room, Academic Building, and Central Field, while some competitions will be conducted online. The event has so far established collaboration with 25 student clubs and organizations from different universities and textile colleges across the country. These include KUET Textile Club, BUP Career Club, Textile Club-MBSTU, DUET Textile Career & Research Club, NITER Science Society, BUFT Career Development Club, Daffodil AI Club, Southeast University Textile Club (SEUTC), Green University Textile Club (GUTC), Sonargaon University Textile Club, and RTEC Research Club, among others. The competition aims to encourage students to engage in research and innovation while developing practical and sustainable solutions to challenges faced by the textile sector. It will also provide participants with a platform to showcase their creative ideas, technical knowledge, and problem-solving abilities. At the university level, the competition will feature project exhibition, research-based poster presentation, quiz competition, textile case competition, treasure hunt, essay writing and an artificial intelligence-based video-making competition. articles.s: The global Tencel fiber products market is expanding as apparel brands and textile manufacturers increase their use of lower-impact cellulosic fibers. According to Verified Market Reports, the market...
articles.x: The global Tencel fiber products market is expanding as apparel brands and textile manufacturers increase their use of lower-impact cellulosic fibers. According to Verified Market Reports, the market was valued at $3.5 billion in 2025. It is projected to reach $6.15 billion by 2033, growing at a 7.8% CAGR from 2026 to 2033. The growth is supported by demand for sustainable materials, stronger traceability requirements and advances in fiber technology. Tencel products include Lyocell and Modal fibers, which are used across apparel, home textiles and technical applications. A separate 2026 market analysis gives a more detailed view of the fabric segment. According to PW Consulting, the Tencel fiber fabric market reached $3.67 billion in 2025 and could reach $5.94 billion by 2032, at a 7.15% CAGR. Lyocell fiber fabric held the largest share at 59.8%. Apparel remains the largest end-use segment. Apparel and clothing generated about $2.37 billion, or 64.7% of the Tencel fiber fabric market, in 2025. Home textiles followed with $927.7 million, or 25.3%. Technical textiles accounted for $365.4 million, or 10%. Asia-Pacific remains the largest regional market. It generated about $1.64 billion in Tencel fiber fabric revenue in 2025. Europe followed at $929.8 million, while North America reached $656.8 million. The broader fiber market also shows stronger demand for regenerated cellulose. According to Lenzing, global production of lyocell, modal, and viscose increased about 4% to 8.7 million tons in 2025. Lyocell and modal output increased at a double-digit rate. Technology remains a major differentiator. TENCEL™ Lyocell uses a closed-loop process that recovers more than 99.8% of the solvent. articles.x: DHAKA – Bangladesh is set to quadruple polyester-chip capacity at a local producer, in a bid to reduce reliance on imported synthetic textile inputs. The move comes as garment makers seek to expand beyond cotton and move into new product segments. The Asian Development Bank (ADB) has signed a US$50mloan with Modern Syntex Limited, part of TK Group, to expand its polyester-chip manufacturing operation in the Mirsarai Economic Zone near Chattogram. The project will increase the plant’s capacity from 107 tonnes to 407 tonnes a day. It is designed to produce high-intrinsic-viscosity polyester chips for higher-value textile and apparel applications, with commercial operations targeted for 2027. The investment comes as Bangladesh’s garment industry remains heavily weighted towards cotton, while manufacturers look to capture more orders for man-made-fibre products. Industry estimates put man-made-fibre apparel at about 25 per cent of Bangladesh’s garment export revenues, compared with around 70 per cent of global clothing consumption. Polyester demand in Bangladesh is estimated to be growing by about 10 per cent a year. The Business Standard reported in September that annual local demand is around 140,000–160,000 tonnes for polyester staple fibre, while demand for polyester yarn is estimated at 500,000–550,000 tonnes. The same report said Modern Syntex already produces polyester staple fibre, filament yarn and PET chips, and meets nearly 21% of the country’s demand for polyester products. It also reported that a significant share of domestic demand is still met through imports. The ADB-backed expansion is therefore part of a broader effort to build domestic capacity, rather than Bangladesh’s first move into polyester production. articles.o: Paul Schlack Prize for Senbis bioplastics researcher
articles.s: Momo Naeimirad of Netherlands-based Senbis Polymer Innovations has received the 2026 Paul Schlack Prize for research into the relationship between the performance and biodegradation of melt-spun bioplastic fibres. Presented at the 65th Dornbirn Global Fiber Congress held in Austria from September 16
articles.x: Momo Naeimirad of Netherlands-based Senbis Polymer Innovations has received the 2026 Paul Schlack Prize for research into the relationship between the performance and biodegradation of melt-spun bioplastic fibres. Presented at the 65th Dornbirn Global Fiber Congress held in Austria from September 16-18, the award recognised Naeimirad’s PolyBioDeg research into how the structure and properties of melt-spun bioplastic fibres influence both their mechanical performance during use and their subsequent biodegradation. Naeimirad is affiliated with Senbis and the University of Amsterdam. The Paul Schlack Prize is one of the fibre industry’s longest-established awards for young researchers. First awarded in 1971 and named after Paul Schlack, the inventor of polyamide 6, it is intended to encourage research and development in the manufacture, processing and application of man-made fibres in Europe. The €3,000 prize is awarded annually at Dornbirn following assessment by an independent jury. Naeimirad’s work addresses an increasingly important challenge for biodegradable polymers – achieving the mechanical and processing performance required during a product’s useful life while ensuring that the material can subsequently biodegrade under appropriate environmental conditions. It is an issue closely related to the wider development programme of Senbis at its base in Emmen, the Netherlands. The company used Dornbirn’s Innovation Day and Forum to present its GreenPearls range of biodegradable compounds for fibre and filament production. The materials are being engineered specifically around individual fibre-forming processes, with the aim of overcoming some of the processing and performance limitations traditionally associated with biodegradable polymers. articles.x: With its state-of-the-art manufacturing facility in Ranipet now fully operational, AMANN Group is moving into a new phase of growth in India—combining global thread expertise with local manufacturing, faster delivery, application support and a growing portfolio of sustainable and high-performance solutions. Sanjeev Grewal, Regional Business Director – Asia, Middle East & Pacific , Amann Group For AMANN Group, India is no longer simply another market in its global network. It is emerging as a strategically important manufacturing and consumption centre, with opportunities extending across apparel, home textiles, footwear, leather and technical applications. The German thread specialist, which began its Indian journey with a trading operation in Chennai in 2007, has now taken a significant step forward by establishing a modern manufacturing facility at Ranipet in Tamil Nadu. The transformation reflects AMANN’s confidence in the long-term potential of the Indian textile and allied industries. After spending years understanding the market, its customers and their requirements, the company commenced construction of the Ranipet plant in 2022. Commercial production began towards the end of 2024, following a two-year delay caused by the pandemic. The facility has since completed its ramp-up phase and is now fully equipped to serve the Indian market with AMANN’s portfolio of products. articles.o: Getting to grips with silk
articles.s: A robotic hand developed by Chinese firm Agilink has been taught foundational Suzhou embroidery techniques by master craftswoman Fu Xianghong, including separating silk threads, threading a needle, stretching fabric on an embroidery hoop and stitching. The demonstration puts a robotic hand to work w
articles.x: A robotic hand developed by Chinese firm Agilink has been taught foundational Suzhou embroidery techniques by master craftswoman Fu Xianghong, including separating silk threads, threading a needle, stretching fabric on an embroidery hoop and stitching. The demonstration puts a robotic hand to work with one of the most delicate and deformable materials it can encounter. A silk thread can bend, slip and change shape with slight changes in contact. Splitting silk requires one finger to separate individual strands while others maintain support and tension. Twisting thread meanwhile requires opposing fingertips to maintain contact while allowing the thread to turn. Threading a needle and stitching add further demands on positioning, force and coordination. The OmniHand 3 Ultra combines 21 active degrees of freedom with a fully direct-drive architecture and tactile sensing across the fingertips, finger pads and palm. Vision-based tactile sensors at each fingertip detect changes in the contact surface, providing feedback as the hand handles thin, deformable materials. “A single silk thread gives OmniHand 3 Ultra’s fingertip dexterity a visible measure,” said Qiao Tianjie, vice president of Agibot and CEO of Agilink. “It also reveals the possibility of handing more delicate work to machines.” The demonstration comes as Agilink reaches a new stage of commercial scale. Spun out from Agibot in January 2026, the company has shipped more than 15,000 dexterous hands to date. In August, its OmniHand series competed across all eight dexterous-hand events at the World Humanoid Robot Games, winning seven gold, four silver and three bronze medals. articles.s: As the global textile machinery industry prepares to meet at ITMA ASIA in Shanghai this November, Swedish textile technology companies are responding to a rapidly changing market with investment, innovation and new solutions. Growing competition from Asia, geopolitical uncertainty, new regulations a
articles.x: As the global textile machinery industry prepares to meet at ITMA ASIA in Shanghai this November, Swedish textile technology companies are responding to a rapidly changing market with investment, innovation and new solutions. Growing competition from Asia, geopolitical uncertainty, new regulations and the accelerating impact of AI and digitalisation are reshaping the industry. Against this backdrop, TMAS members have had a busy 2026, with new facilities, product launches and technologies addressing automation, productivity, recycling and more resource-efficient textile manufacturing. Following a record 2025 and a number of bolt-on acquisitions, ACG Kinna has inaugurated a 1,000-square-metre expansion at its headquarters in Skene in response to growing demand for its complete textile and finished product line automation services. Imogo, a pioneer in industrial spray dyeing, has opened a new showroom, test centre and production hub in Kinnahult. Imogo introduced its first Dye-Max prototype in 2019 and completed its first industrial-scale installation in 2021. The new facility now enables brands and manufacturers to move from laboratory development to validated commercial production in one location. The centre features Imogo’s patented spray application technology, combining the Mini-Max laboratory system with a fully operational industrial-scale Dye-Max line for fabrics up to 2.4 metres wide and a production capacity of approximately 3 tons per day. Using as little as 0.7 litres of dye liquor per kilogram of fabric, Dye-Max delivers major reductions in water, energy, chemicals and wastewater compared with conventional dyeing. articles.o: NITER Students Gain Textile Technology and Industrial Exposure Through China Training Programme
articles.s: Eight students from the National Institute of Textile Engineering and Research (NITER) have successfully completed an international training programme in China, gaining practical exposure to advanced textile technologies, industrial operations, academic practices and cultural heritage. The training
articles.x: Eight students from the National Institute of Textile Engineering and Research (NITER) have successfully completed an international training programme in China, gaining practical exposure to advanced textile technologies, industrial operations, academic practices and cultural heritage. The training programme was organised under the initiative of the Bangladesh Textile Mills Association (BTMA), providing the participating students with an opportunity to experience China’s advanced textile manufacturing ecosystem beyond classroom-based learning. During the programme, the students explored modern textile production systems, automation, quality control and industrial management practices. Their exposure covered several key areas of textile manufacturing, including spinning technology, woven fabric dyeing, man-made fibre dyeing, fabric structure and textile design. As part of the industrial visits, the students visited Shengshan Group (至山集团), where they observed modern woven fabric dyeing operations and industrial production processes. They also gained insights into the integrated technologies and production capabilities used in China’s advanced spinning sector. The programme also included academic and cultural sessions at Zhejiang Agriculture and Business College. The students participated in sessions covering Chinese 3D media, tea culture and tea processing, Chinese language, traditional armour culture, and artificial intelligence-driven vehicle technology. At Shaoxing Secondary Technical School, the students received hands-on exposure to traditional natural indigo dyeing and printing techniques. articles.x: Author: Ahmed Javed Jamal, Country Manager, Silkflex Bangladesh Limited How a screen-printing unit uses energy, how low-cure chemicals help, which savings are evidence-backed , and what to do first. Bangladesh has 883 textile printing units, and in most of them the largest energy user is the conveyor dryer or tunnel oven at the end of the line. Many of those units also deal with unreliable power, so every kilowatt-hour and every cubic meter of gas counts. articles.o: CISUTAC helps advance textile circularity
articles.s: The CISUTAC project has concluded after four years of work across the European textile value chain, releasing a package of technologies, open data, consumer research and policy recommendations designed to support the transition towards a circular textile and clothing sector. The final results were p
articles.x: The CISUTAC project has concluded after four years of work across the European textile value chain, releasing a package of technologies, open data, consumer research and policy recommendations designed to support the transition towards a circular textile and clothing sector. The final results were presented on 22 and 23 September at the ECOSYSTEX Conference in Antwerp, where project partners outlined progress in repair, disassembly, recycling, consumer behaviour and policy development. CISUTAC tested new repair, disassembly and recycling technologies under real operating conditions. These included methods to significantly reduce the time needed for full zipper repairs, automated disassembly systems for difficult-to-recycle protective equipment and trials showing that recycled fibres can be spun into yarns with sufficient strength for use in new garments. The project has also produced open tools and datasets intended to make textile sorting faster and more consistent. Alongside the technical work, CISUTAC carried out large-scale consumer research supported by national awareness campaigns and local guidelines. The aim was to identify the factors influencing decisions to repair, reuse and purchase second-hand textiles, while exploring ways of encouraging more circular consumption habits. Policy work formed the third major strand of the project. Assessments of possible future scenarios for the European textile sector were used to develop recommendations covering waste management, public procurement, ecodesign, standardisation and Extended Producer Responsibility.
