articles.o: The Next Generation of Fiber Will Not Be Defined by the Claim
articles.s: As new EU rules raise the evidentiary bar for environmental claims from 27 September, Good Earth Cotton® has built an evidence-led model over eight years based on primary farm-level data, independently verified outcomes, and fiber physically verified at source. From 27 September, new measures implem
articles.x: As new EU rules raise the evidentiary bar for environmental claims from 27 September, Good Earth Cotton® has built an evidence-led model over eight years based on primary farm-level data, independently verified outcomes, and fiber physically verified at source. From 27 September, new measures implementing the European Union’s Empowering Consumers for the Green Transition Directive, known as EmpCo, begin to apply across EU Member States. The rules raise the evidentiary threshold for environmental claims, including restricting generic environmental claims that cannot demonstrate recognized environmental performance. For Good Earth Cotton® (GEC), this regulatory shift reflects the direction of its evidence-led model: moving beyond practice-based assumptions and broad environmental claims toward measured outcomes, primary farm-level data, independent verification, and fiber physically verified at source. European Commission analysis has found that 53% of green claims examined in the EU market provide vague, misleading or unfounded information, 40% have no supporting evidence, and half of green labels offer weak or non-existent verification. The regulatory direction is clear: environmental claims are increasingly expected to be supported by credible evidence. EmpCo’s significance extends beyond its individual prohibitions. It reflects a broader shift from environmental claims toward substantiation — placing greater emphasis on what can be evidenced before a claim is made. For fibre, that distinction matters. Cotton accounted for approximately 19% of global fibre production in 2024, representing around 24.5 million tonnes, while recycled cotton accounted for approximately 1% of global cotton production, at around 300,000 tonnes. articles.s: Cynergy Limited has signed an agreement with Dutch-Bangla Pack Limited (DBPL) to develop a 608 kWp rooftop solar power project at DBPL’s manufacturing facility in Gazaria, Munshiganj. Established in 2007, Dutch-Bangla Pack Limited is a Netherlands–Bangladesh joint venture and a 100% export-oriented
articles.x: Cynergy Limited has signed an agreement with Dutch-Bangla Pack Limited (DBPL) to develop a 608 kWp rooftop solar power project at DBPL’s manufacturing facility in Gazaria, Munshiganj. Established in 2007, Dutch-Bangla Pack Limited is a Netherlands–Bangladesh joint venture and a 100% export-oriented manufacturer of Flexible Intermediate Bulk Containers (FIBCs/Big Bags) for the food, pharmaceutical and industrial sectors. Under the project, a 608 kWp rooftop solar PV system will be installed at DBPL’s industrial facility. The solar installation is expected to supply renewable electricity directly to manufacturing operations, helping reduce dependence on grid electricity and associated carbon emissions. DBPL operates as a vertically integrated manufacturing facility with High Care Cleanroom capabilities and holds internationally recognized certifications, including ISO 9001, ISO 14001, ISO 45001, FSSC 22000 and SA8000 . According to Cynergy, the project represents another step toward expanding solar energy adoption across Bangladesh’s export-oriented manufacturing sector. The company said its team will focus on maintaining high standards of engineering, safety, quality and project execution. The 608 kWp installation will also contribute to transforming industrial rooftops into clean-energy assets, supporting the sector’s transition toward more sustainable manufacturing. articles.x: REMSCHEID, Germany— September 24, 2026 — Maintenance and service processes in chemical fiber spinning plants have a significant impact on product quality, equipment availability, and workplace safety. With three new retrofittable solutions, Barmag helps producers make manual work processes more efficient, safer, and more reproducible. Maintenance as a competitive advantage The portfolio includes the automatic knife sharpening machine, the wiping robot for automated spinneret cleaning both in filament spinning and in the staple fiber process, and the electric Spinpack changer for motor-assisted replacement of spinning packages. Together, these solutions aim to standardize maintenance processes and sustainably improve the performance of existing production facilities. Automated cleaning for stable processes The automatic knife sharpening machine ensures consistently high cleaning quality for spinnerets and helps producers increase the performance of their spinning systems. Standardized grinding results reduce process fluctuations, increase cleaning efficiency, and extend the service life of key components. Barmag’s automatic knife sharpening machine ensures consistently high-quality grinding results, thereby helping to reduce process fluctuations. This leads to reduced maintenance requirements, higher equipment availability, and improved productivity. Customer experience shows increases in the full-bobbin rate of up to 12 percent, in take-up efficiency of up to 28 percent, and an extension of spinneret service life of up to 51 percent. At the same time, cleaning cycles can be reduced by up to 53 percent. The wiping robot performs spinneret cleaning fully automatically both in filament spinning and in the staple fiber process. articles.o: Fair and Vibrant PC Elections Held at Fakir Knitwears Ltd. and Fakir Eco Knitwears Ltd
articles.s: Setting a strong benchmark for workplace democracy and industrial harmony, Fakir Knitwears Ltd. and Fakir Eco Knitwears Ltd. successfully completed their Participation Committee (PC) elections on September 22, 2026. The election process was carried out across both facilities in a free, fair, transpa
articles.x: Setting a strong benchmark for workplace democracy and industrial harmony, Fakir Knitwears Ltd. and Fakir Eco Knitwears Ltd. successfully completed their Participation Committee (PC) elections on September 22, 2026. The election process was carried out across both facilities in a free, fair, transparent, and vibrant atmosphere. The election saw enthusiastic participation from the workforce, reflecting high engagement and trust in the collective representation process. • Fakir Knitwears Ltd.: A total of 93 candidates contested for 15 designated seats. Following an orderly and competitive vote count, 24 representatives were declared victorious. • Fakir Eco Knitwears Ltd.: The contest featured 27 candidates vying across 3 seats, resulting in the election of 12 worker representatives. The entire electoral procedure was closely observed by Mr. Sofiqul Islam, Assistant Director of the Department of Inspection for Factories and Establishments (Labour Office). During his visit, Mr. Islam inspected the voting booths, monitored the polling process firsthand, and commended the management, election commission, and workers for organizing such a peaceful, systematic, and credible election. The successful formation of the new Participation Committees marks another significant milestone for the Fakir Group, strengthening worker-management collaboration, ensuring effective social dialogue, and reinforcing a fair, inclusive workplace culture. articles.o: Study shows hemp can improve comfort and performance in denim
articles.s: Hemp is gaining attention in denim not only as a lower-impact fiber alternative but also as a way to improve fabric performance. A new study by textile engineering researchers at Istanbul Technical Un...
articles.x: Hemp is gaining attention in denim not only as a lower-impact fiber alternative but also as a way to improve fabric performance. A new study by textile engineering researchers at Istanbul Technical University in Türkiye found that adding hemp to stretch denim can improve moisture management, thermal comfort, and tactile properties. Figure: Companies including Levi’s, Lucky Brand, and Naked & Famous have used hemp in denim products. Courtesy: Collected Published in the Research Journal of Textile and Apparel , the study examined hemp in single-core and dual-core stretch yarns. Researchers tested cotton and elastane blends as well as cotton, T400, and elastane blends. They evaluated seven denim fabric compositions in both untreated and rinsed conditions. The tests covered moisture management, thermal performance, and fabric handle. The results showed that hemp improved several moisture-related properties. These included air permeability, water absorption, vertical and transfer wicking, drying efficiency, and relative water vapor permeability. The improvements were particularly notable in fabrics made with single-core yarn blends. Hemp also influenced the denim's thermal behavior. The fiber increased thermal absorptivity, which can create a cooler feel against the skin. Hemp has already gained traction among denim brands. Companies including Levi’s, Lucky Brand, and Naked & Famous have used hemp in denim products. However, its relatively coarse fiber has generally limited its share in denim blends, with many products using around 20% to 30% hemp. For example, Fashion for Good’s Beyond50 Denim project explored technologies to increase hemp content to 50% or more by making hemp fibers better suited for apparel applications. articles.o: UTS adds Shima Seiki technology for advanced knit prototyping
articles.s: The Advanced Fabrication Research Lab (AFRL) at the University of Technology Sydney (UTS) has expanded its textile research capabilities with new Shima Seiki knitting and 3D design technology. Figure...
articles.x: The Advanced Fabrication Research Lab (AFRL) at the University of Technology Sydney (UTS) has expanded its textile research capabilities with new Shima Seiki knitting and 3D design technology. Figure: WHOLEGARMENT technology can produce knitted products in one piece, reducing the need for conventional cut-and-sew assembly.Courtesy: Collected. The research facility has installed a Shima Seiki SWG-XR WHOLEGARMENT computerized flat knitting machine along with the SDS-ONE APEX4 3D design system. The new setup is designed to support seamless knit development from digital design to physical prototypes. It will give researchers an integrated environment to develop and test knitted structures for different applications. The technology will support research across fashion, architecture, product design, engineering, and sustainability. WHOLEGARMENT technology can produce knitted products in one piece, reducing the need for conventional cut-and-sew assembly. The SDS-ONE APEX4 system adds 3D design capabilities to the workflow. Researchers can develop and visualize knitted products digitally before moving to machine-based prototyping. The investment is expected to strengthen UTS's research into advanced knitted structures and broaden the use of knitting beyond conventional apparel applications. articles.x: HUNTERSVILLE, N.C. — September 25, 2026 — Microban International, a global supplier of product protection technologies, has partnered with mountain sports specialist ORTOVOX to incorporate Microban odor-capture technology into its debut mountain bike collection, the Sequence Series. articles.x: The UK’s post-consumer textile waste is driving a new industry effort to build large-scale recycling infrastructure. New Look, Marks & Spencer (M&S), and Sainsbury’s Tu Clothing have joined The Circuit, an initiative focused on recovering and processing textiles that can no longer be reused. Figure: The Circuit aims to collect, sort, and pre-process these textiles into feedstock for existing and emerging fiber-to-fiber recycling technologies. Courtesy:Collected The UK generated about 1.4 million tons of post-consumer textiles in 2024. Nearly half of this volume is estimated to be non-reusable, creating a growing need for systems that can recover textile fibers at scale. The Circuit aims to collect, sort, and pre-process these textiles into feedstock for existing and emerging fiber-to-fiber recycling technologies. Circle-8 Textile Ecosystems is developing the infrastructure and commercial framework behind the initiative. Its model includes automated textile sorting and pre-processing facilities located close to where textiles reach end of use. The first phase is scheduled to begin in January 2027 at Oxfam’s site in Batley, Yorkshire. The phase will focus on automated sorting, traceability, identifying recycling opportunities, and developing relationships with recyclers. Oxfam will operate the automated sorting equipment and separate reusable textiles from materials that can no longer be worn or reused. The organization will also bring its long experience in textile collection, reuse, and recovery. New Look, M&S, and Sainsbury’s Tu Clothing are among the founding retail partners. articles.x: Ethical Trading Initiative Bangladesh organized a Rapid Energy Transition Conference in Dhaka focusing on “Powering Security, Sustainability & Growth in Bangladesh RMG”, at the Bangladesh Military Museum in Dhaka. The event brought together Business Associations, Manufacturers, Brands and Sectoral experts to discuss how Bangladesh’s RMG sector can accelerate the transition towards renewable energy and industrial decarbonization. Nishat Hamid , Chairman, Standing Committee on Energy Optimization, BGMEA and Director, Shasha Garments & EOS Textile Mills, stressed that the next few years will be decisive for Bangladesh’s competitiveness following LDC graduation stating: “RE is no longer just an environmental agenda, buyer requirement or a CSR strategy, it is fundamental to our core cost and market competitiveness for global survival.” She highlighted the need for predictable tariffs, access to technically viable renewable energy solutions and green finance, effective regulatory frameworks, and bankable Power Purchase Agreements (PPAs) as critical pillars for enabling factories to make the transition. Kazy Mohammad Iqbal Hossain, South Asia Regional Sustainability Manager, Lindex HK Ltd, also spoke at the event. The session was further enriched by keynotes from Priyong Sabastini from ETI Bangladesh and Chief Executive, Hasan Mehedi from CLEAN BD, alongside a solidarity address by Development Anthropologist, Dr. UKM Shawkat Ara Begum, who all highlighted the profound social and economic dividends of moving toward a low-carbon sector. articles.x: Same-store retail spends across India climbed 9.6% year-on-year in August, up from 7.1% in July. That is the finding of the second edition of SANKET (Spends & Key Emerging Trends), the quarterly like-for-like tracker published jointly by the Retailers Association of India (RAI) and Innoviti. The report draws on more than 70 million transactions at over 100,000 checkout points, across 2,800-plus towns and 10,000-plus PIN codes. It is the strongest monthly reading since April, and it settles a question that had hung over Q1: whether the slowdown earlier this year reflected weakening demand or simply a run of bad timing. The August numbers say the latter. The strength is not confined to one category or one region. Grocery & General Retail led the field at 9.9%, up from 7.5% in July. Fashion & Lifestyle turned around sharply, from 4.5% to 8.5%, the biggest swing of any category this quarter. Jewellery & Accessories climbed to 8.4%, its best reading since April’s Akshaya Tritiya spike. Consumer Electronics was the outlier, holding flat at 5.0% — a category still working through the drag of a weak rupee on import costs, even as festive demand starts to build. Geographically, the West (10.7%) and South (9.7%) kept their lead, but the North posted the sharpest single-month rebound of any zone, up 3.0 percentage points from July. “ These numbers tell us business is promising right now, and the recovery is genuinely encouraging — it’s broad enough to trust, not a one-category story ,” said Kumar Rajagopalan, CEO, Retailers Association of India . “ August is really a precursor to the festive season, and if this pace holds, retailers have good reason to plan with confidence heading into it. articles.x: BRUSSELS — September 24, 2026 — CEMATEX has selected 20 emerging start-ups from nine countries to receive the CEMATEX Start-Up Grant and showcase their innovations at Start-Up Valley during ITMA 2027 in Hanover. Their participation will be fully funded by CEMATEX, giving promising early-stage companies access to the world’s leading textile and garment technology platform. The selected start-ups span six product areas: Colourants & Chemicals, Fibres, Yarns & Fabrics, Garment Making, Recycling, Software & Automation, and Testing. While they address different challenges across the value chain, they share a common focus on sustainability and circularity. Across their technologies, sustainability is increasingly embedded in the way new materials, processes and production systems are being developed, rather than treated as a standalone consideration. The innovations address challenges ranging from chemistry and resource consumption to textile recycling, traceability, and production efficiency. Meet the 20 start-ups The 20 recipients of the CEMATEX Start-Up Grant are: Amphico, BioFluff, Eeden, EverDye, Fibarcode, Gemell Technology, Innovo Fiber, NunoX, Re.Solution, Recyc’Elit, Refiberd, ReSpin, Revoltech, RubyLab, Sages, Silana, Solena Materials, Sparxell, SwitchDye and Tintte . Their innovations can be seen in solutions addressing some of the textile and garment industry’s persistent sustainability challenges. Amphico is developing alternatives to substances the industry has long relied upon. Its PFAS-free membrane is designed to keep performance fabrics waterproof and breathable, while its colour platform introduces colour through weaving rather than dyeing. articles.o: Shima Seiki supports University of Technology Sydney innovation
articles.s: Shima Seiki’s advanced flat knitting technology is helping researchers and students at the University of Technology Sydney (UTS) explore new possibilities in 3D knitting, sustainable manufacturing and interdisciplinary design. The university’s Advanced Fabrication Research Lab (AFRL) is using a Shim
articles.x: Shima Seiki’s advanced flat knitting technology is helping researchers and students at the University of Technology Sydney (UTS) explore new possibilities in 3D knitting, sustainable manufacturing and interdisciplinary design. The university’s Advanced Fabrication Research Lab (AFRL) is using a Shima Seiki SWG-XR WHOLEGARMENT flat knitting machine and SDS-ONE APEX4 design system to support research, education and collaboration with industry. AFRL applies advanced digital manufacturing technologies including 3D knitting, robotics and 3D printing across fields extending beyond fashion and textiles to architecture, product design, engineering, healthcare and sustainability. As research and industry collaboration at the facility expanded, AFRL identified a need for technology capable of developing and prototyping seam-free knitted products and complex structures. The installation of the SWG-XR and APEX4 established an integrated environment extending from design through to prototyping. © Shima Seiki The SWG-XR is now used daily at the facility and enables researchers to develop three-dimensional knitted products featuring complex structures without conventional cutting and sewing processes. According to Shima Seiki, AFRL selected its technology because of the capabilities of WHOLEGARMENT knitting, the compatibility between the SWG-XR machine and APEX4 design system, and the company’s track record in the textile industry. Support from Shima Seiki’s Australian distributor Ramsay McDonald Australia also influenced the university’s decision. Researchers and technical staff have subsequently received training at Shima Seiki’s headquarters and through the company’s Shimanavi e-learning system. articles.o: Demand to Retain Decision to Withdraw Bonded Facility for Importing 10–30 Count Yarn
articles.s: Workers, officials and employees in the local spinning industry have demanded that the decision to withdraw the bonded facility for importing 10–30 count cotton yarn be kept in force. At the same time, exporters have demanded that the facility for importing the raw materials required by them be cont
articles.x: Workers, officials and employees in the local spinning industry have demanded that the decision to withdraw the bonded facility for importing 10–30 count cotton yarn be kept in force. At the same time, exporters have demanded that the facility for importing the raw materials required by them be continued. The demand was raised at a press conference organized by the Dhaka Reporters Unity (DRU) on Wednesday. Salma Group’s Chief Operating Officer (COO), Ajhar Ali, presented a written statement on behalf of the workers, officials and employees working in the spinning sector. On September 7, the Ministry of Commerce asked the local yarn-producing industry to withdraw the bonded facility for importing 10–30 count cotton yarn in order to protect the industry. However, it allowed such yarn to be imported against bank guarantees when required by the relevant garment factories. The Ministry of Commerce later suspended this order. At the press conference, the participants demanded that this decision be retained. According to them, if the facility remains operational, the use of locally produced yarn will increase. This could increase local value addition and reduce foreign-currency expenditure on yarn imports. At the same time, they believe that the bonded facility would reduce opportunities for illegally selling or diverting imported yarn in the local market. The press conference said that during the 2022–23 fiscal year, the quantity of imported 10–30 count cotton yarn was 216 million kilograms. In the 2024–25 fiscal year, it increased to 460 million kilograms. In other words, imports of this category of yarn increased by approximately 113% within two fiscal years. articles.x: Italian textile machinery manufacturers will strengthen their engagement with Taiwan’s textile industry at TITAS 2026, as renewed investment in machinery points to growing demand for flexible, resource-efficient production technologies. The Taiwan International Textile & Garment Machinery Show takes place in Taipei from 6-8 October 2026, bringing together technology suppliers and textile manufacturers from Taiwan and the wider Asian market. ACIMIT, the Association of Italian Textile Machinery Manufacturers, says Italy’s presence at the exhibition reflects the long-standing relationship between the two countries’ textile industries and the importance Taiwanese manufacturers continue to place on quality, technological development and specialised production. According to the association, the beginning of 2026 saw a strong recovery in Italian textile machinery exports to Taiwan following a period of adjustment in the global market. ACIMIT believes the rebound demonstrates renewed investment by Taiwanese textile manufacturers as they modernise production and target higher-value markets. Italian machinery suppliers are particularly well positioned to address Taiwan’s requirements because of their focus on flexible and customised manufacturing solutions. Taiwan’s textile industry has traditionally maintained a strong presence in the upstream stages of the supply chain, with spinning technologies accounting for a significant proportion of local demand for Italian equipment. articles.t: EU의 MELANGE 프로젝트는 섬유단계 착색을 섬유 순환성의 중심에 두었습니다.
articles.o: EU’s MELANGE project puts fiber-stage coloration at the center of textile circularity
articles.s: Textile coloration is moving upstream as Europe seeks to reduce the water and chemical footprint of textile production. Figure: MELANGE will test whether this upstream approach can deliver measurable...
articles.x: Textile coloration is moving upstream as Europe seeks to reduce the water and chemical footprint of textile production. Figure: MELANGE will test whether this upstream approach can deliver measurable resource savings while maintaining product performance, design flexibility, and commercial acceptance.Courtesy: Collected The EU-funded MELANGE project, led by Aalto University in Finland, aims to shift coloration from dyeing and finishing toward the fiber stage, targeting up to 50% lower water and chemical use than conventional finishing-stage processes. Launched in August 2026, the project will run until July 2029 with €3.97 million in Horizon Europe funding. Nine partners from research, fiber production, spinning, weaving, design, policy and industry networking are involved. The shift addresses a major environmental burden. The European Environment Agency (EEA) estimates that EU household textile consumption required about 6 billion m³ of blue water in 2022, with 85% consumed outside Europe, mainly in Asia. MELANGE will explore fiber-stage coloration, including spun-dyed and solution-dyed fibers. In synthetic fiber production, pigments can be added to the polymer before extrusion, potentially eliminating a separate wet dyeing stage. The 50% reduction is a project target, not yet a proven outcome. The project will also explore an approach inspired by Italy’s Prato textile district, where pre-colored recycled fibers can be blended by shade. This could make color variation part of product design while reducing repeated color correction and re-dyeing. MELANGE goes beyond technology. At the centre of the discussion was the government's recent decision on imports of 10–30 count cotton yarn. Industry representatives maintain that the decision can revive underused spinning capacity, safeguard jobs and reduce foreign-currency spending, and they urged the government to keep it in force. articles.x: CEMATEX has selected 20 start-ups from nine countries for fully funded participation in the Start-Up Valley at ITMA 2027 in Hanover from next September 16-22. The companies will exhibit technologies across six areas of textile and garment manufacturing – colourants and chemicals, fibres, yarns and fabrics, garment making, recycling, software and automation and testing. The 20 recipients are Amphico, BioFluff, Eeden, EverDye, Fibarcode, Gemell Technology, Innovo Fiber, NunoX, Re.Solution, Recyc’Elit, Refiberd, ReSpin, Revoltech, RubyLab, Sages, Silana, Solena Materials, Sparxell, SwitchDye and Tintte. Although their technologies address different stages of the textile value chain, sustainability and circularity feature strongly across the selection, alongside automation, advanced materials and more efficient manufacturing. Among the companies selected, Amphico is developing a PFAS-free membrane for waterproof and breathable performance fabrics, as well as a technology that introduces colour through weaving rather than conventional dyeing. Other start-ups are targeting the heavy consumption of water, energy and chemicals associated with textile wet processing. SwitchDye, a University of Leeds spin-out, has developed CO2-responsive dyes intended to reduce chemical, water and energy requirements while operating with existing dyeing equipment. Recycling technologies also feature prominently. French start-up Recyc’Elit is developing a chemical recycling process for blended textiles that recovers polyester as monomers while separating materials including cotton and elastane. US-based Refiberd is tackling a different part of the recycling problem. articles.x: Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BGMEA) launched its Japan Desk to strengthen economic relations with Japan and expand bilateral trade and investment opportunities, particularly in the apparel sector. Japanese Ambassador to Bangladesh SAIDA Shinichi formally inaugurated the desk at the BGMEA Complex in Uttara, with BGMEA President Mahmud Hasan Khan and senior representatives of Japanese business organisations and companies present. The new desk will serve as a one-stop platform for Japanese buyers and investors, facilitating business connections, investment and order management, particularly for small and medium-sized orders, according to BGMEA. The initiative aims to promote greater diversification of Bangladesh’s apparel export markets and products while creating stronger and longer-term business partnerships between the two countries. Speaking at the inauguration, Ambassador SAIDA congratulated BGMEA on establishing the Japan Desk and expressed hope that it would help further accelerate bilateral trade. He also stressed the importance of export diversification for sustainable economic growth. BGMEA President Mahmud Hasan Khan said the association does not consider excessive dependence on a single sector or traditional markets desirable. “BGMEA is placing the highest priority on product and market diversification. The Japanese market holds significant potential for Bangladesh’s apparel sector, and the Japan Desk has been established to realise that potential,” he said. He identified lead time, or the ability to deliver products within the shortest possible period, as one of the major challenges for Bangladesh’s apparel exporters in the Japanese market. Their technologies address challenges ranging from chemistry and resource consumption to textile-to-textile recycling, traceability, materials development and manufacturing efficiency. Among them, Amphico is developing a PFAS-free membrane designed to provide waterproof and breathable performance for fabrics. The company is also developing a colour platform that introduces colour through weaving rather than conventional dyeing. SwitchDye is targeting the significant water, energy and chemical demands associated with textile dyeing. articles.x: Key insights Burkina Faso opened the $30 million TEXFORCES-BF textile complex in Bobo-Dioulasso. Brazil’s Guara Circular has recycled 181 tons of textile waste into new yarns since March 2025. Both developments show how domestic processing can retain more value within textile-producing economies. Burkina Faso and Brazil are taking different routes to the same textile challenge- keeping more value inside domestic supply chains. Figure: The government of Burkina Faso estimates its potential annual output at 20 million meters of fabric, 6 million knitted garments, 6 million uniforms, 6 million T-shirts, and 1 million pairs of socks. Courtesy: Collected Burkina Faso has opened a $30 million integrated textile complex in Bobo-Dioulasso as it seeks to turn more of its cotton into finished products at home. Brazil, meanwhile, is expanding textile-to-textile recycling to keep cotton waste within its own industrial system. The latest move in Burkina Faso is the Textile des Forces du Burkina Faso (TEXFORCES-BF), inaugurated on 9 September at Logofourousso. The 30-hectare facility combines weaving, knitting, dyeing, finishing and garment production. It will initially process more than 12 tons of cotton fiber per day. Government estimates put its potential annual output at 20 million meters of fabric, six million knitted garments, six million uniforms, six million T-shirts and one million pairs of socks. The factory will supply security forces and the civilian market, linking domestic cotton directly with finished apparel. The scale reflects a clear import substitution challenge. articles.x: Functional Fabric Fair powered by Performance Days has announced its Expert Talks education programme for its Fall 2026 edition, taking place from 26-28 October at the Oregon Convention Center in Portland, Oregon. The three-day programme opens on 26 October with the Day 0 OIA Catalyst Conference, developed in partnership with the Outdoor Industry Association (OIA), followed by two days of sourcing and Expert Talks sessions on 27-28 October. The programme is aimed at designers, product developers and material decision-makers across the performance, outdoor and sports apparel sectors, with discussions covering performance innovation, regulatory developments, circularity and trends influencing the Fall 2027/28 seasons. Nearly 20 Expert Talks sessions are scheduled, with Stewart Sheppard, founder and principal consultant of S2 Consulting, returning as host. The programme will bring together specialists from textile companies, brands, industry organisations and consultancies to examine both technical developments and wider changes affecting the textile supply chain. Among the subjects on the opening day will be Summer 2028 and Winter 2028/29 performance colour trends, European Digital Product Passport requirements, textile data, bio-based materials, artificial intelligence-assisted prototyping, antimicrobial technologies and polyester circularity. A panel led by Hyosung TNC will explore the roadmap towards adoption of bio-based materials, with Malvina Hoxha of Hyosung TNC and Ajay Chadha of REI Co-op among the participants. articles.x: President Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir on Wednesday called upon all stakeholders, including BGMEA, BKMEA and BTMA, to work together to address the existing challenges and problems facing the country’s apparel sector. The President made the call when a delegation of the Bangladesh Knitwear Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BKMEA), led by its President Mohammad Hatem, met him at Bangabhaban. President’s Press Secretary Md Sarwar Alam briefed reporters after the meeting. During the meeting, Mirza Fakhrul said coordinated initiatives are necessary to keep the country’s growing economy moving while ensuring that all stakeholders receive equitable benefits. He said the current government has adopted business-, industry- and economy-friendly policies to strengthen the national economy, create employment opportunities and provide businesses with opportunities to recover and grow. “Growing industries and businesses need necessary protection to remain sustainable,” the President said, stressing the importance of reducing bank lending rates to encourage investment in the country. He also urged industry owners to explore alternative energy sources, including solar power, to help address the ongoing energy crisis. Mirza Fakhrul said the government is working to keep the country’s growing economy vibrant. He recalled with appreciation the contribution of knitwear manufacturers and exporters to earning foreign currency for the country and thanked them for their role. Referring to the restoration of democracy in the country, the President said any problem facing the country should be resolved through democratic processes and discussion in Parliament. articles.s: Textile ETP, The European Technology Platform for the Future of Textiles and Clothing, has launched a new strategy setting out how Europe’s textile and apparel industry can accelerate the transition towards biobased and circular materials while strengthening its manufacturing base. articles.x: Textile ETP, The European Technology Platform for the Future of Textiles and Clothing, has launched a new strategy setting out how Europe’s textile and apparel industry can accelerate the transition towards biobased and circular materials while strengthening its manufacturing base. The Bioeconomy Innovation Strategy for the European Fibres, Textiles, and Apparel Industry was unveiled during the fourth ECOSYSTEX Conference in Antwerp. It was developed by Textile ETP between February and August 2026 together with experts from across the European biotextile value chain through its Circular & Biobased Textiles Innovation Hub. The strategy argues that Europe must reverse five decades of increasing dependence on fossil-based textile materials and develop stronger domestic value chains for renewable fibres, bio-processing and circular production. It identifies sustainability, strategic resilience and competitiveness as three converging pressures driving the transition. Textile ETP notes that rising global fibre consumption continues to be met largely through fossil-based synthetics, while more than 90% of global polyester capacity is already located in Asia. According to the organisation, this concentration leaves Europe increasingly dependent on a relatively small number of non-European suppliers for strategically important textile raw materials. At the same time, Textile ETP believes advances in biomaterials and bioprocessing could create new opportunities for European manufacturers to differentiate through innovation, intellectual property and higher-value production. “Europe’s textile bioeconomy is not only a sustainability opportunity, it is an industrial opportunity,” said Marina Crnoja-Cosic, President of Textile ETP. “Reversing decades of rising fossil dependence can s

articles.x: The Nigeria Sovereign Investment Authority (NSIA) and its partners have commercially launched a $300 million Distributed Renewable Energy (DRE) Fund to mobilize private-sector investment in renewable energy and expand electricity access for underserved communities and businesses. The launch, announced on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York, marks the transition of the fund from its structuring phase to active capital deployment. The initiative brings together the NSIA, Sustainable Energy for All (SEforALL) and Africa50 , an infrastructure investment platform established by the African Development Bank and African states. The fund is designed to finance distributed renewable energy solutions, including mini-grids and standalone solar systems, particularly in communities and businesses that remain underserved by conventional electricity infrastructure. It also supports Mission 300, the initiative to connect around 300 million people across Africa to electricity by 2030. World Bank commits initial $25 million The World Bank Group is a founding partner of the initiative and has committed an initial $25 million through the International Development Association (IDA), according to the NSIA. Aminu Umar-Sadiq, Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer of NSIA, said the commercial launch reflects the growing investment potential of Nigeria’s distributed renewable energy market. He said the fund comes at a critical point as distributed renewable energy becomes increasingly important to closing electricity-access gaps, supporting economic activity and strengthening energy security. The event will also feature technologies designed to reduce water, chemical, and energy use. The event comes as textile manufacturers face growing pressure to improve efficiency while meeting sustainability and traceability requirements. articles.t: MMCF 부문은 공급, 투자 동향의 변화를 보고 있습니다.
articles.o: MMCF sector sees changing supply, investment trends
articles.s: The global man-made cellulosic fiber (MMCF) sector is going through a period of change as feedstock supply risks and concerns over oversupply affect investment decisions, according to Canopy’s 2026 Ho...
articles.x: The global man-made cellulosic fiber (MMCF) sector is going through a period of change as feedstock supply risks and concerns over oversupply affect investment decisions, according to Canopy’s 2026 Hot Button Progress Report. Figure: Canopy’s assessment comes as the MMCF industry faces uncertainty around conventional feedstock supply. Concerns about oversupply are also influencing investment across the sector. The environmental nonprofit is calling for faster adoption of next-generation fibers as the industry responds to changing market and environmental pressures. According to the report, green shirt-rated producers now represent 53% of global MMCF capacity. This is down one percentage point from 2025. However, the performance of individual producers improved. Of the 28 producers assessed by Canopy, 22 achieved green shirt status in 2026. This means 79% of the assessed producers qualified for green shirt status, compared with 70% in 2025. The results show a mixed picture for the MMCF sector. Canopy’s assessment comes as the MMCF industry faces uncertainty around conventional feedstock supply. Concerns about oversupply are also influencing investment across the sector. The report highlights the need for the industry to accelerate the development and adoption of next-generation fiber solutions. These technologies are expected to play a growing role in reducing pressure on conventional forest-based feedstocks and supporting a more sustainable fiber supply. The latest findings also underline the importance of looking beyond the number of companies meeting sustainability benchmarks. The capacity represented by those producers remains a key factor in measuring the overall progress of the MMCF industry.

articles.o: Filo focuses on stronger supply chains
articles.s: The need for a more united, innovative and responsible textile and fashion sector was placed firmly in the spotlight at the opening ceremony of the 66th edition of Filo, held at Fiera Milano Rho earlier this month. Under the theme ‘Weaving the Future: balance for a stronger, more competitive textile
articles.x: The need for a more united, innovative and responsible textile and fashion sector was placed firmly in the spotlight at the opening ceremony of the 66th edition of Filo, held at Fiera Milano Rho earlier this month. Under the theme ‘Weaving the Future: balance for a stronger, more competitive textile and fashion supply chain’, industry representatives explored how closer collaboration across the value chain could help companies navigate challenging market conditions while maintaining investment in innovation, sustainability and skills. Opening the event, Filo head Paolo Monfermoso acknowledged the difficult environment currently facing the industry, although he pointed to encouraging participation at the exhibition. “The sector is going through a challenging situation, with circumstances varying from company to company,” Monfermoso said. He added that exhibitor numbers were in line with the February edition, while buyer registrations on the opening morning provided grounds for optimism. Pier Francesco Corcione, general director of Biella Industrial Union (UIB), stressed the continuing importance of B2B exhibitions as practical business development platforms. According to Corcione, growing demands for innovation and collaboration make opportunities for meaningful networking increasingly important. Filo, he said, places the textile supply chain at the centre of this process by encouraging dialogue between its different participants and promoting expertise, sustainability and research. Emanuele Ramella Pralungo, president of the Province of Biella, highlighted Filo’s role in showcasing Italian yarn expertise and Made in Italy manufacturing, while calling for collaboration between different parts of the sector to address increasingly complex challenges. articles.o: Monforts ATC helps advance finishing innovation
articles.s: Monforts is helping textile manufacturers turn new ideas into industrial reality at its Advanced Technology Centre (ATC) in Mönchengladbach, where customers can trial fabrics, finishing technologies and new processes under full-scale production conditions. Covering 1,200 square metres at the company
articles.x: Monforts is helping textile manufacturers turn new ideas into industrial reality at its Advanced Technology Centre (ATC) in Mönchengladbach, where customers can trial fabrics, finishing technologies and new processes under full-scale production conditions. Covering 1,200 square metres at the company’s headquarters, the ATC houses two full Montex finishing lines engineered to accommodate a diverse range of processes. The centre also includes a Thermex range for the continuous dyeing of denim and other woven fabrics, a full colour kitchen and several laboratory-scale systems for smaller batch trials. “The ATC allows our customers to test their own textiles and technical fabrics on Monforts dyeing and finishing machines under fully confidential, real production conditions,” said Monforts Marketing Manager Nicole Croonenbroek. “Using the results from these trials, we are also able to make recommendations for improving many fabric finishes.” Technical textiles One of the centre’s Montex lines is specifically configured for technical textiles, where flexibility is increasingly important because manufacturers can be required to process materials with very different properties and performance requirements in rapid succession. Applications range from substrates for digitally printed soft signage and carbon fabrics for high-performance composites to filter media designed for extreme temperatures and flame-retardant barrier fabrics. The technical textiles line incorporates a Montex four-chamber horizontal-chain stenter and an explosion-proof coating application chamber, enabling treatments involving organic solvents and other volatile materials. articles.o: TMAS technology behind the perfect little black dress
articles.s: The little black dress may be one of fashion’s simplest and most enduring garments, but achieving its characteristic clean lines depends on manufacturing precision of the kind supplied by Swedish textile machinery specialist and TMAS member Svegea. Ever since Audrey Hepburn appeared in Givenchy’s ce
articles.x: The little black dress may be one of fashion’s simplest and most enduring garments, but achieving its characteristic clean lines depends on manufacturing precision of the kind supplied by Swedish textile machinery specialist and TMAS member Svegea. Ever since Audrey Hepburn appeared in Givenchy’s celebrated creation in Breakfast at Tiffany’s, the LBD has become a wardrobe staple across generations. Its appeal lies partly in its apparent simplicity, but producing a dress that retains its shape, sits cleanly around the neckline and withstands repeated wear requires considerable attention to details that are largely invisible to the wearer. One of those details is bias binding. Bias binding is produced from strips of fabric cut diagonally across the material rather than along its straight grain. Cutting on the bias gives the strip greater flexibility, allowing it to follow curved necklines, armholes and other edges without puckering or distorting the garment. It can be used to enclose raw edges, reinforce areas subjected to movement and provide a clean internal finish. While largely unnoticed by the wearer, accurately produced and applied binding can consequently make an important contribution to both the appearance and durability of a garment. For a home sewer, bias strips can be cut and prepared manually but in industrial garment production, where thousands of identical pieces may be required, the challenge is quite different. Consistency of width and cut becomes critical, while manufacturers must also control material use and maintain production speeds. It is here that TMAS member Svegea has established a specialist position with automated equipment for bias binding and other fabric cutting operations. articles.o: Benninger Advances Sustainable Dyeing with FabricMaster and SynthMaster in Bangladesh
articles.s: Swiss textile machinery manufacturer Benninger has introduced its latest discontinuous dyeing technologies, FabricMaster and SynthMaster, to the Bangladesh textile industry, focusing on resource efficiency, process consistency, and gentle fabric handling. The technologies were showcased at a technic
articles.x: Swiss textile machinery manufacturer Benninger has introduced its latest discontinuous dyeing technologies, FabricMaster and SynthMaster, to the Bangladesh textile industry, focusing on resource efficiency, process consistency, and gentle fabric handling. The technologies were showcased at a technical seminar titled “The sustainable way of discontinuous dyeing: Fast, cost-effective, and zero footprints,” held on 17 September 2026 at Hotel Le Méridien Dhaka. Benninger and its agent for discontinuous dyeing machinery in Bangladesh, Global Hitech, jointly organized the seminar. Photo: A portion of the team from Global HiTech More than 120 textile industry professionals attended the event, including representatives from dyeing, finishing, and textile manufacturing companies. The seminar provided an opportunity for industry professionals to learn about the latest developments in discontinuous dyeing and the technologies being developed to address the changing requirements of modern textile production. With more than 160 years of experience in textile machinery and finishing technologies, Benninger presented FabricMaster and SynthMaster as solutions for dyehouses facing increasingly diverse fabric types, rising resource-efficiency requirements, and the need for consistent quality. Industry focus on efficient and controlled dyeing Opening the seminar, Saad Omar Fahim, CEO of Global Hitech, highlighted the growing importance of reducing water and energy consumption in Bangladesh’s textile processing sector while maintaining productivity and product quality. He said that investment in advanced machinery alone is not enough to achieve sustainable improvements at factory level. articles.s: Indian textile industry is entering a new phase of transformation where diversification, technology adoption, sustainability and value addition will be the key drivers of long term global competitiveness. While India… The post SIMA Chairman urges Textile Industry to accelarate automation and value a
articles.x: Indian textile industry is entering a new phase of transformation where diversification, technology adoption, sustainability and value addition will be the key drivers of long term global competitiveness. While India has traditionally has been built on natural fibres, particularly cotton, the rapidly evolving global market demands a stronger presence across the entire textile value chain including MMF, Technical Textiles, Recycled Fibres, Sustainable products and value-addition to further strengthen India’s position in the global Textile and Apparel market. The future growth of the Indian textile industry will depend not only on expanding capacity, but producing high value products with greater efficiency through Innovation, productivity, advanced technology, sustainability and market diversification. These measures will enable the industry to maximise the emerging opportunities arising from India’s Free Trade Agreements. In a Press Release issued recently, the re-elected Chairman of SIMA, Mr Durai Palanisamy, expressed this gratitude to the NDA Government for always giving high priority for the textile industry by announcing numerous growth oriented policies including • Rationalisation of GST across the textile value chain. • Withdrawal of QCOs on cotton, MMF fibres, filaments and yarns. • Retention of the annual banking system and reduction of related charges, in relation to power. • Extension of export obligation period under Advance Authorisation. • Launch of the Mission for Cotton Productivity. • Revisions to the PLI Scheme, including lower investment and turnover thresholds. • Progress on FTAs with the EU, UK, New Zealand, Oman and other countries. • Export credit support, RoDTEP restoration and extension of RoSCTL. • Temporary exemption of cotton from 11% import

articles.s: CARY, N.C. — September 23, 2026 — INDA, the Association of the Nonwoven Fabrics Industry, in partnership with International Filtration News, has announced the finalists for the FiltXPO™ 2026 Innovation Awards. The awards recognize innovative new products introduced to the filtration industry since t
articles.x: CARY, N.C. — September 23, 2026 — INDA, the Association of the Nonwoven Fabrics Industry, in partnership with International Filtration News, has announced the finalists for the FiltXPO 2026 Innovation Awards. The awards recognize innovative new products introduced to the filtration industry since the last FiltXPO event in 2025. The FiltXPO Innovation Awards celebrate advancements in filtration technology for air and gas and water and liquid applications. Entries are evaluated on creativity, novelty of approach, uniqueness and technical sophistication. The winners will be announced during FiltXPO 2026, the premier global event for the filtration industry, Oct. 28-29 at the Minneapolis Convention Center in Minneapolis. The FiltXPO 2026 Innovation Award finalists are: FiltXPO Innovation in Air/Gas Filtration Award Hifyber: CombiNano Leanfil Oy: Leanfil® Solberg Manufacturing, Inc.: Fully Automated Liquid Management System FiltXPO Innovation in Water/Liquid Filtration Award Acuriant Technologies Inc.: CUF Flow – More Water, Same Footprint Ahlstrom: Ahlstrom OptiPad Gessner, a Mativ Brand: GESSNER PFAS Filter Media Voting for the winner in each category is open on the International Filtration News website. Winners will be announced Oct. 28 at FiltXPO 2026. To vote, visit: https://www.filtnews.com/filtxpo-innovation-awards/ For more information about the Finalists, visit: https://www.filtxpo.com/awards To register for FiltXPO 2026, visit: https://www.filtxpo.com/ Posted: September 23, 2026 Source: INDA, the Association of the Nonwoven Fabrics Industry

articles.s: India’s textile and apparel industry is facing a fresh export risk as new US legislation gives Washington authority to impose additional tariffs of up to 100% on countries buying Russian oil and gas....
articles.x: India’s textile and apparel industry is facing a fresh export risk as new US legislation gives Washington authority to impose additional tariffs of up to 100% on countries buying Russian oil and gas. Figure: India’s apparel exports declined 2.74% year over year to $1.20 billion, even as textile exports recorded stronger growth, according to data cited by the Confederation of Indian Textile Industry (CITI). The Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 , signed into law on September 18 , gives the US President this tariff authority. However, the additional duty is not automatic. The US has yet to determine the targeted countries, tariff rates, product coverage, or implementation schedule. For India’s textile and apparel exporters, the uncertainty comes at a sensitive time. The US is a major export market, while India’s apparel shipments are already losing momentum. India’s combined textile and apparel exports declined 0.24% year over year to $15.08 billion during April–August 2026. Textile exports increased 6.94% to $8.93 billion, but apparel exports fell 9.1% to $6.15 billion, according to industry data. Apparel weakness raises exposure The latest figures show a clear divergence between India’s textile and apparel performance. Upstream textile exports are growing, while finished apparel exports are contracting. The pressure continued in August. India’s apparel exports declined 2.74% year over year to $1.20 billion, even as textile exports recorded stronger growth, according to data cited by the Confederation of Indian Textile Industry (CITI). This makes the potential US tariff risk more significant for garment manufacturers. Any additional duty could increase the landed cost of Indian products and put further pressure on supplier margins. articles.s: ZÜRICH, Switzerland — September 22, 2026 — The winners of the ITMF Sustainability & Innovation Awards 2026 will present their project at the upcoming ITMF & IAF Conference 2026 which will be held from 14 – 15 October 2026 in Fortaleza, Brazil and will be co-hosted by ABIT (Brazilian Textile & Indust
articles.x: ZÜRICH, Switzerland — September 22, 2026 — The winners of the ITMF Sustainability & Innovation Awards 2026 will present their project at the upcoming ITMF & IAF Conference 2026 which will be held from 14 – 15 October 2026 in Fortaleza, Brazil and will be co-hosted by ABIT (Brazilian Textile & Industry Industry Association). The objectives of the ITMF Sustainability & Innovation Awards are to recognize sustainable and innovative achievements in the textile industry with focus on innovation, design, development, and production under the strictest standards of sustainability and respect for the environment. articles.x: UK delegation visits Vancot Limited; a concern of Shin Shin Group, highlights strong UK market engagement and sustainability ambitions. The British High Commission has reaffirmed its commitment to maintaining strong trade relations with Bangladesh, with the UK market set to remain open to Bangladeshi exporters following the country’s graduation from Least Developed Country (LDC) status. The assurance came during a visit by the British High Commission delegation, led by the Deputy High Commissioner James Goldman, to Vancot Limited, a manufacturing facility of Shin Shin Group, where the delegation held discussions on Bangladesh’s apparel exports, sustainability, technological advancement, investment and future UK-Bangladesh trade relations. During the visit, the Deputy High Commissioner highlighted the benefits available to Bangladeshi exporters under the UK’s Developing Countries Trading Scheme (DCTS) and said the existing level of market access would remain unchanged during the three-year transition period following Bangladesh’s LDC graduation. “Bangladesh enjoys duty-free access for 99.8% of products exported to the UK under our Developing Countries Trading Scheme, and that access will stay exactly the same during the three-year transition period after Bangladesh graduates from LDC status,” the Deputy High Commissioner said. He further noted that after the transition period, 92% of products, including garments, will continue to enter the UK market duty-free. “What does that mean for businesses in Bangladesh and their UK partners? It means certainty and confidence to invest, grow and plan for the future,” he said. articles.x: The Monforts Advanced Technology Centre (ATC), initially opened in 2013 and subsequently expanded, continues to be an invaluable resource to customers from around the world in achieving new standards in fabric finishing. articles.o: Brazil scales cotton-to-cotton recycling through an integrated textile hub
articles.s: Brazil is moving textile recycling closer to the factory floor. Fashion retailer Riachuelo has launched Guara Circular, Northeast Brazil’s first industrial-scale textile recycling hub, creating a clos...
articles.x: Brazil is moving textile recycling closer to the factory floor. Fashion retailer Riachuelo has launched Guara Circular, Northeast Brazil’s first industrial-scale textile recycling hub, creating a closed-loop route for cotton waste generated within its own production network. The project integrates textile waste separation, fiber opening, and spinning. The factory produces about 40% of Riachuelo’s merchandise and is Latin America’s largest integrated textile plant. The scale is already measurable. Guara Circular has transformed 181 tons of textile waste into new yarn and plans to reuse more than 1.2 million kg of 100% cotton cutting scraps from the factory. The project was developed with Cotton Move and Evotex. The recycled material is now moving into products. Riachuelo launched a collection of more than 41,000 pieces, including jeans made from 100% cotton with 25% recycled fiber. The move also addresses a wider industry challenge. Mechanical cotton recycling can reduce dependence on virgin fiber, but repeated processing can shorten fibers and affect yarn quality. Blended materials, elastane contamination and inconsistent waste quality add further complexity. Riachuelo’s model is significant because it links waste generation, recycling, spinning, and product manufacturing within one industrial ecosystem. Brazil’s textile recycling market was estimated at about $169.2 million in 2026, with cotton identified as its largest material segment. The next challenge will be scaling this model beyond controlled factory waste to post-consumer textiles, where collection, sorting, and fiber quality become more difficult. articles.o: Technology Transforming the Fashion Value Chain @ ASW’26
articles.s: Technology is rapidly transforming the fashion value chain, moving beyond automation on the factory floor to influence almost every stage of the business – from product design, development and merchandising to manufacturing, supply-chain management and retail. AI, 3D product development, digital wor
articles.x: Technology is rapidly transforming the fashion value chain, moving beyond automation on the factory floor to influence almost every stage of the business – from product design, development and merchandising to manufacturing, supply-chain management and retail. AI, 3D product development, digital workflows, ERP and data-driven decision-making are helping companies accelerate product development, improve accuracy, optimise resources and respond faster to changing market demands. At the same time, automation, intelligent production systems, traceability and digital communication are creating greater visibility and efficiency across the supply chain. The real advantage today is not technology in isolation, but how different technologies can connect processes, people and data across the value chain. For brands and manufacturers, this means shorter development cycles, fewer physical samples, better resource utilisation, improved production planning and greater responsiveness to increasingly demanding customers. ASW’26 will bring together technology providers showcasing solutions across this evolving landscape – from design and product development to manufacturing, AI, supply-chain management and retail. The event provides industry professionals an opportunity to see these technologies in action, understand their practical applications and explore how they can create a measurable business advantage. articles.o: Candour Techtex signs MOU with Ratanmoti Texfab for Coating and Lamination of Fabrics for Defence Applications
articles.s: Candour Techtex Limited (CTL), Malegaon, has announced that it has entered into a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) with Ratanmoti Texfab (India) Pvt. Ltd. (RMTF), Kolhapur, for a long-term arrangement relating… The post Candour Techtex signs MOU with Ratanmoti Texfab for Coating and Lamination of F
articles.x: Candour Techtex Limited (CTL), Malegaon, has announced that it has entered into a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) with Ratanmoti Texfab (India) Pvt. Ltd. (RMTF), Kolhapur, for a long-term arrangement relating to the coating and lamination of fabrics intended for applications in the Indian Defence Industry. Under the proposed arrangement, RMTF will supply fabrics to CTL, which will undertake the required coating and lamination processes at its manufacturing facilities, in accordance with the applicable specifications and quality requirements. The processed fabrics will thereafter be supplied by RMTF to Aerial Delivery Research and Development Establishment (ADRDE), Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO). The MOU represents an important development for CTL as its coating and lamination capabilities are proposed to become part of the supply chain serving ADRDE/DRDO through RMTF. The association provides the Company with an opportunity to participate in the development and supply chain for specialised coated and laminated textile materials intended for defence-related applications. Through this arrangement, CTL will contribute its technical expertise and manufacturing capabilities in the processing, coating and lamination of technical fabrics, with a focus on consistently meeting the specified technical, quality and performance requirements applicable to such specialised applications. Brand-Promotion The proposed association also aligns with CTL’s broader objective of expanding the application of its processing capabilities into technical textiles, specialised industrial applications and defence-related textile requirements. The Company believes that its experience in coating and lamination can support the growing requirement for engineered textile materials

articles.o: Turning new ideas into industrial reality at the Monforts ATC
articles.s: The Monforts Advanced Technology Centre (ATC), initially opened in 2013 and subsequently expanded, continues to be an invaluable resource to customers from around the world in achieving new standards in… The post Turning new ideas into industrial reality at the Monforts ATC appeared first on The Tex
articles.x: The Monforts Advanced Technology Centre (ATC), initially opened in 2013 and subsequently expanded, continues to be an invaluable resource to customers from around the world in achieving new standards in fabric finishing. Covering an area of 1,200 square metres, the Monforts ATC at the company’s headquarters in Mönchengladbach houses two full MONTEX finishing lines, engineered to accommodate an extremely diverse range of processes, in addition to a THERMEX range for the continuous dyeing of denim and other woven fabrics, a full colour kitchen and a number of lab-scale systems for smaller batch trials. “The ATC allows our customers to test their own textiles and technical fabrics on Monforts dyeing and finishing machines under fully confidential, real production conditions,” says the company’s Marketing Manager Nicole Croonenbroek. “Using the results from these trials, we are also able to make recommendations for improving many fabric finishes.” Technical textiles A highly-controlled and contained environment was a key consideration when constructing the special MONTEX line for technical textiles at the ATC. “Technical textiles are extremely diverse in their end-use applications and manufacturers can be called upon to quickly produce a succession of materials with widely differing properties and performance applications – often within a single shift,” explains Monforts Textile Technologist Saskia Bollhöfer. “These range from substrates for digitally-printed soft signage to carbon fabrics for today’s high-performance composites, and from filter media which must perform in extreme temperatures to flame retardant barrier fabrics. These very different materials all require expert coating and finishing for maximum efficiency and the technology to allow for ultimate flexibility

articles.o: Fashion influences one third of world’s farmland report says
articles.s: Almost a third of the world’s farmland is influenced by the fashion industry, according to new research from the University of Oxford’s Smith School of Enterprise and the Environment. The report, produced with DIRT Charity, estimates that fashion influences 30.15% of global agricultural land – aroun
articles.x: Almost a third of the world’s farmland is influenced by the fashion industry, according to new research from the University of Oxford’s Smith School of Enterprise and the Environment. The report, produced with DIRT Charity, estimates that fashion influences 30.15% of global agricultural land – around 1.45 billion hectares – when leather and wool production are included alongside textile crops such as cotton, hemp and flax. The figure is substantially higher than previous estimates based largely on land devoted directly to textile crops. The researchers estimate that leather accounts for 876 million hectares, wool 528.4 million hectares, cotton 34.7 million hectares, linen and hemp 5.9 million hectares and silk 2.3 million hectares. The Climate and Agricultural Impact of Textile Production report also argues that the environmental impact of a textile can depend more heavily on how its raw material is produced than on the type of fibre itself. © DIRT Charity According to the research, variations within a single material can be greater than those between different materials, potentially limiting the usefulness of fibre content alone as an indicator of environmental impact. Life-cycle studies reviewed for the report, for example, put the carbon footprint of leather at between 8.5 and 152 kg CO2e per square metre. Two mycelium-based leather alternatives assessed were also found to differ twentyfold in emissions. One was assessed at 2.76 kg CO2e per square metre, representing a substantial reduction compared with the approximately 33 kg CO2e cited for bovine leather. Another, produced using electricity from a coal-intensive grid, was assessed at 57 kg CO2e per square metre. articles.t: HeiQ와 Archroma가 ITMF 상을 수상했습니다.
articles.o: HeiQ and Archroma win ITMF award
articles.s: HeiQ and Archroma have won the ITMF International Collaboration Award 2026 in recognition of their partnership to advance innovation, sustainability and competitiveness across the global textile industry. The award recognises the companies’ work in bringing next-generation antimicrobial and odour-co
articles.x: HeiQ and Archroma have won the ITMF International Collaboration Award 2026 in recognition of their partnership to advance innovation, sustainability and competitiveness across the global textile industry. The award recognises the companies’ work in bringing next-generation antimicrobial and odour-control technologies to textile manufacturers, brands and retailers worldwide, combining HeiQ’s material technology expertise with Archroma’s global commercial and technical platform. According to the companies, the partnership has created a model for scaling textile innovation internationally, allowing mills and brands to access advanced functional technologies more efficiently while benefiting from global technical support. “Our collaboration demonstrates what can be achieved when two organisations with complementary strengths unite around a shared purpose,” said Raquel Vaz Vieira, Executive Vice President, HeiQ Advanced Materials. “This award is not only a recognition of what has been achieved so far, but also an encouragement to continue pushing the boundaries of sustainable textile innovation. We thank ITMF for this honour and our customers, partners, and teams across both organisations whose commitment made this collaboration a success.” Dhirendra Gautam, Vice President, Marketing at Archroma, added: “This recognition from ITMF validates our belief that innovation has greater impact when it is made accessible at scale. articles.s: Bangladesh has amended the Import Policy Order, removing prior approval requirements for yarn and fabric imports. Export‑oriented garment manufacturers can now import directly without clearance from t...
articles.x: Bangladesh has amended the Import Policy Order, removing prior approval requirements for yarn and fabric imports. Export‑oriented garment manufacturers can now import directly without clearance from the Ministry of Commerce. The Ministry of Commerce issued a notification on Sunday (September 20), announcing the amendment, providing relief to garment exporters who had raised concerns over the additional approval requirement. Courtesy:Collected The condition had been introduced in the new Import Policy Order that came into effect in August. Business leaders and entrepreneurs had criticized the requirement, saying it was making business operations more difficult and increasing production costs. Exporters said several consignments of raw materials had already arrived at ports but could not be released because importers were unable to obtain the required approval from the Ministry of Commerce on time. They expect the amendment to accelerate customs clearance and cargo release processes and resolve the complications faced by exporters. Mohammad Hatem, President of the Bangladesh Knitwear Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BKMEA), said the new IPO had made prior approval from the Ministry of Commerce mandatory for imports of yarn and fabrics for the hosiery and knitwear sectors. “As a result, exporters whose raw material consignments had already arrived at the port could not release them, creating various complications for overall exports. We hope the policy amendment will resolve the issue,” he added. Local textile mills currently supply around 80% of the yarn and fabric required by Bangladesh’s knitwear manufacturers, while the sector is also reported to have sufficient production capacity to meet its overall demand. articles.x: John Smedley has launched The Original Muse, its Autumn/Winter 2026 campaign inspired by the natural world and the relationship between nature, fibres, design and craftsmanship that has shaped the British knitwear manufacturer for more than 240 years. The company marked the launch with an intimate cocktail event at Farm Shop in Mayfair, London, bringing together collaborators, creatives and friends of the brand. Guests included musicians Reuben James and Wilfred Cisse, actor Lara Peake, Dennis Okwera, Danny Lomas, Reuben Larkin, Kit Clarke, Brett Staniland and Scott Staniland. The Original Muse campaign features actor and poet Kit Clarke and artist and poet Robert Montgomery, who explore a return to nature as a source of creative inspiration. © John Smedley Across five films – Returning to the Land, The Human Difference, Rooted in Simplicity, The Sublime and In Natural Harmony – poetry and knitwear are brought together through themes of artistry, human touch and craftsmanship. For John Smedley, nature provides both the raw materials and creative starting point for its knitwear. Natural fibres form the foundation of its products, while colours, textures and landscapes influence the development of its collections. The company says this relationship is reflected in its considered approach to manufacturing and its focus on producing knitwear designed for longevity. “Being in nature, sharing wisdom and stories, with a friend and with all the nature that surrounded us, reminded me that the most beautiful things are often the quiet, consistent ones,” said Kit Clarke. articles.t: Lectra는 Apogy를 통해 AI 업스트림을 구현합니다.
articles.o: Lectra takes AI upstream with Apogy
articles.s: Lectra is moving beyond its traditional strength in patternmaking and production software with the launch of Apogy, a cloud-based platform designed to bring the fragmented stages of fashion product development into a single system. Three years in development, Apogy is intended to connect the work th
articles.x: Lectra is moving beyond its traditional strength in patternmaking and production software with the launch of Apogy, a cloud-based platform designed to bring the fragmented stages of fashion product development into a single system. Three years in development, Apogy is intended to connect the work that takes place between an initial garment concept and a prototype ready for industrial production – encompassing design information, pattern development, digital prototyping, approvals and collaboration with suppliers. The Paris-based company says the platform is its first to make extensive use of agentic AI, with software agents able to carry out specific tasks and retrieve and act on information rather than simply responding to individual user commands. For fashion companies, the more immediate issue Apogy is attempting to address is the amount of product information currently moving between separate systems, departments and suppliers as a garment progresses towards production. Collection cycles have become shorter while brands are dealing with more product variants, geographically dispersed supply chains and increasing requirements for traceability and regulatory information. Lectra believes this has left product development as one of the less integrated parts of the fashion industry’s digital infrastructure. Shared environment Apogy provides a shared environment in which designers, product developers, patternmakers, suppliers and other participants can work from the same product data and follow changes as they are made. Concepts can be generated and developed from text prompts, sketches and images, while 3D simulation and photorealistic rendering are intended to reduce the number of physical samples required during development and speed up approval decisions. articles.o: Italian Textile Machinery at TITAS 2026: Strategic partnership and tailor-made solutions for the Taiwanese market
articles.s: The excellence and innovative capabilities of Italian textile machinery technology are coming to Taipei for TITAS 2026 (Taiwan International Textile & Garment Machinery Show), the leading event fo...
articles.x: The excellence and innovative capabilities of Italian textile machinery technology are coming to Taipei for TITAS 2026 (Taiwan International Textile & Garment Machinery Show), the leading event for the island’s textile industry and the wider Asian region, scheduled to take place from 6 to 8 October 2026. Italy’s presence at this key event reflects its commitment to strengthening a long-standing and strategic relationship with a local manufacturing industry that has always placed great emphasis on quality and technological research. The Taiwanese market is undergoing a period of profound transformation and evolution. Following a period of global adjustment, the beginning of 2026 saw an extraordinary and vigorous turnaround in exports by Italian machinery manufacturers to the island. This strong sign of renewed momentum confirms that Taiwan’s textile industry is actively seeking reliable technology partners to support its plans for recovery and modernization. The strength of Italian technologies lies in their ability to adapt with exceptional flexibility to the most sophisticated requirements. In Taiwan, where production has historically been concentrated in the upstream stages of the textile supply chain, Italian spinning solutions continue to account for by far the largest share of local interest, alongside solid demand for finishing machinery and related accessories. This concentration confirms that the flexibility and high degree of customization offered by Italian technology are among the differentiating factors most highly valued by Taiwanese manufacturers, who need to diversify their production and develop high value-added market niches.
